A bar that we pull at its ends carries the load by stretching. In every cross section one part pulls the other with the same force along the axis, and the stress came out in chapter 2 as the force divided by the area of the cross section. Many structures, however, carry a load that does not point along the axis but pushes across it. The girder of a bridge carries traffic that presses it down, a diving board bends under the diver, a ceiling rests on joists loaded by its weight, a shaft in a machine carries wheels hanging on it. How does a body carry a load that pushes across it?

We have already seen three pictures. A bar clamped in a wall and pushed down at its free end bends (figure 2.5). The forces across a cut do not all pull along the axis: the upper part of the material pulls the neighbouring part toward itself, the lower part pushes it, and the part at the wall holds the rest of the bar up. Chapter 2 only described these forces and promised to compute them. A strip that bends so that the fibres above the middle get longer and below it shorter in proportion to the distance from the middle, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), bends without gaps between the bands (figure 1.143). Chapter 1 gave the displacement field of such a strip and predicted that a bent slender body bends this way. The truss of chapter 4 (definition 4.4) is a model of a structure with pins. In a real structure the bars are usually welded at the joints, so they also carry some bending, and there we promised to compute it.

The goal of the chapter is the path from the loads to the displacements and stresses of a slender body that carries a load across it. For given loads and supports we shall compute how large the force across the body is and how strongly the forces try to bend the body in every cross section, what the stress in the material is, where every point of the body axis moves to, and how much energy the body stores. We reach this by two paths, the path of forces and the path of energy, just as for bars in chapter 4. The model of such a body is a simplification. So for each of its assumptions we shall measure on numerical examples what it costs us, and so say how far we may trust the model.

The route of the chapter is this. In the first section we say how to describe a slender body that carries a load across it, how it is supported and loaded, and choose two examples that will stay with us to the end. Then we compute the internal forces and moments along the body. In the next section we find how the points of the body move if the cross sections stay plane. For stresses we also need the mean position of the points of the cross section and the integral of the square of the height over the cross section, and then come the sections on stresses in bending and on shear stresses. From forces, deformations and material we build an equation for the unknown deflection of the axis, prepare the mathematics for solving it, and compute the deflection in both examples. The second path starts with virtual work. Since it brings in for the first time the search for a function that is the minimum of an integral, the mathematics that makes this possible follows, then the energy of the body and virtual forces, with which we also solve cases in which equilibrium alone does not give the reactions. The sections on the corrected model that also allows for shear deformation (Timoshenko) and on structures made of several rigidly joined parts at the end of the chapter extend the model, and the last section collects all the assumptions and their cost.

5.1 Beams and their model (nosilec in njegov model)

In this section we answer the question how to describe a slender body that carries a load across it, what holds it and what loads it, and which numbers are enough to describe it. With the answer we set up the model that the chapter will refine, and we choose two bodies on which we shall try every new idea with numbers. The axis \(x\) points along the body from its left end, the axis \(y\) vertically up, the axis \(z\) toward the reader, so that the triple \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) is right-handed, as in chapters 1 and 2.

5.1.1 Line structures (linijske konstrukcije)

Structures are divided by shape (figure 5.1). A line structure (linijska konstrukcija) is made of bodies that are much longer in one direction than in the other two. We already know the bar: forces act only at its ends or along its axis, so it carries only axial force (definition 4.4). A cable (vrv, kabel) is a very flexible bar that carries only tension. A slender body that also carries load across it, as we shall see in the definition below, is the subject of this chapter. Several such bodies that are rigidly joined to each other make a structure of rigidly joined bodies, which one of the last sections of this chapter treats. A surface structure (ploskovna konstrukcija) has one dimension, the thickness, much smaller than the other two. If it is flat we call it a plate (plošča), if it is curved a shell (lupina). Both have their own chapters (18, 22). When all three dimensions are comparable we have a massive body (masivno telo), such as a cube or the base of a machine. For such a body we must solve the equations of elasticity in all three directions at once. The division follows EP §2.5.1 (pp. 71-72).

For us the slender body that carries a load across it is the most important. In the model we shall replace the cross section by a point on the axis, so we must first say what the axis is. A cross section (prečni prerez) is here the plane surface that we get by cutting the body perpendicular to its axis, as in chapter 2 (figure 2.5). For a symmetric cross section, such as a rectangle or a double T, the centre of the cross section lies where its axes of symmetry meet. The general rule, valid for every cross section, we shall state later in this chapter, when we can compute the mean position of the points of the cross section. For now we take bodies with a symmetric cross section and the axis through the centres of the cross sections.

Definition 5.1 Beam (nosilec)

A beam (nosilec) is a body with a straight axis that has length \(L\) along it and the same cross section everywhere, and the dimensions of the cross section are much smaller than \(L\). The axis (os) is the line through the centres of the cross sections, the cross section (prečni prerez) is the plane perpendicular to it. The beam is loaded by forces that also have a component perpendicular to the axis, and supported at its ends or at several places.

Source: EP §2.5.1 (p. 71), ONATE2 §1.2 (PDF p. 33), SADD §D.3 (PDF p. 574).

How long must a beam be compared with its cross section? EP says that a beam has a very large ratio of length to the dimensions of the cross section, "say, 10 to 100 or more" (EP §2.5.1, p. 71). The ratio \(L/h\), where \(h\) is the height of the cross section in the plane in which the beam bends, we call slenderness (vitkost). The beams of the chapter will have \(L/h = 25\) and \(L/h = 50\) (figure 5.2).

Why does slenderness allow a simpler model? The forces across a cross section gave three numbers in chapter 2: the force along the axis, the force across it and the moment (figure 2.5). The model will replace the whole cross section by them and, about how the cross section deforms, will only assume that it stays plane (we study this in the next section), instead of solving the equations of elasticity in all three directions. How close this is to the truth depends on slenderness. For our steel strip we shall compute later in the chapter, at the Timoshenko beam, that because of the cross sections, which in truth do not stay quite plane, the displacement of the end of the cantilever grows by 0,125 % at \(L/h = 25\) and by 19,5 % at \(L/h = 2\). The share falls with the square of the ratio \(h/L\). EP summarizes that such theories give results "accurate enough for engineering analysis and design" (EP §2.5.1, p. 72). One cost is already visible. The cross section is a point on the axis in the model, so the model does not say how the forces are distributed over the cross section near a support or near the place where a load acts. The exact solution of the plane problem of a beam is also not necessarily valid near the ends of the beam (SADD example 8.2, PDF p. 171).

Besides slenderness the model makes one more restriction. All loads and supports lie in the plane \(xy\) and the cross section is symmetric about the axis \(y\). Then the beam only bends in this plane, without twisting about the axis and without bending sideways (EP §2.5.1, p. 72, ONATE2 §1.2.1, PDF p. 33). What happens with unsymmetric cross sections and with beams loaded in two planes we state as a limit of the model in the last section of the chapter.

5.1.2 Supports and loads (podpore in obremenitve)

Loads first, then supports. Three kinds of loads act on a beam (figure 5.3). A point force (točkovna sila) acts at one point of the axis. For it we already have the force vector (definition 2.1), here with components \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\). But how do we describe a load that acts over the whole length or over part of it, like weight or snow on a roof? Let \(q(x)\) be the force per unit length of the beam in the direction \(y\) at the place \(x\). With it we write how much force a small piece of the beam takes, and write the sum as an integral. We did similarly for a bar with the axial load (definition 4.74).

Definition 5.2 Distributed transverse load (porazdeljena prečna obtežba)

Let the beam lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\). A distributed transverse load (porazdeljena prečna obtežba) is a continuous function \(q\) on the interval \([0, L]\) whose input is the place \(x\) on the axis and whose output is the force per unit length of the beam in the direction of the axis \(y\) at that place, in newtons per metre. The load is positive when it points up. On the part of the beam between the places \(x_1 < x_2\) acts, in the direction of the axis \(y\), the force

\[\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{5.1}\]

and its moment about the point \((0, 0, 0)\) has the component \(z\)

\[\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} t\,q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{5.2}\]

Source: ONATE1 §2.2 (PDF pp. 66-67), EP §2.5.2 (p. 72, figure 2.5.2), where the symbol is \(q\). The moment follows from definition 2.32 for the force \(q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) at the point \((t, 0, 0)\).

The moment of the load is the sum of the moments of the small forces \(q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), each at the point \((t, 0, 0)\). For \(\vek r = (t, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek F = (0, q\,\mathrm{d}t, 0)\) the vector product is \(\vek r\times\vek F = (0, 0, t\,q\,\mathrm{d}t)\), the other two components are zero. The weight of the beam is an example. Steel has density \(\rho\), the beam has cross-section area \(A\), so the mass of a unit of length is \(\rho A\) and the weight of a unit of length is \(\rho A g\). The weight points down, so \(q = -\rho g A\) (a constant along the whole length for a beam with the same cross section). The uniform load \(q(x) = -q_0\) with \(q_0 > 0\) has by (5.1) the resultant \(-q_0 L\) and by (5.2) the moment \(-q_0 L^2/2\), equal to the moment of the force \(-q_0 L\) at the point \(x = L/2\).

The third kind of load is a pair of opposite forces. The forces \(\vek F\) and \(-\vek F\) at the ends of a ruler, across it, have zero resultant, yet they turn the ruler (figure 2.3). A lever welded across a beam loads it in the same way if two opposite forces push it. Such a pair is named in the definition.

Definition 5.3 Couple (dvojica sil)

A couple (dvojica sil) is a pair of forces \(\vek F\) and \(-\vek F\) that act at different points \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) and do not lie on the same line.

Source: ONATE2 §1.2.1 (PDF p. 33), where point forces and moments act on a plane beam. The definition of a couple is ours.

Since the resultant is zero, by lemma 2.34 on the independence of the moment of the point, the moment of such a pair of forces does not depend on the point about which we compute it. Let us state it with one vector.

Lemma 5.4 Moment of a couple (moment dvojice)

Let the forces \(\vek F\) and \(-\vek F\) act at the points \(A_1\) and \(A_2\). Then their total moment about every point \(O\) equals

\[\vek M_0 = \overrightarrow{A_2 A_1}\times\vek F , \tag{5.3}\]

the vector from the point where \(-\vek F\) acts to the point where \(\vek F\) acts, vector-multiplied by the force \(\vek F\).

Proof

We shall show that we may choose the point \(O\) to be \(A_2\), and then a single term remains.

  1. The resultant of the forces is \(\vek F + (-\vek F) = \vek 0\), so by lemma 2.34 the total moment does not depend on the point about which we compute it. We take \(O = A_2\).
  2. The force \(-\vek F\) acts at the point \(A_2\), the vector from \(A_2\) to \(A_2\) is zero, and its moment is \(\vek 0\times(-\vek F) = \vek 0\) (item 3 of lemma 2.31, used with the number zero).
  3. The force \(\vek F\) acts at the point \(A_1\), its moment about \(A_2\) is by definition 2.32 equal to \(\overrightarrow{A_2 A_1}\times\vek F\). This is the total moment.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

So a couple acts only through the vector \(\vek M_0\), not through where exactly the forces are. Take the forces \(\vek F = (0, 500, 0)\) N at the point \(A_1 = (0{,}05, 0, 0)\) m and \(-\vek F\) at \(A_2 = (-0{,}05, 0, 0)\) m. The vector from \(A_2\) to \(A_1\) is \((0{,}1, 0, 0)\) m, so by (5.3)

\[\vek M_0 = (0{,}1, 0, 0)\times(0, 500, 0) = (0, 0, 50)\ \text{N m} .\]

The couple has only the component \(z\), because both forces lie in the plane \(xy\). We get the same vector if we double the force and halve the distance, since the product does not change. The vector \(\vek M_0\) points in the positive direction of the axis \(z\), toward the reader, and the couple turns the beam counterclockwise as seen by a reader looking toward the negative axis \(z\). A point couple (točkovna dvojica) \(M_0\) on a beam is the limit of such a pair of forces when the distance between the forces shrinks to zero and the forces grow so that \(M_0\) stays the same. Then it loads the beam only with the moment \(M_0 = (\vek M_0)_{\mathrm{z}}\) and with zero resultant (ONATE2 §1.2.1, PDF p. 33).

How is a beam supported? A beam lies on a wall, lies on columns, or is clamped in a wall. A support prevents some displacements and therefore acts on the beam with forces or couples that we call reactions (reakcije). They are external forces, since they act from outside, and they are not known in advance, because the support produces just as much of them as it takes to prevent the displacement. For a plane beam we know three typical supports (figure 5.4).

Definition 5.5 Beam supports (podpore nosilca)

The supports of a plane beam in the plane \(xy\) are three idealizations.

  1. A clamp (vpetje, fixed support) prevents displacement in the directions \(x\) and \(y\) and rotation in the plane. The reactions are a force \((R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}})\) and a couple \(M_{\mathrm{A}}\) (component \(z\)).
  2. A fixed pin support (nepomična členkasta podpora, pin) prevents displacement in the directions \(x\) and \(y\) and allows rotation. The reactions are the components of a force \((R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}})\).
  3. A roller support (pomična členkasta podpora, roller) prevents displacement only in the direction perpendicular to the base along which the support rolls, here the direction \(y\). It allows displacement along the base and rotation. The reaction is one force \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Source: SADD §D.3, figure D.5 (PDF p. 575). The symbols of the reactions are ours.

Each of the three is an idealization and each has a real counterpart. A clamp is the end of a beam welded to a thick plate or built into a wall. A real beam turns a little in the clamp, because the base bends a little, and here we set this rotation to zero. A pin support is a bolt in a hole that allows rotation, but has play and friction. A roller support is a beam lying on rollers or on a greased plate, and the rollers give no force at all along the beam. Which idealization is more suitable depends on the structure. The differences for real supports we estimate in the last section of the chapter, where we shall have numbers.

The reactions are unknown. When can we compute them from equilibrium? The whole beam is in equilibrium with the external forces and the reactions (definition 2.3). For a beam in the plane \(xy\) the force and position vectors lie in the plane, so the moment \(\vek r\times\vek F\) has only the component \(z\), and the two equations, (2.2) and (2.35), give together three equations: the components \(x\) and \(y\) of the forces and the component \(z\) of the moments about a chosen point. The choice of the point for the moments does not change the number of equations, since by the first equation the resultant is zero and by lemma 2.34 the moment does not depend on the point.

Definition 5.6 Statically determinate beam (statično določen nosilec)

A plane beam is statically determinate (statično določen) when the three equations of equilibrium of the whole beam determine all the reactions of the supports uniquely. It is statically indeterminate (statično nedoločen) when it has more unknown reactions than there are independent equations of equilibrium, and for given loads the equations have infinitely many solutions. It is a mechanism (mehanizem) when the supports allow a rigid displacement, so equilibrium for general loads is not possible.

Source: EP example 3.2.6 (p. 122) says of a frame "this is a determinate structure", because all the external reactions follow from the equilibrium of the whole structure, and EP example 3.2.3 (pp. 115-116) says of a shaft clamped between two rigid walls "this is an indeterminate structure", because there is one equation of equilibrium and two unknown torques. The two examples use the words only in a worked example, the definition for a beam in the plane is ours, of the same kind as for the truss (chapter 4, section 4.7.5).

Counting the reactions says where the beam belongs, if the supports prevent all rigid displacements. A rigid displacement (definition 1.11) of a plane body has three free parts: displacement in the direction \(x\), displacement in the direction \(y\) and rotation. If the supports prevent all three and the beam has exactly three unknown reactions, it is statically determinate. If it has more than three, it is statically indeterminate. If the supports do not prevent some rigid displacement, it is a mechanism, even if there are not few reactions. Such is a beam on two roller supports. Both give only a force in the direction \(y\), so no reaction balances a horizontal force and the beam slides along its axis (figure 5.5). We saw the same idea for the truss in section 4.7.5: three unknown forces in the bars, but only two equations of equilibrium of the joint, so equilibrium itself could not tell the true forces.

5.1.3 Two beams that will stay with us (dva nosilca, ki nas bosta spremljala)

Now let us choose concrete beams that we shall use throughout the chapter. They have the same cross section and the same material, they differ in the supports. The cross section is a steel strip of width \(b = 20\) mm in the direction \(z\) and height \(h = 40\) mm in the direction \(y\), standing on its edge (figure 5.6). The area is \(A = b\,h = 800\ \text{mm}^2 = 8\cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\). We choose the rectangle because we know how to integrate it. The material is the steel of the book: modulus of elasticity \(E = 196\) GPa (section 3.1.2), yield strength \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa (definition 2.7) and density \(\rho = 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3\). The weight per unit length is by definition 5.2 \(\rho g A = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 8\cdot 10^{-4} = 61{,}2\) N/m.

The first beam is a cantilever (konzola, cantilever). Its length is \(L = 1\) m, so \(L/h = 25\). At \(x = 0\) it is clamped, and at the free end \(x = L\) a force \(F = 500\) N pushes it down (figure 5.7). The weight of the beam is \(61{,}2\) N, which is 12 % of the force. So we treat the weight separately, at the deflection, which we shall compute later in the chapter. The reactions of the clamp we compute from the equilibrium of the whole beam.

The unknowns are \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{A}}\). The force \(\vek F = (0, -500, 0)\) N acts at the point \(B = (1, 0, 0)\) m, the clamp is at the point \(A = (0, 0, 0)\).

  1. Equilibrium of forces ((2.2)): \((R_{\mathrm{x}},\ R_{\mathrm{y}} - 500,\ 0) = \vek 0\) N. So \(R_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(R_{\mathrm{y}} = 500\) N.
  2. Equilibrium of moments about \(A\) ((2.35)). The moment of the force \(\vek F\) is by definition 2.32 \((1, 0, 0)\times(0, -500, 0) = (0, 0, -500)\) N m. The moment of the reactions is \((0, 0, M_{\mathrm{A}})\), since the force \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) acts at \(A\), the vector from \(A\) to \(A\) is zero, and the force \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\) is zero.
  3. Component \(z\): \(M_{\mathrm{A}} - 500 = 0\), so \(M_{\mathrm{A}} = 500\) N m.

So the clamp holds the beam with a force of 500 N up and a couple of 500 N m counterclockwise. The direction says what the clamp does: the load pushes the free end down and tries to turn the beam clockwise, and the clamp turns it back. We got the reactions from equilibrium alone, without any datum about the material, so the cantilever is statically determinate (definition 5.6).

The second beam is the simply supported beam (prostoležeči nosilec, simply supported beam). Its length is \(L = 2\) m, so \(L/h = 50\). At \(x = 0\) it lies on a fixed pin support, at \(x = L\) on a roller support (figure 5.8). We load it in two ways. In the first there is a uniform load \(q = -q_0\) with \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m, which is \(1000\) N/m down along the whole length. In the second there is a force \(F = 1\) kN down at the middle.

The unknowns are \(R_{\mathrm{Ax}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{Ay}}\) at the pin support and \(R_{\mathrm{By}}\) at the roller support. Let us compute the reactions for the uniform load.

  1. Forces, component \(x\): \(R_{\mathrm{Ax}} = 0\), since there is no other force in the direction \(x\). Component \(y\): \(R_{\mathrm{Ay}} + R_{\mathrm{By}} - q_0 L = 0\) by (5.1), since the resultant of the load is \(-q_0 L = -2000\) N.
  2. Moments about \(A\), component \(z\). The force \(R_{\mathrm{By}}\) acts at \((L, 0, 0)\), its moment is \((L, 0, 0)\times(0, R_{\mathrm{By}}, 0) = (0, 0, L\,R_{\mathrm{By}})\). The moment of the load is by (5.2) \(-q_0 L^2/2 = -2000\) N m. The force \(R_{\mathrm{Ay}}\) acts at \(A\) and has no moment. So \(L\,R_{\mathrm{By}} - q_0 L^2/2 = 0\).
  3. From step 2, \(R_{\mathrm{By}} = q_0 L/2 = 1000\) N, and from step 1, \(R_{\mathrm{Ay}} = q_0 L - R_{\mathrm{By}} = 1000\) N.

Each support carries half of the load, because the load lies symmetrically about the middle. For the force \(F = 1\) kN at the middle the moment about \(A\) is \(L\,R_{\mathrm{By}} - F L/2 = 0\), so \(R_{\mathrm{By}} = F/2 = 500\) N and \(R_{\mathrm{Ay}} = 500\) N. Here too the reason is symmetry. The beam is statically determinate.

For comparison take a propped cantilever (podprta konzola, propped cantilever), the same beam with \(L = 2\) m, clamped at \(x = 0\) and supported on a roller support at \(x = L\), loaded by the uniform load \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m down. The reactions are \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\), four unknowns. Equilibrium gives \(R_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}} = q_0 L - R_{\mathrm{B}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{A}} = q_0 L^2/2 - L\,R_{\mathrm{B}}\), so three equations for four unknowns. For every choice of the number \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\) the remaining reactions are such that the beam is in equilibrium:

\[\begin{aligned} R_{\mathrm{B}} &= 0 \text{ N}: & R_{\mathrm{y}} &= 2000\ \text{N} , & M_{\mathrm{A}} &= 2000\ \text{N m} , \\ R_{\mathrm{B}} &= 1000\ \text{N}: & R_{\mathrm{y}} &= 1000\ \text{N} , & M_{\mathrm{A}} &= 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The first case is an ordinary cantilever with the load along the whole length, the second is a simply supported beam with a clamp without a couple. Equilibrium does not know which number \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\) is the true one. The deformation of the beam will tell, in three ways: with the equation for the deflection, with virtual forces and with energy, all later in this chapter. We shall then check the result: \(R_{\mathrm{B}} = 750\) N, \(R_{\mathrm{y}} = 1250\) N, \(M_{\mathrm{A}} = 500\) N m.

The question of the section was what a beam is, what holds it and what loads it. The answer is a model: a straight axis, a slender beam, a plane problem, three idealized supports and three kinds of loads. The equilibrium of the whole beam gives the reactions for the cantilever and the simply supported beam, but not for the propped cantilever. And what happens inside the beam? Equilibrium of the whole does not say this, and the next section answers it.

5.2 Internal forces in a beam (notranje sile v nosilcu)

In chapter 2 we cut a beam clamped in a wall in thought (figure 2.5). One part of the beam acts on the other across the cut with forces that are distributed over the whole cross section and have a longitudinal and a vertical part. The chapter promised that we would describe them with three numbers and define them exactly in this chapter. We do this now. There are two questions. What are these numbers and how do we compute them from the load? How do they change along the beam? The answer to the first says exactly what we are describing, the answer to the second says how to find these quantities in all cross sections at once, without cutting the beam anew for every cross section.

The beam lies along the axis \(x\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = L\), the axis \(y\) points up, the axis \(z\) toward the reader (section 5.1). The cross section is a rectangle with height \(h\) in the direction \(y\) and width \(b\) in the direction \(z\), its centre (središče) lies on the axis of the beam. The centre of a rectangle is the intersection of its diagonals. For now we can compute an integral over the area of a cross section only over a rectangle (definition 4.8), so we state the lemma on internal forces for a rectangular cross section. The mathematics section on the cross section, which follows in this chapter, extends the integral to cross sections made of rectangles, such as the letter T and the double T. There we shall see that the centre of a rectangle is also the mean position of its points, and that for composite cross sections this mean position replaces the centre. The lemma holds for such cross sections too, as corollary 5.19 in this chapter shows. All loads lie in the plane \(xy\), which is a plane of symmetry of the cross section: it divides the cross section into two mirror halves, one at \(z > 0\) and the other at \(z < 0\). The displacements are small compared with the lengths, so we write equilibrium on the shape of the beam before loading, as in chapter 4.

From history

Galileo broke a bar built into a wall, as we saw in chapter 1 (figure 1.6). He then asked what happens when the bar is not built in but lies on two supports and the force acts at any point between them (TIMO, PDF p. 22). He found that the effect of the force on breaking is greatest under the force and proportional to the product \(a b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are the distances of the force from the two supports (TIMO, PDF p. 22). We can see the reason from equilibrium. For a support spacing \(a + b\) the left support carries the force \(F b/(a + b)\), and its moment about the point under the force is \(F a b/(a + b)\). The spacing does not change, so this moment is proportional to \(a b\). The product of two numbers with a given sum is largest when the numbers are equal, since \((a + b)^2/4 - a b = \big((a - b)/2\big)^2 \ge 0\). The smallest force that breaks the bar is therefore the one acting at the middle between the supports (TIMO, PDF p. 22).

Because the effect of the force on breaking is smaller near the supports than at the middle, Galileo noticed that material can be saved if the cross section is made smaller toward the supports (TIMO, PDF p. 22). For a cantilever of rectangular cross section he also derived the shape in which the strength is the same everywhere. The effect of the force on breaking grows with the distance from the free end, and the resistance of a cross section grows with the square of its depth. The depth must therefore grow with the square root of the distance, which gives a parabola (TIMO, PDF p. 22). So the effect of the force on breaking is not the same in all cross sections of the bar, and we must know it in each cross section separately.

Let us return to the question of the section: which forces and moments act across one cross section of a beam, and how they change from cross section to cross section along the beam.

5.2.1 Three numbers in a cross section (tri števila v prerezu)

We cut the beam at \(x\) and look at the face of the cut that belongs to the part on the side of smaller \(x\). Its outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The part on the side of larger \(x\) acts on this part across the face, and per unit area at a point \(Q\) of the face acts the traction vector (definition 2.20)

\[\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\]

with the components of stress from definition 2.25. The components are functions of the point \(Q\) on the face and also of the place \(x\). We chose the same side for the axial force (definition 2.5), so we need not remember anything new: the force that we describe is always the force of the part on the side of larger \(x\) on the part on the side of smaller \(x\).

Besides the resultant (rezultanta) of these forces, that is the internal force (definition 2.4), we are interested in how strongly the forces try to rotate the part. The resultant does not tell this: the same resultant, acting at the centre of the cross section or at its edge, rotates differently. So we add to it the moment of the distributed forces. We compute it about the centre of the cross section \(C(x) = (x, 0, 0)\). The moment of a force depends on the point about which we compute it, since the resultant is different from zero (lemma 2.34 holds only for a zero resultant). The centre of the cross section lies on the axis of the beam. We shall need this when we move the moment from one cross section to another.

Definition 5.7 Shear force (prečna sila)

Let \(\vek F(x)\) be the internal force (definition 2.4) in the cross section of the beam at \(x\), that is the resultant of the forces with which the part of the beam on the side of larger \(x\) acts across the cross section on the part on the side of smaller \(x\). Let us write it by components, \(\vek F(x) = (N,\ V_{\mathrm{y}},\ V_{\mathrm{z}})\). We called the first component \(N\) the axial force (definition 2.5). The shear forces (prečni sili) are the components \(V_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{z}}\), perpendicular to the axis of the beam. In a plane problem, where all loads lie in the plane \(xy\), \(V_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and we denote the shear force \(V := V_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Source: EP (2.5.6) (p. 74), CM (7.3.28) (PDF p. 309), SADD app. D (PDF pp. 576-577). All three know the shear force only in the plane. EP and CM have the same sign as we do, SADD the opposite one (see the paragraph on the books below). The vector form is ours.

Definition 5.8 Bending moment (upogibni moment)

Let \(\vek M(x)\) be the internal moment (notranji moment) in the cross section of the beam at \(x\), that is the moment about the centre of the cross section \(C(x)\) of the forces with which the part of the beam on the side of larger \(x\) acts across the cross section on the part on the side of smaller \(x\). As in lemma 2.35, it is the sum of the moments of the small forces \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\) over the pieces of the face, as the pieces are made smaller. Let us write it by components, \(\vek M(x) = (M_{\mathrm{x}},\ M_{\mathrm{y}},\ M_{\mathrm{z}})\). The components \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the bending moments (upogibna momenta), since they bend the beam about the axes \(y\) and \(z\). The component \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the moment about the axis of the beam, the torque (torzijski moment), which twists the beam, and chapter 16 deals with it. In a plane problem \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = M_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and we denote the bending moment \(M := M_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Source: EP (2.5.6) (p. 74), CM (7.3.28) (PDF p. 309), SADD app. D (PDF pp. 576-577). All three know only the component about the axis perpendicular to the plane of bending. EP and CM have the opposite sign to ours, SADD the same one (see the paragraph on the books below). The vector form is ours.

The definitions are written with a resultant and a moment, while the stresses are distributed over the cross section. Which stresses make up \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M\)? The answer is in lemma 5.9. The cross section is a rectangle, so the integral over the area is the integral over a rectangle from definition 4.8.

Lemma 5.9 Internal forces from stresses (notranje sile iz napetosti)

Let the cross section of the beam at \(x\) be the rectangle \(A = \{(x, y, z) : -h/2 \le y \le h/2,\ -b/2 \le z \le b/2\}\) with centre \(C = (x, 0, 0)\), and let the components of stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) be continuous functions on \(A\). Then

\[N = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad V_{\mathrm{y}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad V_{\mathrm{z}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{5.4}\]
\[\begin{aligned} M_{\mathrm{x}} &= \int_{\mathrm{A}} (y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A , \\ M_{\mathrm{y}} &= \int_{\mathrm{A}} z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A , \\ M_{\mathrm{z}} &= -\int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A . \end{aligned} \tag{5.5}\]

So in a plane problem \(V = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(M = -\int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Proof

We must show that the sums of the small forces and of their moments, as the surface is divided, are Riemann sums of the functions that appear in the formulas. We write the force by components and compute the moment with the vector product.

  1. We divide the surface \(A\) by a grid into small rectangles with area \(\Delta A\) and choose a point \(Q = (x, y, z)\) in each. Across a rectangle acts a force that for a small piece is approximately \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\), with the traction vector at \(Q\) by definition 2.20.
  2. The sum of the forces is \(\sum \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\). Each of its three components is a Riemann sum of the continuous function \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) or \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) on the rectangle. By theorem 4.9, for a rectangle, each approaches the integral over \(A\) as the grid is refined, and \(\vek F\) is this limit. The components are equation (5.4).
  3. The vector from \(C\) to \(Q\) is \(\vek r = (0, y, z)\). The moment of the force \(\vek t\,\Delta A\) about \(C\) is by definition 2.32 and equation (2.32) equal to \(\vek r \times \vek t\,\Delta A\) with
    \[\vek r\times\vek t = (y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}},\ \ z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - 0\cdot\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \ 0\cdot\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}) .\]
  4. Each component of this vector is a continuous function on \(A\), since it is a sum of products of continuous functions (the components of stress) with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The sum of the moments of the pieces is therefore by step 2 a Riemann sum of each component and approaches the integral, which is (5.5).

Source: EP (2.5.6) (p. 74) and CM (7.3.28) (PDF p. 309) give the same integral for \(N\) and \(V\) and for \(M\) with the opposite sign, SADD (PDF p. 576) has \(M = -\int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A\) like us. The proof is not from a source.

Let us test the lemma on a stress that in the cross section \(b = 20\) mm, \(h = 40\) mm is linear in the height, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y\), with no shear stresses. For \(k > 0\) the upper part of the cross section (\(y > 0\)) is in tension, the lower in compression. By the lemma \(N = k\int_{-\mathrm{b}/2}^{b/2}\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} y\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\), since the contributions of the upper and of the lower part cancel, and the moment is

\[M_{\mathrm{z}} = -k\,b\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = -k\,\frac{b\,h^3}{12} , \qquad \frac{b\,h^3}{12} = 1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4 .\]

For \(k = 4{,}6875\cdot 10^{9}\) Pa/m the stress at the upper edge, where \(y = 0{,}02\) m, equals \(93{,}75\) MPa, and \(M_{\mathrm{z}} = -500\) N m. So a stretched upper edge means a negative moment. A positive bending moment means the opposite, the lower edge is stretched. The cantilever has the same picture at the clamp when we load it at the free end with a force \(500\) N downward: the upper fibres stretch, the lower ones shorten. That the cantilever has the moment \(-500\) N m there is shown by equilibrium in the next section. That the stress is really linear in \(y\) is shown by the section on stresses in bending, here we only tested the lemma.

The plane problem now gets its justification. The loads lie in the plane of symmetry of the cross section, so the picture of the stresses is mirror symmetric about the plane \(xy\) (figure 5.9). The normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) have the same value at \(z\) and \(-z\), the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), which points in the direction \(z\), the opposite one. In the lemma the integrands for \(V_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) are therefore odd functions of \(z\) (\(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\)), and their integral over \(z \in [-b/2, b/2]\) is zero. What remains is

\[N(x), \qquad V(x), \qquad M(x) ,\]

the axial force, the shear force and the bending moment, the three numbers that chapter 2 announced. Each is a function of the place \(x\) with one number as input and one as output. We also call them stress resultants (rezultante napetosti), because we get them from the stresses. The symmetry of the stresses is an assumption that we shall check when we know the stresses.

The books write these numbers differently. EP has the axis \(z\) up and CM the axis \(y\) up, and they define \(M\) as \(\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(\int y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) respectively (EP (2.5.6), p. 74, CM (7.3.28), PDF p. 309). Their \(M\) is therefore \(-M_{\mathrm{z}}\) by our definitions, and their shear force equals \(V_{\mathrm{y}}\) (in EP with the symbol \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) for the vertical shear stress). CM has in (7.3.26) and (7.3.27) text about the direction \(z\) and the axis \(y\), although (7.3.28) uses \(y\) for the vertical direction: the symbols are not consistent (PDF p. 309). SADD has the same \(M\) as we do, and its shear force is \(-V_{\mathrm{y}}\) (SADD (D.5), (D.6), (D.8), PDF pp. 576-578). For every borrowed equation we therefore derive the signs from our definitions and do not copy them from the book. Why such a choice? We describe all three quantities on the side that we chose for the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xj}}\) in chapter 2, that is on the face with normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). So there is no special rule for beams to remember, all other signs we get by computation.

The positive directions of \(N\), \(V\) and \(M\) on both sides of the cut are shown in figure 5.10. On the face with normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) a positive \(N\) and \(V\) point in the direction \(+x\) and \(+y\), a positive \(M\) in the direction \(+z\), that is toward the reader. On the opposite face, with normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the stress is by lemma 2.21 the opposite one, and so all three point in the opposite directions.

5.2.2 Internal forces from equilibrium (notranje sile iz ravnovesja)

How do we compute these forces if we do not know the stresses? From equilibrium. If a beam is in equilibrium, so is each of its parts (section 2.1), also when we cut it off in thought. On the cut-off part act the external loads and the forces of the cross section that we are looking for. The procedure is this.

  1. We cut the beam at \(x\) and choose the part on the side of larger \(x\), from the cut to the end \(x = L\).
  2. We draw all forces and moments on it. On the face of the cut the part on the side of smaller \(x\) acts on our part. The face has the outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so by lemma 2.21 the force on it is \(-\vek F(x)\), and the moment about the centre \(C(x)\) is \(-\vek M(x)\) (each vector \(\vek r\times\vek t\) changes sign with \(\vek t\)).
  3. We write equilibrium of forces (2.2) and of moments (2.35). We compute moments about the centre of the cross section \(C(x)\), since then the internal moment appears by itself.

Why do we choose the part on the side of larger \(x\)? For a cantilever clamped at \(x = 0\) the end at \(x = L\) is free and has no support. The cut-off part therefore carries only known loads and we do not need the reactions of the clamp.

Cantilever. A cantilever of length \(L = 1\) m, clamped at \(x = 0\), loaded at the free end \(x = L\) with a force \(500\) N downward, so \(\vek F_{\mathrm{p}} = (0, -500, 0)\) N (section 5.1.3, figure 5.11). The part from the cut at \(x\) to the end has length \(L - x\). On it act the force of the cross section \(-\vek F(x) = (-N, -V, 0)\) and the force at the end \((0, -500, 0)\) N.

  1. Equilibrium of forces (2.2), component \(x\): \(-N = 0\), so \(N = 0\).
  2. Component \(y\): \(-V - 500 = 0\), so \(V = -500\) N, in every cross section.
  3. The moment of the force at the end about \(C(x)\): the vector from \(C(x)\) to the point of application is \((L - x)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and by (2.32) it is \((L - x)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times(-500\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = -500\,(L - x)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) N m. The moment of the cross section is \(-\vek M(x) = (0, 0, -M)\).
  4. Equilibrium of moments (2.35), component \(z\): \(-M - 500\,(L - x) = 0\), so
    \[M(x) = -500\,(L - x)\ \text{N m} = -F\,(L - x) . \tag{5.6}\]

At the clamp \(M(0) = -500\) N m, at the free end \(M(L) = 0\). The shear force is negative because the part at the wall must hold the cut-off part up: the force of the cross section on it is \(-V = +500\) N, as figure 2.5 shows. The moment is negative, so the beam is stretched at the top, as in the test of the stress above. The stress with \(93{,}75\) MPa at the upper edge from the test therefore has exactly the moment that the cantilever carries at the clamp.

Simply supported beam with a force at the middle. A beam of length \(L = 2\) m lies on a fixed pin support at \(x = 0\) and on a roller support at \(x = L\) (definition 5.5, section 5.1.2). At the middle acts a force \(1\) kN downward, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{p}} = (0, -1000, 0)\) N at \(x_0 = 1\) m. There are no horizontal loads, so by equilibrium of forces in the direction \(x\) the horizontal reaction of the fixed pin support is zero. The reactions are vertical, \(R_{\mathrm{A}}\) at \(x = 0\) and \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\) at \(x = L\), each in the direction \(+y\). From equilibrium of the whole beam, moments about \(x = 0\) (component \(z\)): \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\,L - 1000\cdot 1 = 0\), so \(R_{\mathrm{B}} = 500\) N, and from the forces \(R_{\mathrm{A}} + R_{\mathrm{B}} - 1000 = 0\), so \(R_{\mathrm{A}} = 500\) N. A reaction is an external force on the beam, like the force at the end of the cantilever.

The internal forces have different forms to the left and to the right of the force at the middle, since the cut-off part from the cut to the end contains the force at the middle only for \(x < 1\) m (figure 5.13).

  • A cut at \(x > 1\) m. The cut-off part, from \(x\) to \(L\), has only the reaction \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\). Forces: \(-V + R_{\mathrm{B}} = 0\), so \(V = 500\) N. Moments about \(C(x)\): \(-M + R_{\mathrm{B}}\,(L - x) = 0\), so \(M = 500\,(2 - x)\) N m.
  • A cut at \(x < 1\) m. The cut-off part contains also the force \(1\) kN at the middle. Forces: \(-V + R_{\mathrm{B}} - 1000 = 0\), so \(V = -500\) N. Moments: the force at the middle has the lever arm \((1 - x)\), and \(-M + R_{\mathrm{B}}\,(L - x) - 1000\,(1 - x) = 0\), so \(M = 500\,(2 - x) - 1000\,(1 - x) = 500\,x\) N m.

The shear force is \(-500\) N on the left half and \(+500\) N on the right half, and the moment grows from zero at the pin to \(500\) N m at the middle and falls to zero at the roller support. The jump of the shear force at the force at the middle is \(500 - (-500) = 1000\) N, as much as the force, and the moment at \(x = 1\) m is continuous, \(500\cdot 1 = 500\cdot(2 - 1) = 500\) N m. Why this is so is shown by the lemma on the jump of the shear force in the section on a piece of a beam below. We get the same result with the part on the side of smaller \(x\), since the internal forces in the same cross section are the same. Then we would need the reaction \(R_{\mathrm{A}}\), and the force of the cross section on this part would be \(+\vek F(x)\) and not \(-\vek F(x)\). SADD (D.5) (PDF p. 576) gives for the same beam, with a force \(P\) at \(a\) and \(b = L - a\), \(V_{\mathrm{SADD}} = P\,b/L\) to the left of the force and \(M_{\mathrm{SADD}} = P\,b\,x/L\), which for \(P = 1000\) N, \(a = b = 1\) m, \(L = 2\) m is exactly our \(-V\) and \(M\).

Simply supported beam with a uniform load. We load the same beam with a uniformly distributed load \(q = -q_0\), \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m, pointing downward (definition 5.2). The force of the load on the part between \(x\) and \(L\) is \(\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q\,\mathrm{d}t = -q_0\,(L - x)\). Its moment about \(C(x)\) is the sum of the moments of the small forces \(q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) on the segment, which lie at the distance \(t - x\) from \(C(x)\). Since \((t - x)\,q(t)\) is a continuous function, the sums are Riemann sums, and the moment is the integral

\[\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L (t - x)\,q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = -q_0\int_{\mathrm{x}}^L (t - x)\,\mathrm{d}t = -q_0\,\frac{(L - x)^2}{2} , \tag{5.7}\]

in the direction \(z\). This is the moment of the force \(-q_0\,(L - x)\) that would act at the middle of the cut-off part, at the distance \((L - x)/2\) from \(C(x)\), since \(-q_0\,(L - x)\cdot (L - x)/2 = -q_0\,(L - x)^2/2\). The reactions are equal by symmetry, \(R_{\mathrm{A}} = R_{\mathrm{B}} = q_0\,L/2 = 1000\) N.

  1. Forces on the cut-off part from \(x\) to \(L\): \(-V + R_{\mathrm{B}} + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\), so \(V = R_{\mathrm{B}} - q_0\,(L - x) = q_0\,(x - L/2)\).
  2. Moments about \(C(x)\), component \(z\): \(-M + R_{\mathrm{B}}\,(L - x) - q_0\,(L - x)^2/2 = 0\), so
    \[M = \frac{q_0\,L}{2}\,(L - x) - \frac{q_0}{2}\,(L - x)^2 = \frac{q_0}{2}\,x\,(L - x) . \tag{5.8}\]

The shear force is a linear function (figure 5.14): \(V(0) = -1000\) N, \(V(L/2) = 0\), \(V(L) = +1000\) N. The moment is a parabola, zero at the supports, at \(x = 0{,}5\) m it is \(375\) N m. Where is it largest? We shall find out when we know the relation between \(M\) and \(V\) (example below). All three loads are chosen so that the largest moment is the same, \(500\) N m: a force \(500\) N on a cantilever of length \(1\) m, a force \(1\) kN at the middle of a beam of length \(2\) m (moment \(F\,L/4\)) and a load \(1\) kN/m on the same beam (moment \(q_0 L^2/8\)). This is a choice and not a law. It lets us compare later the stresses and displacements of the three beams at the same largest moment.

Self weight. A steel bar \(20\times 40\) mm has the cross-sectional area \(A = 8\cdot 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\), the density of steel is \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m\(^3\) and \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\). Its weight per unit length is the load \(q = -\rho g A = -61{,}21\) N/m, uniform and downward. For a cantilever of length \(1\) m the same procedure as for a uniform load gives \(V(x) = -61{,}21\,(L - x)\) N and \(M(x) = -61{,}21\,(L - x)^2/2\) N m. At the clamp \(V(0) = -61{,}21\) N and \(M(0) = -30{,}61\) N m, which is \(6{,}1\) % of the moment due to the force \(500\) N. A simply supported beam of length \(2\) m has \(M_{\max} = \rho g A\,L^2/8 = 30{,}61\) N m.

5.2.3 Equilibrium of a piece of a beam (ravnovesje kosa nosilca)

For the three beams we got \(V\) and \(M\) as functions of the place. For a uniform load \(V\) is linear and \(M\) a parabola, for a force at the middle \(V\) is constant on each half and \(M\) linear. Is the relation between them and the load the same for all? Let us differentiate. For a uniform load \(V' = q_0 = -q\) and \(M' = (q_0/2)\,(L - 2x) = -q_0\,(x - L/2) = -V\). For the cantilever with a force at the end \(V' = 0 = -q\), since between the clamp and the end there is no load, and \(M' = 500\) N \(= -V\). For a force at the middle on each half \(V' = 0\) and \(M' = \pm 500 = -V\) (the upper sign on the left, the lower on the right). So the pattern is \(V' = -q\) and \(M' = -V\). Why exactly this, each time with a minus? The answer is shown by the equilibrium of a short piece of a beam, which does not depend on the particular load. The approach is the same as for the axial force in lemma 4.75, only that now besides the axial force we have also the shear force and the moment.

We describe the load with a force per unit length that acts on the axis of the beam, \(\vek q(x) = (q_{\mathrm{x}}, q, q_{\mathrm{z}})\). The component \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the axial load (definition 4.74), \(q\) is the transverse load in the direction \(+y\) (definition 5.2), \(q_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the transverse load in the direction \(z\), defined in the same way. Each component is a continuous function of the place \(x\). A load can also act off the axis, for example at the upper edge. Then we replace it by a force on the axis and a distributed couple (porazdeljeni moment) \(\vek m(x)\), the moment of couples per unit length (definition 5.3). In our examples \(\vek m = \vek 0\). Let the load be continuous, and let there be no point forces and couples on the piece under consideration.

Lemma 5.10 Equilibrium of a piece of a beam (ravnovesje kosa nosilca)

Let the beam be in equilibrium and let the continuous distributed load \(\vek q\) and the distributed couple \(\vek m\) act on the piece between the cross sections \(x_1 < x_2\), without point forces and couples. The internal force \(\vek F\) and the internal moment \(\vek M\) (definitions 5.7 and 5.8) are then continuous functions on \([x_1, x_2]\) and

\[\vek F(x_2) - \vek F(x_1) = -\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} \vek q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{5.9}\]
\[\vek M(x_2) - \vek M(x_1) = -\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} \big(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(t) + \vek m(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{5.10}\]

In a plane problem, \(\vek F = (N, V, 0)\), \(\vek M = (0, 0, M)\), \(\vek q = (q_{\mathrm{x}}, q, 0)\), \(\vek m = (0, 0, m)\), we have \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F = (0, 0, V)\) and

\[\begin{aligned} N(x_2) - N(x_1) &= -\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} q_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}t , \\ V(x_2) - V(x_1) &= -\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} q\,\mathrm{d}t , \\ M(x_2) - M(x_1) &= -\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} \big(V(t) + m(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t . \end{aligned} \tag{5.11}\]
Proof

We write equilibrium of the piece, first the forces, then the moments about the centre of the left cross section. In the moments a term with \(\vek F(x_2)\) appears, which we transform into an integral with the derivative and the fundamental theorem of calculus.

  1. On the piece act: across the right face, with the outward normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the force \(\vek F(x_2)\) and the moment \(\vek M(x_2)\) about \(C(x_2)\). Across the left face, with the outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the traction vector is by lemma 2.21 the opposite one, so the force is \(-\vek F(x_1)\) and the moment \(-\vek M(x_1)\) about \(C(x_1)\). The load: the force \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t\), by components by definitions 4.74 and 5.2, and the moment \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\vek m\,\mathrm{d}t\), by components by the definition of the distributed couple above.
  2. Equilibrium of forces (2.2): \(\vek F(x_2) - \vek F(x_1) + \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\). This is (5.9).
  3. The moment of the forces on the right face about \(C(x_1)\) is the sum of the moments of the small forces \(\vek t\,\Delta A\). The vector from \(C(x_1)\) to the point of application is \((x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek r\), where \(\vek r\) is the vector from \(C(x_2)\) to the point of application. By items 2 and 3 of lemma 2.31 the sum of the moments is \((x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\sum\vek t\,\Delta A + \sum\vek r\times\vek t\,\Delta A\), in the limit \((x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(x_2) + \vek M(x_2)\). The limits exist by steps 2 and 4 of lemma 5.9 when the stresses are continuous.
  4. The small force of the load \(\vek q(t)\,\Delta t\) has the vector from \(C(x_1)\) to the point of application on the axis equal to \((t - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The function \((t - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek q(t)\) is continuous, so the sums of the moments are Riemann sums and the moment of the load is \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} (t - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  5. Equilibrium of moments (2.35): \(\vek M(x_2) - \vek M(x_1) + (x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(x_2) + \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}(t - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t + \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\vek m\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\).
  6. Steps 1 and 2 hold for every piece inside \([x_1, x_2]\). Let \(x \in [x_1, x_2]\). For the piece from \(x_1\) to \(x\) we get \(\vek F(x) = \vek F(x_1) - \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 2, each component is continuous on \([x_1, x_2]\) and differentiable with the derivative \(-\vek q\), so \(\vek F' = -\vek q\).
  7. By the product rule (lemma 1.81, items 3 and 4) \(\big((t - x_1)\,\vek F(t)\big)' = \vek F(t) - (t - x_1)\,\vek q(t)\), and this derivative is continuous. By the fundamental theorem, item 1, \((x_2 - x_1)\,\vek F(x_2) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\vek F\,\mathrm{d}t - \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}(t - x_1)\,\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  8. The vector product with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is linear (lemma 2.31, items 2 and 3) and the integral is linear (lemma 3.39, item 1), by components. Step 7 therefore gives \((x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(x_2) + \int(t - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek q = \int\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F\,\mathrm{d}t\). We insert it into step 5 and get (5.10). The continuity of \(\vek M\) follows from (5.10) for \(x_1\) and \(x\) and from the fundamental theorem.
  9. In a plane problem by (2.32) \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F = (1, 0, 0)\times(N, V, 0) = (0\cdot 0 - 0\cdot V,\ 0\cdot N - 1\cdot 0,\ 1\cdot V - 0\cdot N) = (0, 0, V)\). The components of (5.9) and (5.10) are therefore (5.11).

Source: The proof is not from a source. Equilibrium of an element: EP (2.5.3)-(2.5.5) (p. 74), CM (7.3.25)-(7.3.27) (PDF p. 309), SADD (PDF p. 576), with the opposite sign for \(V\) and \(M\) in the first two, as described at the definitions.

The lemma says that between two cross sections the shear force changes by the load on this piece, and the moment by the area under \(V\). Let us test it on the beam with a uniform load, where \(V = q_0\,(x - L/2)\) and \(M = (q_0/2)\,x\,(L - x)\). On the piece from \(x_1 = 0{,}5\) m to \(x_2 = 1{,}5\) m \(V(1{,}5) - V(0{,}5) = 500 - (-500) = 1000\) N and \(-\int q\,\mathrm{d}t = q_0\cdot 1 = 1000\) N. The moment: \(M(1{,}5) - M(0{,}5) = 375 - 375 = 0\) and \(-\int_{0{,}5}^{1{,}5} q_0\,(t - 1)\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\), since the areas to the left and to the right of \(t = 1\) cancel. On the piece from \(x_1 = 0\) to \(x_2 = 1\) m \(M(1) - M(0) = 500\) N m and \(-\int_0^1 1000\,(t - 1)\,\mathrm{d}t = 500\) N m.

We do not need the piece to be arbitrarily long. When we shrink it, we get the derivative.

Corollary 5.11 Differential relations between the load, the shear force and the moment (diferencialne zveze)

Let \(\vek q\) and \(\vek m\) be continuous on an open interval \((a, b)\), without point forces and couples on it. Then \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M\) are differentiable on \((a, b)\) and

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}\vek F}{\mathrm{d}x} + \vek q = \vek 0 , \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}\vek M}{\mathrm{d}x} + \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F + \vek m = \vek 0 . \tag{5.12}\]

In a plane problem

\[N' = -q_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad V' = -q , \qquad M' = -V - m . \tag{5.13}\]
Proof

We get the derivative from the lemma on a piece that we shrink.

  1. Let \(x \in (a, b)\) and \([x_1, x_2] \subset (a, b)\) a piece that contains \(x\). By lemma 5.10 \(\vek F(x) = \vek F(x_1) - \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t\), and by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 2, \(\vek F\) is differentiable with the derivative \(-\vek q\) (continuous).
  2. The function \(t \mapsto \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(t) + \vek m(t)\) is continuous, and by the lemma \(\vek M(x) = \vek M(x_1) - \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x}\big(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F + \vek m\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\). By the fundamental theorem \(\vek M' = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F - \vek m\).
  3. In a plane problem \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F = (0, 0, V)\) (step 9 of the lemma), which gives (5.13).

Source: The proof is not from a source. EP (2.5.3)-(2.5.5) (p. 74) and CM (7.3.25)-(7.3.27) (PDF p. 309) have \(N' = -f\), \(V' = -q\) and \(V = M'\) with their \(M = -M_{\mathrm{z}}\), which for us is \(M_{\mathrm{z}}' = -V_{\mathrm{y}}\). SADD (PDF p. 576) has \(V = M'\) with \(V_{\mathrm{SADD}} = -V_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Why does the relation \(M' = -V\) have a minus? Let us look at a short piece \([x, x + \Delta x]\) and a positive \(V\) on the right face (figure 5.15). The force \(V\) on the right face points up and has, about the centre of the left face, the lever arm \(\Delta x\) in the direction \(+x\). Its moment is \(\Delta x\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times V\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = V\,\Delta x\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), so it rotates the piece counterclockwise. The piece is in equilibrium, so this rotation is balanced by the difference of the internal moments: \(M(x + \Delta x) - M(x) + V\,\Delta x \approx 0\). This is the reason for the minus. The moment is not constant by itself, but changes exactly by the moment of the shear force of the right face about the left one. For the cantilever: \(V = -500\) N, the moment grows from \(-500\) N m at the clamp to \(0\) at the end (figure 5.12), so \(M' = +500\) N \(= -V\).

For \(m = 0\) from (5.13) follows also \(M'' = -V' = q\). For a uniform load downward, \(q = -q_0\), we therefore have \(M'' = -q_0 < 0\) and \(M\) is a parabola with the peak up, as we got it. The moment is, up to a linear term, the double integral of the load. Later we shall link the moment also with how strongly the axis of the beam curves.

Where is the moment largest? For the beam with a uniform load \(M\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), so by theorem 1.73 it attains its largest value. This is not at the end points, where \(M(0) = M(L) = 0\), since \(M(0{,}5\ \text{m}) = 375\) N m. The largest value is therefore at an interior point \(x^*\), where \(M\) is differentiable, and by lemma 1.82 \(M'(x^*) = 0\). By (5.13) \(V(x^*) = 0\) there. The shear force \(V = q_0\,(x - L/2)\) is zero only at \(x^* = L/2 = 1\) m, where \(M = q_0 L^2/8 = 500\) N m. The largest moment is therefore where the shear force is zero. For the beam with a force at the middle \(V\) is nowhere zero and \(M\) has a peak at the force, where it is not differentiable.

What about a point force? The lemma on a piece requires that there be no point forces on the piece. For the beam with a force at the middle we saw that the shear force jumps at the force and that the moment is continuous. Why is shown by lemma 5.12.

Lemma 5.12 Jump of the shear force and the moment (skok prečne sile in momenta)

Let a point force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{p}} = (F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, F_{\mathrm{z}})\) and a point couple with the moment \(\vek M_{\mathrm{p}}\) act at an interior point \(x_0\) of the axis, and let continuous \(\vek q\) and \(\vek m\) act on the intervals \([x_1, x_0)\) and \((x_0, x_2]\), which extend to continuous functions on \([x_1, x_0]\) and \([x_0, x_2]\), without other point loads. Then the left and right limits \(\vek F(x_0^{\pm})\) and \(\vek M(x_0^{\pm})\) exist and

\[\vek F(x_0^+) - \vek F(x_0^-) = -\vek F_{\mathrm{p}} , \qquad \vek M(x_0^+) - \vek M(x_0^-) = -\vek M_{\mathrm{p}} . \tag{5.14}\]

In a plane problem with a point force \(F_{\mathrm{p}}\) in the direction \(y\) and a couple with the moment \(M_0\) in the direction \(z\): \(V\) jumps by \(-F_{\mathrm{p}}\), \(M\) jumps by \(-M_0\). For a point force alone, without a couple, \(M\) is continuous.

Proof

On a shorter piece around \(x_0\) we write equilibrium with the point loads and let the piece shrink to the point.

  1. Existence of the limits. By lemma 5.10, applied to the piece \([x, x_2]\), for \(x_0 < x < x_2\) we have \(\vek F(x) = \vek F(x_2) + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^{x_2}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t\). As \(x\) approaches \(x_0\) from the right, the right-hand side approaches, by the continuity of the integral (fundamental theorem, item 2, for \(\vek q\) extended by a continuous function on \([x_0, x_2]\)), \(\vek F(x_2) + \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x_2}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t\). So \(\vek F(x_0^+)\) exists. In the same way, with the lemma on the piece \([x_1, x]\) for \(x_1 < x < x_0\), \(\vek F(x_0^-)\) exists. The function \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F + \vek m\) therefore extends on each side to a continuous function on the closed interval. By (5.10) \(\vek M(x) = \vek M(x_2) + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^{x_2}(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F + \vek m)\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(\vek M(x_0^{\pm})\) exist too.
  2. Let \(x_1 < x_0 < x_2\). Equilibrium of forces on the piece \([x_1, x_2]\), which contains the force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{p}}\): \(\vek F(x_2) - \vek F(x_1) + \vek F_{\mathrm{p}} + \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\vek q\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\). We split the integral at \(x_0\) into the integrals of the continuous extensions over \([x_1, x_0]\) and \([x_0, x_2]\) (item 2 of lemma 3.39). Each component of each is by item 3 of the same lemma, with the bounds \(-c\) and \(c\), at most \(c\,(x_2 - x_1)\) in absolute value, where \(c\) is the largest absolute value of the components of the extensions, and tends to zero. When \(x_1 \to x_0^-\) and \(x_2 \to x_0^+\), we get the first equation (5.14).
  3. Moments about \(C(x_1)\): as in step 5 of lemma 5.10 the force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{p}}\) has the lever arm \((x_0 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the couple the moment \(\vek M_{\mathrm{p}}\) (the moment of a couple is the same about every point, lemma 5.4), so \(\vek M(x_2) - \vek M(x_1) + (x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(x_2) + (x_0 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{p}} + \vek M_{\mathrm{p}} + \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\big((t - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek q + \vek m\big)\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\).
  4. When \(x_1 \to x_0^-\) and \(x_2 \to x_0^+\): \(\vek F(x_2)\) is bounded by step 1, so \((x_2 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F(x_2)\) tends to zero, so does \((x_0 - x_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{p}} \to \vek 0\), and the integral tends to zero by item 3 of the lemma on the properties of the integral. What remains is \(\vek M(x_0^+) - \vek M(x_0^-) + \vek M_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\), the second equation of (5.14).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The jump of the shear force at a point force is seen in SADD (D.5) (PDF p. 576), where \(V_{\mathrm{SADD}}\) for a force \(P\) jumps from \(P\,b/L\) to \(-P\,a/L\), that is by \(-P\), and \(V = -V_{\mathrm{SADD}}\) jumps by \(+P\), which for \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -P\) is exactly \(-F_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Let us test it on the beam with a force at the middle (figure 5.16). The force is \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -1000\) N at \(x_0 = 1\) m, so \(V\) jumps by \(-F_{\mathrm{y}} = +1000\) N, from \(-500\) N to \(+500\) N, as we computed. The jump is exactly such that a short piece around \(x_0\) is in equilibrium: the neighbouring parts act on it with \(-V(x_0^-) = +500\) N and \(V(x_0^+) = +500\) N, both upward, and the force \(1000\) N points downward. The moment is continuous, \(M(1^-) = M(1^+) = 500\) N m. The piece is short, so the lever arm of the forces at \(x_0\) about its centre is small, and the moment of the forces cannot jump if there is no couple.

What about a couple? The same simply supported beam, at the middle we load it with a couple with the moment \(M_0 = 100\) N m in the direction \(z\), counterclockwise, with no other loads. From equilibrium of the beam: \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\,L + M_0 = 0\) (component \(z\) about \(x = 0\)), so \(R_{\mathrm{B}} = -50\) N and \(R_{\mathrm{A}} = +50\) N. By the procedure with equilibrium of a part: \(V = -50\) N along the whole length. On the right half \(M = R_{\mathrm{B}}\,(L - x) = -50\,(2 - x)\) N m, on the left, where the part contains the couple, \(M = M_0 + R_{\mathrm{B}}\,(L - x) = 50\,x\) N m. At \(x = 1\) m \(M(1^-) = 50\) N m and \(M(1^+) = -50\) N m. The jump is \(-100\) N m \(= -M_0\), as the lemma claims, and \(V\) is continuous. A couple therefore has a different effect from a force: a force shifts \(V\), a couple shifts \(M\).

The same reasoning gives the conditions at the ends of the beam. At the free end \(x = L\) act a force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and a couple with the moment \(M_0\). On the piece from \(x\) to \(L\) act, besides the force of the cross section \(-\vek F(x)\), these two as well, so \(V(x) = F_{\mathrm{y}} + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q\,\mathrm{d}t\) and, when \(x \to L\), \(V(L) = F_{\mathrm{y}}\). In the same way from the moments about \(C(x)\): \(M(x) = M_0 + (L - x)\,F_{\mathrm{y}} + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L (t - x)\,q\,\mathrm{d}t\), which tends to \(M_0\) as \(x \to L\). For the cantilever with a force \(500\) N downward \(V(L) = -500\) N \(= F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M(L) = 0 = M_0\), as we computed. At the clamped end \(x = 0\) the wall acts on the beam with the force \(-\vek F(0)\) and the moment \(-\vek M(0)\), since the outward normal of the beam there is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). For the cantilever this is a force \(500\) N upward and the moment \(+500\) N m, counterclockwise, which holds the beam against the load at the end.

How the beam bends because of these forces is shown by the next section.

5.3 How a beam bends

Equilibrium gave us the internal forces \(N(x)\), \(V(x)\) and \(M(x)\) in every cross section, but not the shape that the beam takes. For the cantilever of section 5.1.3 we know that the moment at the clamp is \(-500\) N m, and we know nothing about how far the free end sinks. For that we must know where the points of the beam move. A loaded body has a displacement field (definition 1.23) with three unknown functions of three variables. For the bar we replaced it by one function \(u(x)\), because every point of a cross section moved the same way. In a beam the points of a cross section do not move the same way: in bending the fibres on one side get longer and on the other side shorter. We ask how many functions of one variable suffice to describe the displacements of all points of a beam.

We look for the answer in three steps. First we take a load for which symmetry alone gives the answer, pure bending. For other loads symmetry is not enough, so there we assume three properties of the cross sections and prove the form of the displacement field from them. At the end we say where these assumptions do not agree with the material that we know from chapter 3.

5.3.1 Pure bending

Let us start with a load for which every small piece of the middle part of the beam is loaded the same way. A simply supported beam (prostoležeči nosilec) of length \(L = 2\) m, made of a steel bar with a rectangular cross section 20 mm \(\times\) 40 mm, has at a distance \(a = 0{,}5\) m from each support one force \(F = 1\) kN downward (figure 5.17). We call this load four-point bending (štiritočkovni upogib), because the beam receives forces at four places: two reactions and two loads. The reactions are 1 kN each, upward.

We compute the internal forces with a cut, as we learned in section 5.2.2. We take the left part of the beam up to the cut at \(x\) and require that the sum of forces and of moments about the centre of the cut is zero. The force \((N, V, 0)\) and the moment \((0, 0, M)\) act on the left part from the right (the convention of section 5.2.1).

  1. At the left end acts the reaction \((0, 1000, 0)\) N at the point \((0, 0)\). For \(0 < x < a\) this is the only external force on the left part. The sum of forces in the direction \(y\) is \(1000 + V = 0\), so \(V = -1000\) N. The sum of forces in the direction \(x\) gives \(N = 0\).
  2. The moment of the reaction about the centre of the cut is the \(z\) component of the cross product \(\overrightarrow{r} \times \vek F\) with \(\overrightarrow{r} = (-x, 0, 0)\), so \((-x)(1000) - 0 = -1000\,x\) N m. The sum of moments is \(-1000\,x + M = 0\) and \(M = 1000\,x\) N m.
  3. For \(a < x < L - a\) the left part also carries the force \((0, -1000, 0)\) N at the point \((a, 0)\). Now \(V = -1000 + 1000 = 0\). The moment of this force about the cut is \((a - x)(-1000) = 1000\,(x - a)\) N m, so \(-1000\,x + 1000\,(x - a) + M = 0\) and \(M = 1000\,a = 500\) N m.

The middle part of the beam between the loads, 1 m long, therefore has \(N = 0\), \(V = 0\) and \(M = 500\) N m in every cross section, and the nonzero moment is the same everywhere. Such a part of a beam is in pure bending (čisti upogib). The result agrees with the relation \(M' = -V\) of corollary 5.11: for \(x < a\) we have \(V = -1000\) N and \(M' = 1000\) N, in the middle both are zero.

What happens to a cross section in pure bending? Let us recall the strip of section 1.18.3. The thin steel strip had the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) with radius \(R = 10\) m, and the displacement field

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{x\,y}{R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\frac{x^2}{2R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

In it all bands curve the same way and stack without gaps (figure 5.18). Its right end, at \(x = 0{,}2\) m, sinks by \(0{,}2^2/(2 \cdot 10)\) m \(= 2\) mm. We can notice something in it that we did not stress there. We call the segment of a cross section in the plane \(xy\) along which \(x\) and \(z\) are constant and which runs over the whole height of the cross section a normal line (prečnica), because before the load it is perpendicular to the axis. A point on the normal line at \(x\) that was at the height \(y\) moves in the direction \(x\) by \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = (x/R)\,y\). This displacement is proportional to the height \(y\). The normal line therefore does not curve, it stays straight and only tilts: the tilt is \(x/R\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}}/y = x/R\). The cross section stays plane.

Is it so in every pure bending? The answer is yes, and symmetry gives it (figure 5.19). Take a piece of the beam with its middle at \(x_0\) and mirror it in the plane of the cross section at \(x_0\). The mirror image of the piece is the same piece. The load on its ends is also equal to its mirror image: in pure bending there is only a normal stress at both ends, which is equal at both ends at the same point of the cross section and at both ends points either away from the piece or toward it. If the cross section in the middle of the piece bulged to the right, its mirror image would bulge to the left. The mirror image of the deformed piece is again a solution for the same load, and the solution for a given load is unique up to a rigid displacement (lemma 4.133). The deformed piece is therefore equal to its mirror image up to a rigid displacement, so the cross section cannot bulge to either side and must stay in its plane. We state this precisely as follows.

Lemma 5.13 Plane sections in pure bending (ravni prerezi pri čistem upogibu)

Let a segment of a beam be the box \(x_{\mathrm{a}} \le x \le x_{\mathrm{b}}\), \(|y| \le h/2\), \(|z| \le b/2\) (a prismatic segment (prizmatičen odsek): the cross section is the same along the whole length), made of a homogeneous isotropic material with Hooke's law (theorem 3.11), whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero (as in lemma 4.133). There are no body forces and the lateral surface of the segment, \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm b/2\), is free, \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\). Let the displacement field \(\vek u\) of the segment have small strains, be continuously differentiable with continuously differentiable stresses on an open set that contains the segment, and satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.31) at interior points. On every cross section let the stress vector be \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(y, z), 0, 0)\) with the same continuous function \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(y, z)\) (pure bending). Then for every \(x_0\) with \(x_{\mathrm{a}} < x_0 < x_{\mathrm{b}}\) and every piece \(|x - x_0| \le s\) of the segment there exist a field \(\vek w\) with \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(x_0, y, z) = 0\) and a small rigid displacement \(\vek r\) (lemma 4.72) such that on the piece \(\vek u = \vek w + \vek r\). The cross section at \(x_0\) therefore stays plane after the deformation, up to corrections of second order in the small displacements.

Proof

We must show that the mirror field has the same stresses on the same faces as the actual one, and use uniqueness. We take a piece \(K\) of the segment, \(|x - x_0| \le s\), which is a box, and the mirror \(S(x, y, z) = (2x_0 - x, y, z)\). Let \(s_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\) and \(s_{\mathrm{y}} = s_{\mathrm{z}} = 1\) be the signs of the reflection. The map \(S\) takes \(K\) to itself, the right cross face to the left, the left to the right and the lateral surface to itself, and an outward normal to an outward normal, \(\vek n(SP) = (s_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}(P))_{\mathrm{i}}\).

  1. The field \(\vek u\), restricted to \(K\), is a solution for the load \((\vek 0, \bar{\vek t})\), where \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the empty set (the piece is fixed nowhere) and \(\bar{\vek t} = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) on the surface (definition 4.132): requirements 1 and 2 hold by assumption, requirement 3 by the definition of \(\bar{\vek t}\). On the right face (\(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\)) we have \(\bar{\vek t} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(y, z), 0, 0)\), on the left (\(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\)) we have \(\bar{\vek t} = -\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (-\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(y, z), 0, 0)\) at the same \(y\) and \(z\), on the lateral surface \(\vek 0\). The load is continuous on every face.
  2. The mirror field is \(\tilde u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) = -u_{\mathrm{x}}(2x_0 - x, y, z)\), \(\tilde u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{y}}(2x_0 - x, y, z)\) and likewise \(\tilde u_{\mathrm{z}}\) with \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\). By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the derivative with respect to \(x\) of each component \(f(2x_0 - x, y, z)\) equals \(-(\partial f/\partial x)(2x_0 - x, y, z)\), and the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and \(z\) do not change. Therefore \(\tilde\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = s_{\mathrm{i}} s_{\mathrm{j}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(SP)\). For example \(\tilde\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial\tilde u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(SP)\) and \(\tilde\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12(\partial\tilde u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial\tilde u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12(-\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y - \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x)(SP) = -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}(SP)\).
  3. By Hooke's law (3.13) we have \(\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,(\mathrm{tr}\,\tilde{\ten\varepsilon})\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\tilde\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The trace is the same after the reflection, \(\mathrm{tr}\,\tilde{\ten\varepsilon}(P) = \mathrm{tr}\,\ten\varepsilon(SP)\), because the signs on the diagonal are \(s_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = 1\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = s_{\mathrm{i}} s_{\mathrm{j}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Therefore \(\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = s_{\mathrm{i}} s_{\mathrm{j}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(SP)\). The stresses \(\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuously differentiable because the \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are.
  4. The equilibrium equations also hold for \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\). By the chain rule \(\partial\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = s_{\mathrm{i}} s_{\mathrm{j}}\,s_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}})(SP) = s_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}})(SP)\), because \(s_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = 1\) (the derivative with respect to \(x\) gives an extra sign \(s_{\mathrm{x}}\), with respect to \(y\) and \(z\) it does not). The sum over \(j\) is \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) times the left side of equation (2.31) at the point \(SP\), so it is zero, because there are no body forces.
  5. The load of the mirror field is the same. By step 3 we have \((\tilde{\ten\sigma}\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{i}} s_{\mathrm{j}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(SP)\,n_{\mathrm{j}}(P) = s_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\ten\sigma\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{i}}(SP) = s_{\mathrm{i}}\,\bar t_{\mathrm{i}}(SP)\). On the right face \(SP\) is on the left and \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\,\bar t_{\mathrm{i}}(SP) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(y, z), 0, 0) = \bar{\vek t}(P)\), on the left face likewise \((-\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(y, z), 0, 0)\), on the lateral surface \(\vek 0\). The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is therefore a solution for the same load \((\vek 0, \bar{\vek t})\) (requirement 1 of the definition holds, because \(S\) maps \(K\) to itself).
  6. By lemma 4.133, point 2, for the body \(K\) in one piece and the empty \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the difference \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a small rigid displacement.
  7. By lemma 4.134 with \(\alpha = \beta = \tfrac12\) the field \(\vek w = \tfrac12(\vek u + \tilde{\vek u})\) is a solution for the load \(\tfrac12(\vek 0, \bar{\vek t}) + \tfrac12(\vek 0, \bar{\vek t}) = (\vek 0, \bar{\vek t})\). The mirror field of \(\vek w\) is \(\tfrac12(\tilde{\vek u} + \tilde{\tilde{\vek u}}) = \tfrac12(\tilde{\vek u} + \vek u) = \vek w\), because reflecting twice leaves the field unchanged: \(\tilde{\tilde u}_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) = -\tilde u_{\mathrm{x}}(2x_0 - x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)\), and likewise for the other two components.
  8. From \(\tilde w_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the point \((x_0, y, z)\), where \(SP = P\), it follows that \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = -w_{\mathrm{x}}\), so \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(x_0, y, z) = 0\). The points of the cross section at \(x_0\) do not move in the direction \(x\) under the field \(\vek w\) and stay in the plane \(x = x_0\).
  9. The field \(\vek r = \vek u - \vek w = \tfrac12(\vek u - \tilde{\vek u})\) is half of the small rigid displacement of step 6, so it is a small rigid displacement \(\vek r(P) = \delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi \times \overrightarrow{OP}\). Under \(\vek u\) a point \(P\) of the cross section at \(x_0\) goes to the point \(P + \vek w(P) + \delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi \times \overrightarrow{OP}\). The points \(P + \vek w(P)\) lie in the plane \(x = x_0\), and the map \(Q \mapsto Q + \delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi \times \overrightarrow{OQ}\) is linear and so again maps a plane to a plane.
