The point \(P + \vek u(P)\) differs from this map by \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi \times \vek w(P)\), which is of second order in the small displacements. The cross section after the deformation is therefore plane up to corrections of second order.

Source: The proof is not from a source. The same statement is confirmed by SADD Example 8.2 (PDF p. 171-172): for a beam with moments at the ends, which are satisfied only in the statically equivalent sense, the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{x}}\) is linear and all other components are zero, plane sections really stay plane (SADD (8.1.22), PDF p. 172), and the solution is not valid near the ends of the beam.

In four-point bending we assume the hypothesis of the lemma, that on every cross section there is only a normal stress with the same distribution, and we do not prove it: we know only the internal forces \(N = 0\), \(V = 0\) and \(M = 500\) N m, not the stresses. The assumption is supported by SADD Example 8.2, where exactly such a stress is the exact solution of the plane problem (PDF p. 171-172), valid far from the places where the load acts. The proof showed that a cross section cannot bulge in pure bending: the mirror field would bulge it to the other side, and the solution is unique up to a rigid displacement. The proof does not say how a cross section tilts and how the axis curves. We show this in the rest of the section. Symmetry helps only for a load where the stress is the same on all cross sections. For a beam that also has a shear force we cannot mirror cross sections into other cross sections, and symmetry is not enough.

5.3.2 Assumptions of the Euler-Bernoulli beam

From history

Mariotte had to design the pipelines supplying water to the Palace of Versailles, and this made him interested in the bending strength of beams (TIMO, PDF p. 29). Experimenting with wooden and glass rods, he found that Galileo's theory gives too large a breaking force (TIMO, PDF p. 29). In tension tests of various materials he saw that the elongations are proportional to the forces (TIMO, PDF p. 29). We have already met his correction of Galileo's calculation in section 1.1 (figure 1.8). Here we tell how he arrived at it and how he tested it. He started with a lever.

First he took a lever supported at the point \(C\). Three equal weights of 12 pounds hung on its left arm, at distances of 4, 2 and 1 foot from \(C\). They are balanced by a force \(F\) on the right arm, 12 feet from \(C\). From the balance of moments about \(C\), \(F = (12 \cdot 4 + 12 \cdot 2 + 12 \cdot 1)/12 = 7\) pounds (TIMO, PDF p. 29). If the force \(F\) is increased, the lever turns about \(C\). The displacements of the points where the weights hang are proportional to their distances from \(C\), but the forces stay equal, all three 12 pounds (TIMO, PDF p. 29). Mariotte then replaced the weights by three identical wires, each of strength 12 pounds. When the force in the farthest wire reaches 12 pounds, the forces in the other two are proportional to their elongations, so 6 and 3 pounds (TIMO, PDF p. 29). The breaking force is therefore \(F = (12 \cdot 4 + 6 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 1)/12 = 5{,}25\) pounds, not the 7 pounds of the rigid lever (TIMO, PDF p. 29-30). The force in each wire is thus proportional to its distance from the point of rotation, because it is proportional to the elongation, and the elongation to the distance.

He reasoned in the same way for a cantilever. At fracture the cross section turns about the point \(D\), and the forces in the longitudinal fibres are in the same proportion as their distances from \(D\) (TIMO, PDF p. 30). For a rectangular cross section of depth \(h\) and absolute strength \(S\) (the force the cross section carries in tension), the forces in the fibres grow from zero at \(D\) to the largest value at the edge. Their sum is therefore \(S/2\), and the moment about \(D\) is \((S/2)(2h/3) = S h/3\) (TIMO, PDF p. 30). The breaking force is thus two thirds of Galileo's value \(S h/2\) (TIMO, PDF p. 30-31). He tested it on a wooden bar. In tension the bar held \(S = 330\) pounds, and as a cantilever with an arm of \(l = 4\) inches it broke at \(L = 6\) pounds, so \(S : L = 55\). His formula gave 48, Galileo's 32 (TIMO, PDF p. 31). He blamed the difference on time, since the bar in tension might have held 300 pounds if the force had acted long enough (TIMO, PDF p. 31). A repetition with glass rods again showed that his formula predicts better than Galileo's (TIMO, PDF p. 31).

So the idea entered the thinking about bending that the cross section turns as a whole and that the fibres lengthen in proportion to their distance from the point of rotation.

Let us return to the question of the section: how the points of a beam move when it bends. The cross section that turns as a whole, according to Mariotte, is the first answer. Before we write it as an assumption, let us see what we already know about cross sections.

For the cantilever of section 5.1.3 the shear force is \(V = -500\) N in every cross section and the moment changes along the beam. There is no mirror symmetry in the cross section, and the lemma of the previous section says nothing. What do we take as a start? Let us see what is true in pure bending: the normal lines stayed straight (lemma 5.13), and in the strip they also kept their length and stayed perpendicular to the fibres. Let us assume that all this also holds for a beam with a shear force. These are the three assumptions of Euler and Bernoulli (EP, p. 73): after the deformation the normal lines of the beam remain

  • (a) straight,
  • (b) of the same length,
  • (c) perpendicular to the deformed axis of the beam.

CM (PDF p. 308) writes assumptions (b) and (c) with strains: that the normal line keeps its length means \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) (there is no elongation along the normal line), and that it stays perpendicular to the axis means \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) (the right angle between a longitudinal fibre and the normal line does not change, section 1.17.3). The beam is loaded only in the plane \(xy\) and the cross section has this plane as a plane of symmetry, so we also assume \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and that the cross section does not deform in the direction \(z\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). Each assumption has its reason and its cost, which we collect in a later section on the limits of beam theory. We look at the reasons on the cantilever of section 5.1.3.

  • Straightness (a) needs no reason of its own: it follows from (b) and (c), as we prove later in this section. In pure bending it is also proved (lemma 5.13).
  • Equal length (b) means that we neglect the transverse strains. By lemma 3.6 the transverse strain in a fibre under uniaxial stress is \(-\nu\) times the longitudinal one, so at the clamp of the cantilever at most \(0{,}3 \cdot 4{,}78 \cdot 10^{-4} = 1{,}43 \cdot 10^{-4}\). A normal line 40 mm long therefore changes on each half by less than \(20\ \text{mm} \cdot 1{,}43 \cdot 10^{-4} = 2{,}9\ \mu\text{m}\). What this neglect costs we say at the end of the section.
  • Perpendicularity (c) means \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). For the strip of section 5.3.1 it holds. With a shear force the normal lines would tilt relative to the axis by the shear strain, which is small for a slender beam: for the cantilever of section 5.1.3 the largest shear stress, which we compute later in the chapter, is 0,9375 MPa (1 % of the largest longitudinal stress 93,75 MPa from section 5.2.1), the shear strain is \(\tau/G = 0{,}9375\ \text{MPa}/75{,}38\ \text{GPa} = 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-5}\), which is 0,1 % of the slope 0,012 at the free end (we compute it later in the chapter) and 2,6 % of the largest longitudinal strain \(4{,}78 \cdot 10^{-4}\). A more precise estimate comes from a later section on the beam with shear deformation.

We write the assumptions as a definition.

Definition 5.14 Euler-Bernoulli beam model (Euler-Bernoullijev model nosilca)

Let a beam with the axis \(x\) and a rectangular cross section \(|y| \le h/2\), \(|z| \le b/2\) be loaded and supported in the plane \(xy\) (definition 5.1). The displacements of the beam in the Euler-Bernoulli beam model (Euler-Bernoullijev model nosilca) are a displacement field \((u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) which is continuous on the whole beam, whose components have continuous partial derivatives up to second order at the interior points of every piece of the beam between two neighbouring point loads (or of the whole beam if there are none), and which at every interior point of the beam satisfies

\[u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 . \tag{5.15}\]

The strains are the components of the small strain tensor (definition 1.115), computed by (1.63). The conditions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) are assumptions (b) and (c), and the conditions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) together with \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) mean that the deformation is plane and the displacements \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) do not change with \(z\).

Source: EP (p. 73), CM (PDF p. 308). Writing assumption (a) as a consequence of the others is ours (the theorem on the displacement field of a beam later in this section). EP and CM do not write \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) separately, because they choose the displacement field (EP (2.5.1), CM (7.3.22)) already in a form without dependence on \(z\).

5.3.3 Displacement field of a beam

The conditions (5.15) do not write assumption (a) about straight normal lines. Is it hidden in them? What displacement field follows from them? The answer is given by the same procedure as for the strip in section 1.18.3. There we concluded from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) that all points of a normal line move the same way in the direction \(y\), and from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) that \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). We use the same here. The second derivatives of the displacements are continuous only on each piece of the beam between two point loads, since the shear force jumps at a point force (lemma 5.12), while the displacement field is continuous across those points because the beam does not break. We therefore apply the theorem on each piece separately.

Theorem 5.15 Displacement field of a beam (polje pomikov nosilca)

Let \(B = \{(x, y, z) : x_1 < x < x_2, |y| < h/2, |z| < b/2\}\) be the set of interior points of the piece of the beam between neighbouring point loads at \(x = x_1\) and \(x = x_2\) (or of the whole beam, \(x_1 = 0\), \(x_2 = L\), if there are none) and let the displacement field \((u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) satisfy at every point of \(B\) the conditions (5.15) of the Euler-Bernoulli model, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order of the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\). Then there exist functions \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\) on the interval \((x_1, x_2)\), with continuous derivatives up to second order, such that at every point of \(B\)

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = u(x) - y\,v'(x) , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = v(x) , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 . \tag{5.16}\]

The only nonzero component of the strain is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = u'(x) - y\,v''(x) . \tag{5.17}\]
Proof

We must show that \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), that \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) grows linearly with \(y\) and that the coefficient of \(y\) is the derivative of the function \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\). We use corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative along segments inside \(B\), as in steps 1 to 3 of the proof for the strip in section 1.18.3.

  1. From \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial y) = 0\) it follows that \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z = 0\) at every point of \(B\). By corollary 1.85 on the segment from \((x, y, 0)\) to \((x, y, z)\), which lies in \(B\), we have \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, 0)\). Likewise from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\) it follows that \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = 0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, 0)\). The displacements are functions of \(x\) and \(y\) only.
  2. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = 0\), by corollary 1.85 on the segment from \((x, 0)\) to \((x, y)\) it follows that \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y) = u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 0) =: v(x)\). All points of a normal line move the same way in the direction \(y\).
  3. Therefore \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) at the point \((x, y)\) is the limit of the difference quotients \((u_{\mathrm{y}}(x + t, y) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y))/t = (v(x + t) - v(x))/t\), which are equal to those at the point \((x, 0)\), as \(t \to 0\) (definition 1.5). So \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = v'(x)\) for every \(y\), and similarly \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = v''(x)\). The derivatives \(v'\) and \(v''\) are continuous, because they are continuous derivatives of the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  4. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), by (1.63) it follows that \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -v'(x)\).
  5. At constant \(x\) the derivative of the function \(y \mapsto u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y) + y\,v'(x)\) with respect to \(y\) equals \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + v'(x) = 0\) by step 4 (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation). By corollary 1.85 on the segment from \((x, 0)\) to \((x, y)\) this function is constant, equal to its value at \(y = 0\), \(u(x) := u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, 0)\). So \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = u(x) - y\,v'(x)\). The function \(u\) has continuous derivatives up to second order as a restriction of the continuously differentiable component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  6. We compute the strains from (1.63): \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = u'(x) - y\,v''(x)\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) by assumption, and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial z = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) by assumption.

Source: CM (7.3.22), (7.3.23) (PDF p. 308-309), EP (2.5.1), (2.5.2) (p. 73). The sources write the displacement field as an assumption and compute the strains from it. The proof that the field follows from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) is not from the sources, it uses steps 1 to 3 of section 1.18.3.

The proof showed that the straightness of a normal line follows from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\): a point at the height \(y\) moves by \(-y\,v'(x)\) in the direction \(x\), so linearly with the height, and the normal line stays straight. This is assumption (a), which therefore did not need to be written separately. What this field means is shown by figure 5.21. The displacement of the axis is \((u(x), v(x))\). The displacement \(u(x)\) is the displacement of the bar of chapter 4: a point of the axis, \(y = 0\), moves by \(u(x)\) in the direction \(x\). The displacement \(v(x)\) is the deflection of the axis (poves osi), the displacement in the direction \(y\), which is the same for all points of a normal line.

So a point at the height \(y\) moves, besides the displacement of the axis, by \(-y\,v'(x)\) in the direction \(x\) (figure 5.22). What is \(v'(x)\)? It is the slope of the axis: by how much the axis rises per unit length, a ratio of two lengths, a number without a unit. For the cantilever of section 5.1.3 the slope at the free end is \(v' = -0{,}01196\) (we compute it later in the chapter). A point at the top of the cross section, at \(y = 20\) mm, therefore moves at the free end in the direction \(x\) by \(-0{,}020\ \text{m} \cdot (-0{,}01196) = 0{,}239\) mm. This is a horizontal displacement due to the slope, without length changes of the axis.

The normal line stays perpendicular to the axis and tilts by the same ratio as the slope of the axis. Let us show this with the small rotation tensor of section 1.18.3. For the field (5.16) we have by (1.54)

\[\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(-v' - v') = -v'(x) .\]

In a rigid rotation about the axis \(z\) by a small angle \(\varphi\) in radians (the ratio of the arc length to the radius), counterclockwise, the displacement of a point is \(\vek u = \varphi\,(-y, x, 0)\), and \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12(-\varphi - \varphi) = -\varphi\). The material near the axis therefore rotates by \(\varphi = v'(x)\): the normal line rotates by the slope of the axis, so it stays perpendicular to it. For the cantilever of section 5.1.3 the normal line at the free end rotates clockwise, because \(v' < 0\).

The axis curves. How strongly? We already saw the answer for the strip in section 1.18.3: the second derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2\) tells how fast the slope changes along a fibre. For a beam this is \(v''(x)\) and we name this quantity in the definition.

Definition 5.16 Curvature of the axis (ukrivljenost osi)

Let \(v\) be a twice continuously differentiable function on every open interval between neighbouring point loads in \((0, L)\) (or on \((0, L)\) if there are none), the deflection of the axis of a beam. Let the slope be small, \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\). The curvature of the axis (ukrivljenost osi) is the function \(\kappa(x) = v''(x)\) with the unit \(\text{m}^{-1}\), which gives one number for every value of \(x\). The radius of curvature (polmer ukrivljenosti) is \(R(x) = 1/|\kappa(x)|\), where \(\kappa(x) \ne 0\).

Source: CM (7.3.22) (PDF p. 308) has the slope \(\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}x\) in the displacement field. SADD (D.7), (D.8) (PDF p. 578) has the curvature \(1/\rho \approx d^2 v/dx^2\) for small slopes. The exact curvature of the graph of the function \(v\) is \(v''/(1 + v'^2)^{3/2}\) (SADD, PDF p. 578, the formula below (D.7)).

Sign: \(\kappa > 0\) where the slope increases and the axis curves upward (the shape of the letter U), \(\kappa < 0\) where the slope decreases. For the strip of section 1.18.3 we have \(v = -x^2/(2R)\) and \(\kappa = -1/R = -0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\), radius of curvature 10 m, as with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\). Figure 5.23 shows why we call this curvature: on a small piece of the axis the curvature \(\kappa\) means the change of the slope per unit length, and a circular arc of radius \(R\) has the same change of the slope, \(1/R\). The bound \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) is chosen because at it the exact curvature differs from \(v''\) by the factor \((1 + v'^2)^{-3/2} \ge 0{,}985\), so by at most 1,5 %. For the cantilever of section 5.1.3 the largest slope is \(v' = -0{,}01196\), \(v'^2 = 1{,}43 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the factor there is \(1{,}0001430^{-3/2} = 0{,}99979\), the error 0,02 %. For the simply supported beam the largest slope at the support is \(0{,}01594\) (we compute it later in the chapter), \(v'^2 = 2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the error 0,04 %.

The field (5.16) has three parts: \(u(x)\) is the bar of chapter 4, \(v(x)\) the deflection and \(-y\,v'(x)\) the tilt of the cross section. The strain (5.17) thus has two parts: \(u'(x)\) is the axial strain, the same for all \(y\), and \(-y\,v''(x) = -y\,\kappa(x)\) is the bending strain, which grows linearly with the height. For the strip of section 1.18.3 we have \(u = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v'' = y/R\), as in section 5.3.1. At positive curvature the upper fibres get shorter, because the axis curves upward and the inner side of a bend is shorter than the outer, and the upper fibres are on the inner side.

5.3.4 What we neglect here

Assumption (b), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), does not agree with the material. In a fibre pulled only by a longitudinal stress the transverse strain by lemma 3.6 is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which is not zero. Take the clamp of the cantilever of section 5.1.3, where the stress at the top of the cross section is \(+93{,}75\) MPa (section 5.2.1). The longitudinal strain there is \(93{,}75\ \text{MPa}/196\ \text{GPa} = 4{,}78 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the transverse strain is \(-0{,}3 \cdot 4{,}78 \cdot 10^{-4} = -1{,}43 \cdot 10^{-4}\) in the direction \(y\) and the same in the direction \(z\). The width of the cross section, 20 mm, decreases at the top by \(2{,}87\ \mu\text{m}\), by \(1{,}43\ \mu\text{m}\) on each side, and at the bottom, where the longitudinal strain is opposite, it increases by the same. The rectangular cross section turns into a trapezoid (figure 5.24). The normal line also curves because of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\): after integrating \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \nu\,\kappa\,y\) we get \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = v + \nu\,\kappa\,y^2/2\), its end points move by the same amount, and its middle is displaced relative to the end points by \(\nu\,|\kappa|\,h^2/8 = 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}0239\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot (0{,}04\ \text{m})^2/8 = 1{,}4\ \mu\text{m}\). The length of the normal line between its end points therefore does not change, but it stays straight only approximately. We call this anticlastic curvature (antiklastična ukrivljenost).

The model thus requires \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), and a material under uniaxial stress has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). We cannot have both at once. When we compute the stress from the strain we will keep \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and we use \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) only for the form of the displacement field. CM (PDF p. 309) admits this: in the relation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) it takes \(\nu = 0\), but in the relation \(2G = E/(1 + \nu)\) it does not. We still use the model, because what it neglects is small: the transverse strain at the clamp of the cantilever is less than \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the longitudinal one is \(4{,}78 \cdot 10^{-4}\). How large the errors of the results are we collect in a later section on the limits of beam theory.

The second assumption, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), is likewise only approximate when the shear force is \(V \ne 0\). Hooke's law connects the shear stress with the shear strain, and from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) it follows that \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), so also the shear force \(V = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,dA = 0\). The shear force that equilibrium requires would have to be zero. EP (p. 74) calls this an inconsistency of Bernoulli's hypothesis, CM (PDF p. 309) a flaw. Therefore we do not compute the shear stresses from Hooke's law but from the shear force (a later section on shear stresses), and we allow the shear strain, which \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) neglects, in the section on the beam with shear deformation. For the cantilever of section 5.1.3 the largest shear strain is \(\gamma = \tau_{\max}/G = 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-5}\), and its contribution to the deflection of the free end is 0,125 % of the bending part, but for the same bar shortened to \(L = 80\) mm it is 19,5 % (we compute it in a later section on the beam with shear deformation).

5.4 Mathematics: centroid and second moment of a cross section

The stress in a beam changes over the cross section. In tension it is the same everywhere, in bending it is tensile on one side of the cross section and compressive on the opposite side, and in between it passes through zero. The forces and moments of the cross section are therefore integrals of the stress over the cross section, and since the stress will be a constant or proportional to the distance \(y\) from some axis, we will compute three kinds of integrals over the area of the cross section: \(\int \mathrm{d}A\), \(\int y\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(\int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\). For each cross section these are three numbers that we compute once and afterwards only read. The question of this section is what these numbers mean and how to compute them for a given figure.

The cross section (prerez) is a figure in a plane perpendicular to the axis of the beam, that is, in the plane \(x = \text{const.}\). We look at the cross section along the axis \(x\), from the left end of the beam toward the right, so that the axis \(x\) points away from us, the axis \(y\) points up and the axis \(z\) points to the right. This system is right-handed, because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} \times \vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\): the thumb of the right hand points away from us, the index finger up and the middle finger to the right. We describe the points of the figure by the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\), and for now we choose the origin anywhere. As an example we will use the cross section of a steel flat bar, \(b = 20\) mm wide and \(h = 40\) mm high, standing on its edge (the width along \(z\), the height along \(y\)), and next to it three composite figures that often appear in beams, the letter T, the letter L and the double T, which we call the I-section.

5.4.1 Integral over a figure

In chapter 4 we defined the integral over a box as an iterated integral and extended it to bodies assembled from the cells of a grid. For a rectangle in the plane \(x = c\) the two iterated integrals run over the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) (definition 4.8). All the cross sections we will compute are made of rectangles whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes. For such composite figures we can take the same step in the plane: we cut the figure into the cells of a grid and add up the integrals over the cells.

Definition 5.17 Figure made of rectangles (lik iz pravokotnikov)

Let \(R = [y_{\mathrm{a}}, y_{\mathrm{b}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{a}}, z_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a rectangle in the plane with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The partitions \(y_{\mathrm{a}} = y_0 < y_1 < \dots < y_{\mathrm{m}} = y_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{a}} = z_0 < z_1 < \dots < z_{\mathrm{n}} = z_{\mathrm{b}}\) cut \(R\) into the cells \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = [y_{\mathrm{i}-1}, y_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{j}-1}, z_{\mathrm{j}}]\), and this is the grid. A set of points \(L\) is a figure made of rectangles (lik iz pravokotnikov) if it is the union of some cells of this grid, at least one.

  1. The integral of a continuous function \(f(y, z)\) over the figure \(L\) is the sum of the integrals over its cells,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{L}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \sum_{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{ij}} \subseteq \mathrm{L}} \int_{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{ij}}} f\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    where the integral over a cell is the iterated integral of definition 4.8, first over \(z\), then over \(y\). The integral is a number.
  2. The area (ploščina) of the figure \(L\) is the number \(A = \int_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{d}A\).

Source: An analogue of definition 4.11 of chapter 4, in the plane. The definition is not from a source.

By item 2 of lemma 4.10 the area of a rectangle is \(A = (y_{\mathrm{b}} - y_{\mathrm{a}})(z_{\mathrm{b}} - z_{\mathrm{a}})\), which is the familiar area of a rectangle. Our bar therefore has \(A = 20 \cdot 40 = 800\) mm\(^2\).

A figure can be cut into cells in several ways, and also a figure made of a few larger rectangles is cut into the cells of a grid that contains all their sides (figure 5.25). The integral must always be the same, and the following lemma guarantees this. The first part is the same argument as for bodies made of boxes (lemma 4.12), and the second part will let us add up the integral over a composite figure part by part.

Lemma 5.18 The integral over a figure does not depend on the grid (integral po liku ni odvisen od mreže)

Let \(L\) be a figure made of rectangles and \(f\) a continuous function on \(L\).

  1. The integral \(\int_{\mathrm{L}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\) and the area of the figure \(L\) do not depend on the grid by which we cut \(L\) into cells.
  2. Let \(L\) be the union of rectangles \(P_1, \dots, P_{\mathrm{k}}\) with sides parallel to the coordinate axes, whose interiors do not overlap. Then
    \[\int_{\mathrm{L}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \sum_{\mathrm{m}=1}^{k} \int_{\mathrm{P}_\mathrm{m}} f\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  3. The integral over a figure is linear: \(\int_{\mathrm{L}} (\alpha f + \beta g)\,\mathrm{d}A = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{L}} f\,\mathrm{d}A + \beta \int_{\mathrm{L}} g\,\mathrm{d}A\) for continuous functions \(f\), \(g\) and numbers \(\alpha\), \(\beta\).
Proof

We must show that the sum over the cells does not depend on the grid, that it equals the sum over the rectangles of which the figure is made, and that it is linear. We prove the first by adding lines to the grid one at a time, as in lemma 4.12.

1. Independence of the grid.

  1. Let the second grid have one more line, for example \(y = c\) with \(y_{\mathrm{i}-1} < c < y_{\mathrm{i}}\). The line cuts each cell between \(y = y_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(y = y_{\mathrm{i}}\) into two halves, the other cells remain. A half of a cell that is not in \(L\) is not in \(L\) either, because its points that lie on no line of the grid lie in no other cell of the old grid. So \(L\) is the union of the uncut cells and the halves of the cut cells.
  2. By item 3 of lemma 4.10, applied to a rectangle, the integral over a cut cell is the sum of the integrals over the halves. The sum over the cells is therefore the same in both grids. We proceed in the same way for a line \(z = c\).
  3. Let two arbitrary grids for \(L\) be given. We extend both to a common rectangle that contains both original ones, by adding end points to the partitions. The new cells lie outside \(L\), so the sum does not change. The grid that has all the lines of both grids is obtained from each of them by adding lines one at a time. By steps 1 and 2 each of the two grids gives the same sum as this common grid. With \(f = 1\) this holds for the area.

2. Additivity over rectangles.

  1. We take a grid whose lines are all the coordinates of the sides of the rectangles \(P_1, \dots, P_{\mathrm{k}}\). Each \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\) is a union of cells of this grid, because none of its sides is inside a cell. By item 3 of lemma 4.10 the integral over \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\) is the sum of the integrals over the cells in \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  2. Each cell of the figure \(L\) lies in some \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\), because it is in \(L\) and so its interior points lie in some \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\), which is a union of cells. It does not lie in two rectangles, because their interiors would overlap. The sum over the rectangles is therefore the sum over the cells of the figure \(L\) in this grid, which by step 1 of the first part is the sum that defines \(\int_{\mathrm{L}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\).

3. Linearity.

  1. By item 1 of lemma 4.10, applied to a rectangle, the integral over each cell is linear. A sum of linear expressions over the cells is linear.

Source: The proof is not from a source, it is the two-dimensional proof of lemma 4.12.

The lemma says two things. The integral over a figure made of rectangles is a well-defined number, even if we take another cutting for the grid. In addition, we can always compute it over the rectangles of which the figure is made, which we will do for all cross sections. The T-section of figure 5.25 has the area \(A = 1200 + 1600 = 2800\) mm\(^2\) if the web is 20 mm wide and 60 mm high and the flange is 80 mm wide and 20 mm high (we compute both numbers by item 2 of lemma 4.10 as the area of a rectangle).

For the forces and moments of the stress in a cross section we still need a corollary that extends lemma 5.9 from a rectangle to every figure made of rectangles. The moment is computed about a point \(C\) in the plane of the cross section that is not necessarily the centre of a rectangle, so we say so in the statement.

Corollary 5.19 Internal forces from stresses for a composite cross section (notranje sile iz napetosti za sestavljen prerez)

Let the cross section of a beam at \(x\) be a figure \(L\) made of rectangles (definition 5.17), let \(C = (x, 0, 0)\) be a point of its plane from which the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) are measured, and let the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) be continuous functions on \(L\). Then for \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M\) about \(C\) equations (5.4) and (5.5) hold with integrals over \(L\).

Proof

We must show that the forces and moments of the rectangles of which \(L\) is made, added up, give the same as the integrals over \(L\).

  1. Let \(L\) be the union of rectangles \(P_1, \dots, P_{\mathrm{k}}\) with non-overlapping interiors. The force on \(L\) is the sum of the forces on the individual \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\), the moment about \(C\) is the sum of the moments, because the forces and moments of pieces of a surface add.
  2. Steps 1 to 4 of the proof of lemma 5.9 use only that the surface is a rectangle and that the vector from \(C\) to a point of the surface is \(\vek r = (0, y, z)\). They nowhere use the centre of the rectangle. So they hold for every \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\) and give the force \(\int_{\mathrm{P}_\mathrm{m}} \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\) and the moment \(\int_{\mathrm{P}_\mathrm{m}} \vek r \times \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  3. The components of \(\vek t\) and \(\vek r \times \vek t\) are continuous functions on \(L\). By item 2 of lemma 5.18 the sum of the integrals over the \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\) equals the integral over \(L\). Adding over \(m\) gives for \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M\) the same expressions as in the lemma, with integrals over \(L\).

Source: The proof is not from a source, it extends the proof of lemma 5.9.

5.4.2 Centroid

Why do we need the second number, \(\int y\,\mathrm{d}A\)? Take a uniform stress \(\sigma\) pulling the cross section, that is, a force \(\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A\) on each piece of area. The force acts at the point \((0, y, z)\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), \(\vek F = (\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A, 0, 0)\), so its moment about the origin (definition 2.32) is \((0, y, z) \times (\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A, 0, 0) = (0,\ z\,\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A,\ -y\,\sigma\,\mathrm{d}A)\). All the pieces together give the component \(z\) of the moment \(-\sigma \int y\,\mathrm{d}A\) and the component \(y\) of the moment \(\sigma \int z\,\mathrm{d}A\). A uniform tension should be only a force without a moment, so both integrals must be zero. This holds only if the axes pass through the right point of the figure. How do we find it?

Definition 5.20 First moment of area (statični moment)

Let \(L\) be a figure made of rectangles (definition 5.17) in the plane with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) and the origin \(O\). The first moments of the figure \(L\) about the axes \(z\) and \(y\) are the numbers

\[S_{\mathrm{z}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} y\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad S_{\mathrm{y}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} z\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

The unit is length cubed, for example mm\(^3\).

Source: The definition is not from a source.

The index tells the axis about which we count: \(S_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the first moment about the axis \(z\), where \(y\) is the distance from this axis, and \(S_{\mathrm{y}}\) about the axis \(y\), where the distance is \(z\). The first moment is the area weighted by the distance from the axis, so it can be positive, zero or negative, depending on which side of the axis the figure mostly lies.

Definition 5.21 Centroid (težišče)

Let the figure \(L\) made of rectangles have the area \(A > 0\). The centroid (težišče) of the figure \(L\) is the point \(T\) with the coordinates

\[y_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{S_{\mathrm{z}}}{A} , \qquad z_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{S_{\mathrm{y}}}{A} .\]

Source: ONATE2 (Fig. 1.3, PDF p. 35) gives the centre of gravity G of cross sections as known. The definition is not from a source.

The next lemma says that the first moments are zero if we put the origin in the centroid. A plate of equal thickness and density in the shape of the figure therefore stays in balance when supported at the centroid: the weight of a piece of area \(\mathrm{d}A\) is proportional to \(\mathrm{d}A\), and the moment of the weight about an axis through the centroid is proportional to \(\int y'\,\mathrm{d}A\) or \(\int z'\,\mathrm{d}A\), and both are zero.

Lemma 5.22 First moments about axes through the centroid (statična momenta glede na osi skozi težišče)

Let the figure \(L\) made of rectangles have the centroid \(T\) with the coordinates \((y_{\mathrm{T}}, z_{\mathrm{T}})\), and let \(y' = y - y_{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(z' = z - z_{\mathrm{T}}\) be the coordinates about axes through \(T\), parallel to the original ones. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{L}} y'\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \qquad \int_{\mathrm{L}} z'\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]
Proof

We must show that subtracting \(y_{\mathrm{T}} A\) from \(S_{\mathrm{z}}\) leaves exactly zero. The computation is one line.

  1. By linearity (item 3 of lemma 5.18) \(\int_{\mathrm{L}} (y - y_{\mathrm{T}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{L}} y\,\mathrm{d}A - y_{\mathrm{T}} \int_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{d}A = S_{\mathrm{z}} - y_{\mathrm{T}} A\).
  2. By definition 5.21 \(S_{\mathrm{z}} = y_{\mathrm{T}} A\), so the difference is zero. The same holds for \(z'\) and \(S_{\mathrm{y}} = z_{\mathrm{T}} A\).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

From now on, except where we say otherwise, we will use the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) with the origin in the centroid, as is usual for beams. For a rectangle and for a composite figure we compute the centroid as follows.

Lemma 5.23 Centroid of a rectangle and of a union (težišče pravokotnika in sestavljenega lika)
  1. The centroid of the rectangle \([y_{\mathrm{a}}, y_{\mathrm{b}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{a}}, z_{\mathrm{b}}]\) is its centre, \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = (y_{\mathrm{a}} + y_{\mathrm{b}})/2\) and \(z_{\mathrm{T}} = (z_{\mathrm{a}} + z_{\mathrm{b}})/2\).
  2. Let \(L\) be the union of rectangles \(P_1, \dots, P_{\mathrm{k}}\) with areas \(A_{\mathrm{m}}\) and centroids \((y_{\mathrm{m}}, z_{\mathrm{m}})\), whose interiors do not overlap. Then
    \[y_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{\sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}}\,y_{\mathrm{m}}}{\sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}}} , \qquad z_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{\sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}}\,z_{\mathrm{m}}}{\sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}}} .\]
Proof

We must show that the first moment of the figure is the sum of the first moments of the parts, and then that the first moment of a rectangle is the product of the area and the coordinate of the centre.

1. Rectangle.

  1. By definition 4.8 \(S_{\mathrm{z}} = \int_{\mathrm{y}_\mathrm{a}}^{y_{\mathrm{b}}} \big( \int_{\mathrm{z}_\mathrm{a}}^{z_{\mathrm{b}}} y\,\mathrm{d}z \big)\,\mathrm{d}y\). The inner integral is \(y\,(z_{\mathrm{b}} - z_{\mathrm{a}})\), because \(y\) is a constant in the inner integral.
  2. The outer integral is \((z_{\mathrm{b}} - z_{\mathrm{a}}) \int_{\mathrm{y}_\mathrm{a}}^{y_{\mathrm{b}}} y\,\mathrm{d}y = (z_{\mathrm{b}} - z_{\mathrm{a}})\,\dfrac{y_{\mathrm{b}}^2 - y_{\mathrm{a}}^2}{2} = A\,\dfrac{y_{\mathrm{a}} + y_{\mathrm{b}}}{2}\), because \(y_{\mathrm{b}}^2 - y_{\mathrm{a}}^2 = (y_{\mathrm{b}} - y_{\mathrm{a}})(y_{\mathrm{b}} + y_{\mathrm{a}})\) and \(A = (z_{\mathrm{b}} - z_{\mathrm{a}})(y_{\mathrm{b}} - y_{\mathrm{a}})\). So \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = S_{\mathrm{z}}/A = (y_{\mathrm{a}} + y_{\mathrm{b}})/2\). For \(z_{\mathrm{T}}\) the computation is the same, with the roles of the coordinates exchanged by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration.

2. Composite figure.

  1. By item 2 of lemma 5.18 \(S_{\mathrm{z}} = \sum_{\mathrm{m}} S_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{m}}\) and \(A = \sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}}\), where \(S_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{m}}\) is the first moment of the rectangle \(P_{\mathrm{m}}\), because \(f = y\) and \(f = 1\) are continuous functions.
  2. By step 2 of the first part \(S_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{m}} = A_{\mathrm{m}}\,y_{\mathrm{m}}\). So \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = S_{\mathrm{z}}/A = \sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}} y_{\mathrm{m}} / \sum_{\mathrm{m}} A_{\mathrm{m}}\). For \(z_{\mathrm{T}}\) the computation is the same.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

The lemma says that the centroid of a composite figure is a weighted mean of the centroids of the parts, where the weights are the areas. If the figure has a symmetry, the computation becomes even shorter.

Lemma 5.24 Centroid of a symmetric figure (težišče simetričnega lika)

Let \(L\) be a figure made of rectangles that is symmetric about the axis \(y\): the point \((y, z)\) is in \(L\) exactly when the point \((y, -z)\) is in \(L\). Let \(g\) be a continuous function of the variable \(y\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{L}} z\,g(y)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]

In particular \(S_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) (with \(g = 1\)), so the centroid lies on the axis of symmetry.

Proof

We must show that the integrals over cells that are mirror images of each other cancel. We choose a symmetric grid.

  1. To the grid that cuts \(L\) we add the mirror lines \(z = -z_{\mathrm{j}}\). By item 1 of lemma 5.18 the integral does not change, and the grid is now symmetric. The mirror image of a cell of the figure \(L\) is therefore a cell of the grid, and it lies in \(L\), because \(L\) is symmetric.
  2. By definition 4.8 the cell \([y_{\mathrm{i}-1}, y_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{j}-1}, z_{\mathrm{j}}]\) has the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{i}-1}}^{y_{\mathrm{i}}} g(y) \big( \int_{\mathrm{z}_{\mathrm{j}-1}}^{z_{\mathrm{j}}} z\,\mathrm{d}z \big)\,\mathrm{d}y\), because \(g(y)\) is a constant in the inner integral. The inner integral is \((z_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - z_{\mathrm{j}-1}^2)/2\).
  3. The mirror cell is \([y_{\mathrm{i}-1}, y_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [-z_{\mathrm{j}}, -z_{\mathrm{j}-1}]\) and has the inner integral \((z_{\mathrm{j}-1}^2 - z_{\mathrm{j}}^2)/2\), the opposite number. The integrals of the two cells therefore cancel. A cell that lies on the axis, \(z_{\mathrm{j}-1} = -z_{\mathrm{j}}\), is its own mirror image, and its inner integral is \((z_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - z_{\mathrm{j}}^2)/2 = 0\).
  4. The sum over the cells of the figure \(L\) is a sum of pairs and cells on the axis, so it is zero.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

For our bar, lemma 5.24 gives that the centroid is on the axis of symmetry, \(z_{\mathrm{T}} = 0\), and since the figure is symmetric also about the axis \(z\) (exchanging the roles of the coordinates), also \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = 0\) (lemma 5.24 with the roles of the coordinates exchanged), so the centroid is at the centre of the rectangle, as lemma 5.23 also says. Figure 5.26 shows why: the strip at height \(y\) and the strip at height \(-y\) have equal areas, and their contributions \(y\,\mathrm{d}A\) are opposite.

For the letter T the centroid is not at half the height, because the upper part is wider than the lower one. Let us see where it is.

Example 5.25 Centroid of a T-section (težišče prereza T)

The T-section has a web \(20 \times 60\) mm and a flange \(80 \times 20\) mm lying on top of the web, all symmetric about the axis \(y\) (figure 5.27). The total height is 80 mm. We measure heights from the lower edge, \(y = 0\).

  1. The web is the rectangle \([0, 60] \times [-10, 10]\) with the area \(A_1 = 20 \cdot 60 = 1200\) mm\(^2\) and the centroid at the height \(y_1 = 30\) mm (lemma 5.23, item 1). The flange is the rectangle \([60, 80] \times [-40, 40]\) with the area \(A_2 = 80 \cdot 20 = 1600\) mm\(^2\) and the centroid at the height \(y_2 = 70\) mm.
  2. By item 2 of the same lemma the total area is \(A = 1200 + 1600 = 2800\) mm\(^2\) and
    \[y_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{1200 \cdot 30 + 1600 \cdot 70}{2800}\ \text{mm} = \frac{36\,000 + 112\,000}{2800}\ \text{mm} = \frac{370}{7}\ \text{mm} = 52{,}86\ \text{mm} .\]
  3. The centroid is therefore 52,86 mm above the lower edge and \(80 - 52{,}86 = 27{,}14\) mm below the upper one. It lies in the web, because \(52{,}86 < 60\) mm. If the two parts had equal areas, the centroid would be midway between their centroids, at 50 mm. The flange has more area (1600 against 1200 mm\(^2\)), so the centroid is shifted toward it.

5.4.3 Second moment of area of a cross section

In bending the stress grows in proportion to the distance from some axis, \(\sigma = k\,y\), and the component \(z\) of the moment of the stress is, by the computation above, \(-\int y \cdot k y\,\mathrm{d}A = -k \int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\). A third integral appears at once. First we name it, then we compute it for a rectangle and for composite figures.

Definition 5.26 Second moment of area (vztrajnostni moment prereza)

Let \(L\) be a figure made of rectangles in the plane with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) with the origin in the centroid (lemma 5.22). The numbers

\[I_{\mathrm{z}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad I_{\mathrm{y}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad I_{\mathrm{yz}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} y\,z\,\mathrm{d}A\]

are the second moments of area of the cross section about the axes \(z\) and \(y\) and the product of inertia (deviacijski moment) of the cross section. The unit is length to the fourth, for example mm\(^4\) or m\(^4\).

Source: SADD (9.8.18) (PDF p. 276) writes \(I_{\mathrm{x}} = \iint y^2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = -\iint x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\) (with a minus) and \(I_{\mathrm{xy}} = \iint x y\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\). The minus at \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) is a misprint: from (9.8.15) follows \(B\iint x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y + C\iint xy\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y = -P_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is (9.8.16) only if \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = +\iint x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\), and in (9.8.19) the quantity \(I_{\mathrm{x}} I_{\mathrm{y}} - I_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\) uses exactly this positive \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) (Cauchy-Schwarz). So we do not adopt the minus, and our \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) is not negative by item 4 of lemma 4.10 anyway. SADD nowhere uses \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) with a sign as a convention of its flexure formula (PDF pp. 276-277). His axes of the cross section are \(x\) and \(y\), ours are \(y\) and \(z\). ONATE2 (1.5) and Fig. 1.3 (PDF pp. 34 and 35) has \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = \int z^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) with the axis \(z\) up. We have \(y\) up, so for bending in the plane \(x\)–\(y\) it is \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) that matters.

The name is similar to the name from the mechanics of a rigid body, where the moment of inertia (vztrajnostni moment) describes how a body resists rotation. Here it describes how a cross section resists bending, and it has nothing to do with inertia. The name is historical, and we will meet the mechanics of rotating bodies in chapter 8. Here \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a property of the figure. Since the integrand \(y^2\) is non-negative, by item 4 of lemma 4.10 the integral over each cell is non-negative, so \(I_{\mathrm{z}} \ge 0\).

Lemma 5.27 Second moment of a rectangle (vztrajnostni moment pravokotnika)

A rectangle of width \(b\) (along \(z\)) and height \(h\) (along \(y\)) with the origin at the centre, \([-h/2, h/2] \times [-b/2, b/2]\), has

\[A = b\,h , \qquad I_{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{b\,h^3}{12} , \qquad I_{\mathrm{y}} = \frac{h\,b^3}{12} , \qquad I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \tag{5.18}\]
Proof

We must show four integrals, and we compute them as the iterated integrals of definition 4.8, the inner over \(z\), the outer over \(y\). For \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) we use the same computation with the roles exchanged, by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration.

  1. Area: \(\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} \big( \int_{-\mathrm{b}/2}^{b/2} \mathrm{d}z \big) \mathrm{d}y = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} b\,\mathrm{d}y = b\,h\).
  2. For \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) the inner integral is \(\int_{-\mathrm{b}/2}^{b/2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}z = b\,y^2\), because \(y^2\) is a constant in the inner integral.
  3. The outer integral is \(b \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = b \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\Big[ y^3 \Big]_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\), which by the fundamental theorem of calculus equals \(\dfrac{b}{3} \Big( \dfrac{h^3}{8} + \dfrac{h^3}{8} \Big) = \dfrac{b\,h^3}{12}\).
  4. \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = h\,b^3/12\) after exchanging the roles \(y \leftrightarrow z\), \(b \leftrightarrow h\).
  5. For \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}\) the integrand is \(y\,z\) and by lemma 5.24 with \(g(y) = y\) the integral is zero, since the rectangle is symmetric about the axis \(y\).

Source: ONATE2 Fig. 1.3 (PDF p. 35) states \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = b h^3/12\) for a rectangle with the axis \(z\) up, which is our \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\). The proof is not from a source.

For our bar \(b = 20\) mm and \(h = 40\) mm,

\[\begin{aligned} I_{\mathrm{z}} &= \frac{20 \cdot 40^3}{12}\ \text{mm}^4 = 106\,667\ \text{mm}^4 = 1{,}0667 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4 , \\ I_{\mathrm{y}} &= \frac{40 \cdot 20^3}{12}\ \text{mm}^4 = 26\,667\ \text{mm}^4 . \end{aligned}\]

The bar standing on its edge therefore has a second moment four times that of the same bar lying flat, because the ratio \((h/b)^2 = 4\) enters as the square of the ratio of the sides.

Why does \(h^3\) appear in \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\), and not \(h\)? We cut the cross section into strips of height \(\Delta y\). The strip at height \(y\) has the area \(b\,\Delta y\) and contributes \(y^2\,b\,\Delta y\) (figure 5.28). The contribution grows with the square of the distance from the axis, so the strips at the edge count much more than the strips near the axis. For our bar the outer half of the height, \(10\ \text{mm} \le |y| \le 20\ \text{mm}\), contributes

\[2 \cdot 20 \int_{10}^{20} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = 2 \cdot 20 \cdot \frac{20^3 - 10^3}{3}\ \text{mm}^4 = \frac{280\,000}{3}\ \text{mm}^4 ,\]

and the inner half \(20 \int_{-10}^{10} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = 40\,000/3\ \text{mm}^4\). The outer half of the height contributes \(87{,}5\ \%\) of the whole \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 320\,000/3\ \text{mm}^4\), the inner only \(12{,}5\ \%\). This is why we give cross sections a shape in which the material is as far from the axis as possible.

The integral is the limit of sums over strips. If we replace it by the sum over \(n\) strips, with the contribution computed at the middle of each strip, \(\sum y_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,b\,\Delta y\), we obtain for our cross section for \(n = 2, 4, 8\) and \(1000\) strips \(80\,000\), \(100\,000\), \(105\,000\) and \(106\,667\ \text{mm}^4\). The sum is always smaller, because the mean of \(y^2\) over a strip with the centre \(y_{\mathrm{k}}\) and half-height \(\delta\) is \(y_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + \delta^2/3\), which is more than the value at the middle. With more strips the error shrinks, since \(\delta\) gets smaller.

We computed the second moment of the rectangle about axes through its centre. In a composite figure each part has its own centroid and its own axes. We compute them by knowing how to transfer the second moment to a parallel axis, and the following theorem makes this possible.

Theorem 5.28 Parallel axis theorem (Steinerjev izrek)

Let the figure \(L\) made of rectangles have the area \(A\), the centroid \(T\) and the second moments \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}\) about axes through \(T\). Let \(y'\) and \(z'\) be the coordinates about axes parallel to the original ones, with the origin at a point \(O'\) in which the centroid \(T\) has the coordinates \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} I_{\mathrm{z}}' &= \int_{\mathrm{L}} y'^2\,\mathrm{d}A = I_{\mathrm{z}} + A\,d_{\mathrm{y}}^2 , \\ I_{\mathrm{y}}' &= I_{\mathrm{y}} + A\,d_{\mathrm{z}}^2 , \\ I_{\mathrm{yz}}' &= I_{\mathrm{yz}} + A\,d_{\mathrm{y}}\,d_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned} \tag{5.19}\]
Proof

We must show that the difference is \(A\,d^2\), and that the term with \(d\) vanishes. The coordinates in the new system are \(y' = y + d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(z' = z + d_{\mathrm{z}}\), where \(y\) and \(z\) are the coordinates about \(T\).

  1. We expand the square, \(y'^2 = (y + d_{\mathrm{y}})^2 = y^2 + 2 d_{\mathrm{y}}\,y + d_{\mathrm{y}}^2\).
  2. By linearity of the integral (item 3 of lemma 5.18) \(I_{\mathrm{z}}' = \int_{\mathrm{L}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A + 2 d_{\mathrm{y}} \int_{\mathrm{L}} y\,\mathrm{d}A + d_{\mathrm{y}}^2 \int_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{d}A\).
  3. The second integral is zero by lemma 5.22, because the \(y\) are coordinates about the centroid. The third is \(A\). So \(I_{\mathrm{z}}' = I_{\mathrm{z}} + A\,d_{\mathrm{y}}^2\).
  4. For \(I_{\mathrm{y}}'\) the computation is the same with \(z\) in place of \(y\). For \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}'\) we have \((y + d_{\mathrm{y}})(z + d_{\mathrm{z}}) = y z + d_{\mathrm{z}}\,y + d_{\mathrm{y}}\,z + d_{\mathrm{y}} d_{\mathrm{z}}\), and both middle integrals are zero by lemma 5.22, so \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}' = I_{\mathrm{yz}} + A\,d_{\mathrm{y}} d_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source, it is standard.

Let us test it on the bar (figure 5.29). The second moment about the lower edge, that is, about an axis that is \(d_{\mathrm{y}} = 20\) mm below the centroid, is by the theorem

\[I_{\mathrm{z}}' = 106\,667 + 800 \cdot 20^2 = 106\,667 + 320\,000 = 426\,667\ \text{mm}^4 .\]

Directly, with the integral from \(y = 0\) to \(y = 40\) mm, \(20 \int_0^{40} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = 20 \cdot 40^3/3 = 426\,667\ \text{mm}^4\). The results agree. An axis that does not pass through the centroid gives a moment four times larger, because for \(d_{\mathrm{y}} = 20\) mm the term \(A\,d_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = 320\,000\ \text{mm}^4\) is three times larger than \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) itself.

The parallel axis theorem allows us to compute the second moment of a composite figure from its parts. For an I-section 200 mm high, with flanges \(100 \times 10\) mm and a web \(6 \times 180\) mm, the centroid is at the middle, \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = 100\) mm from the lower edge, because the figure is symmetric about the horizontal axis (lemma 5.24, with the roles of the coordinates exchanged).

Example 5.29 Second moment of an I-section (vztrajnostni moment I-profila)

The cross section has three rectangles: the upper flange \(100 \times 10\) mm, the web \(6 \times 180\) mm and the lower flange \(100 \times 10\) mm (figure 5.30). We count the coordinate \(y\) from the centroid (the middle of the height).

  1. The area is \(A = 1000 + 1080 + 1000 = 3080\) mm\(^2\).
  2. A flange has, about its own centroid, by lemma 5.27 \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 100 \cdot 10^3/12 = 8333\) mm\(^4\). The centroid of the flange is at the distance \(d_{\mathrm{y}} = 95\) mm from the centroid of the cross section, so by theorem 5.28, equation (5.19), it contributes \(8333 + 1000 \cdot 95^2 = 8333 + 9\,025\,000 = 9\,033\,333\) mm\(^4\). The two flanges together give \(18\,066\,667\) mm\(^4\).
  3. The web has its centroid at the centroid of the cross section, \(d_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), so its contribution is just \(6 \cdot 180^3/12 = 2\,916\,000\) mm\(^4\).
  4. By item 3 of lemma 5.18 the integral is the sum over the rectangles, so
    \[I_{\mathrm{z}} = 18\,066\,667 + 2\,916\,000 = 20\,982\,667\ \text{mm}^4 = 2{,}098 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{mm}^4 .\]
  5. Let us compare with a rectangle of the same area (3080 mm\(^2\)), 20 mm wide and \(3080/20 = 154\) mm high, which has \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 20 \cdot 154^3/12 = 6\,087\,107\) mm\(^4\). The I-section has a second moment \(20\,982\,667 / 6\,087\,107 = 3{,}45\) times larger for the same mass. The reason is that the flanges, which have almost all the area at the edge, lie \(95\) mm from the axis and each contributes \(9{,}03 \cdot 10^6\) mm\(^4\), while the web, which has \(35\ \%\) of the area, contributes only \(14\ \%\) of the total.

For a circle the computation over rectangles is not possible, because it is not a figure made of rectangles, and its integral has a form that we know how to compute only in polar coordinates. We therefore take the value from a source and postpone the proof to chapter 16. A circle of radius \(R\) has, by ONATE2 (Fig. 1.3, PDF p. 35), the area \(A = \pi R^2\) and \(I = \pi R^4/4\), which for the diameter \(d = 2R\) equals \(I = \pi d^4/64\). A circle of diameter \(d = 32\) mm has the area \(804\) mm\(^2\), almost the same as our bar, and \(I = \pi \cdot 32^4/64 = 51\,472\) mm\(^4\). This is less than half of \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 106\,667\) mm\(^4\) of the bar standing on its edge, because the bar has more material far from the axis.

5.4.4 Principal axes of a cross section

Cross sections with an axis of symmetry \(y\) or \(z\) have \(I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) (lemma 5.24 with \(g(y) = y\), as in item 5 of the proof of lemma 5.27). For a cross section without an axis of symmetry, for example the letter L, we do not know in advance how the second moments change if we turn the axes. We will need this for a beam that bends in the planes \(x\)–\(y\) and \(x\)–\(z\) at the same time (later in this chapter). What happens to the three numbers \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}\) if we turn the axes around the centroid by an angle \(\varphi\)?

We leave the axis \(x\) and turn the axes \(y\) and \(z\) around it by the angle \(\varphi\) in the direction from \(y\) toward \(z\), which is a turn in the positive direction about the axis \(x\). Let \(\bar y\) and \(\bar z\) be the coordinates about the turned axes with unit vectors that have in the old axes the components \((c, s)\) and \((-s, c)\), where \(c = \cos\varphi\) and \(s = \sin\varphi\). As in definition 2.37, these are the rows of the rotation matrix, except that the axes \(y\) and \(z\) take the roles of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) of the definition. A point with the coordinates \((y, z)\) has in the new axes the coordinates

\[\bar y = c\,y + s\,z , \qquad \bar z = -s\,y + c\,z .\]

By theorem 2.42 the components of stress in the plane transform in this way. The second moments \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are integrals of the squares and the product of the coordinates, and in the next theorem we show by computation that they change by the same rule as the stresses.

Theorem 5.30 Rotation of the axes of a cross section (vrtenje osi prereza)

Let the figure \(L\) made of rectangles with the origin in the centroid have the second moments \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}\). About the axes turned by the angle \(\varphi\) the second moments are

\[\begin{aligned} \bar I_{\mathrm{z}} &= c^2\,I_{\mathrm{z}} + s^2\,I_{\mathrm{y}} + 2cs\,I_{\mathrm{yz}} , \\ \bar I_{\mathrm{y}} &= s^2\,I_{\mathrm{z}} + c^2\,I_{\mathrm{y}} - 2cs\,I_{\mathrm{yz}} , \\ \bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} &= -cs\,I_{\mathrm{z}} + cs\,I_{\mathrm{y}} + (c^2 - s^2)\,I_{\mathrm{yz}} . \end{aligned} \tag{5.20}\]

The sum \(\bar I_{\mathrm{z}} + \bar I_{\mathrm{y}} = I_{\mathrm{z}} + I_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on the angle.

Proof

We must show three integrals and a sum. We obtain each by writing the coordinates with the new ones and splitting the integral by linearity (item 3 of lemma 5.18).

  1. \(\bar I_{\mathrm{z}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} (c\,y + s\,z)^2\,\mathrm{d}A = c^2 \int_{\mathrm{L}} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A + 2cs \int_{\mathrm{L}} y\,z\,\mathrm{d}A + s^2 \int_{\mathrm{L}} z^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) equals \(c^2 I_{\mathrm{z}} + 2cs\,I_{\mathrm{yz}} + s^2 I_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  2. \(\bar I_{\mathrm{y}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} (-s\,y + c\,z)^2\,\mathrm{d}A = s^2 I_{\mathrm{z}} - 2cs\,I_{\mathrm{yz}} + c^2 I_{\mathrm{y}}\), the same computation with the sign \(-\) at the middle term.
  3. \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = \int_{\mathrm{L}} (c\,y + s\,z)(-s\,y + c\,z)\,\mathrm{d}A\). The expansion of the product is \(-cs\,y^2 + c^2\,y z - s^2\,y z + cs\,z^2\), so \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = -cs\,I_{\mathrm{z}} + (c^2 - s^2)\,I_{\mathrm{yz}} + cs\,I_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  4. The sum of the first two equations is \((c^2 + s^2)(I_{\mathrm{z}} + I_{\mathrm{y}}) = I_{\mathrm{z}} + I_{\mathrm{y}}\), because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) and the terms with \(2cs\,I_{\mathrm{yz}}\) cancel.

Source: Our sources have no formula for the transformation of second moments. The computation is the same as for the transformation of stress in chapter 2, the proof is ours.

Equations (5.20) have the same form as the first three equations of (2.45) for stresses, with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \to I_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} \to I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \to I_{\mathrm{yz}}\). The matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} I_{\mathrm{z}} & I_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ I_{\mathrm{yz}} & I_{\mathrm{y}} \end{pmatrix}\) is therefore here what the matrix of stress in the plane is. It is symmetric and transforms like the matrix of stress, so the angle we look for is the one at which this matrix is diagonal, that is, \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). Theorem 2.61 on principal directions holds for matrices with three rows, so we show the existence of the angle here directly with the intermediate value theorem, which is shorter than embedding the \(2 \times 2\) matrix in a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and showing that both principal directions lie in the plane of the cross section.

Corollary 5.31 Principal axes of a cross section (glavne osi prereza)

For every figure made of rectangles with the origin in the centroid there is an angle \(\varphi\) between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) at which \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). The axes that belong to this angle are called the principal axes (glavni osi) of the cross section, and the numbers \(\bar I_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\bar I_{\mathrm{y}}\) the principal second moments. If the figure is symmetric about the axis \(y\) or about the axis \(z\), the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are principal axes.

Proof

We must show that the function \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}}(\varphi)\) has a zero. We use the intermediate value theorem.

  1. By equation (5.20) with double angles, \(2cs = \sin 2\varphi\) and \(c^2 - s^2 = \cos 2\varphi\), \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}}(\varphi) = \tfrac12 (I_{\mathrm{y}} - I_{\mathrm{z}})\sin 2\varphi + I_{\mathrm{yz}}\cos 2\varphi\). This is a continuous function of the angle.
  2. At \(\varphi = 0\) the value is \(I_{\mathrm{yz}}\), at \(\varphi = 90^\circ\) it is \(-I_{\mathrm{yz}}\). If \(I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), the axes are already principal. Otherwise the values have opposite signs, and by the intermediate value theorem 2.57 there is an angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) at which \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\).
  3. If the figure is symmetric about the axis \(y\), then \(I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) by lemma 5.24 with \(g(y) = y\), and for symmetry about the axis \(z\) with the roles of the coordinates exchanged. The axes \(y\) and \(z\) are therefore principal, as for \(\varphi = 0\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. Theorem 2.61 holds for \(3 \times 3\) matrices, so this proof replaces it for a \(2 \times 2\) matrix by the intermediate value theorem.

Let us look at what the principal axes look like for a cross section without symmetry, on the letter L.

Example 5.32 Principal axes of an L-section (glavne osi prereza L)

The L-section has a vertical leg \(10 \times 60\) mm (\(z\) from 0 to 10, \(y\) from 0 to 60) and a horizontal leg \(30 \times 10\) mm (\(z\) from 10 to 40, \(y\) from 0 to 10), together the area \(A = 600 + 300 = 900\) mm\(^2\) (figure 5.31).

  1. By lemma 5.23 \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = (600 \cdot 30 + 300 \cdot 5)/900 = 65/3 = 21{,}67\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{T}} = (600 \cdot 5 + 300 \cdot 25)/900 = 35/3 = 11{,}67\) mm.
  2. The centroid of the vertical leg has, with respect to the centroid of the cross section, the coordinates \((d_{\mathrm{y}}, d_{\mathrm{z}}) = (25/3, -20/3)\) mm, and the centroid of the horizontal leg \((-50/3, 40/3)\) mm (the differences \(30 - 65/3\), \(5 - 35/3\) and \(5 - 65/3\), \(25 - 35/3\)). The own second moments by lemma 5.27 are \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 10 \cdot 60^3/12 = 180\,000\) mm\(^4\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = 60 \cdot 10^3/12 = 5000\) mm\(^4\) for the vertical one, and \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 30 \cdot 10^3/12 = 2500\) mm\(^4\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = 10 \cdot 30^3/12 = 22\,500\) mm\(^4\) for the horizontal one, the own products of inertia are zero.
  3. By theorem 5.28 \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = (180\,000 + 600 \cdot (25/3)^2) + (2500 + 300 \cdot (50/3)^2) = 221\,667 + 85\,833 = 307\,500\) mm\(^4\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = (5000 + 600 \cdot (20/3)^2) + (22\,500 + 300 \cdot (40/3)^2) = 31\,667 + 75\,833 = 107\,500\) mm\(^4\) and \(I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 600 \cdot \tfrac{25}{3} \cdot (-\tfrac{20}{3}) + 300 \cdot (-\tfrac{50}{3}) \cdot \tfrac{40}{3} = -33\,333 - 66\,667 = -100\,000\) mm\(^4\).
  4. The product of inertia is not zero, because the figure has no axis of symmetry. The condition \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) is by step 1 of the proof of corollary 5.31 equivalent to \(\tan 2\varphi = 2 I_{\mathrm{yz}}/(I_{\mathrm{z}} - I_{\mathrm{y}})\) for \(\cos 2\varphi \ne 0\), which is \(-200\,000/200\,000 = -1\), so \(2\varphi = 135^\circ\) and \(\varphi = 67{,}5^\circ\).
  5. At this angle \(c^2 = 0{,}1464\), \(s^2 = 0{,}8536\) and \(2cs = \sin 135^\circ = 0{,}7071\), \(c^2 - s^2 = -0{,}7071\). By theorem 5.30 \(\bar I_{\mathrm{z}} = 0{,}1464 \cdot 307\,500 + 0{,}8536 \cdot 107\,500 + 0{,}7071 \cdot (-100\,000) = 66\,079\) mm\(^4\), \(\bar I_{\mathrm{y}} = 348\,921\) mm\(^4\) and \(\bar I_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) (up to rounding). The sum \(66\,079 + 348\,921 = 415\,000 = 307\,500 + 107\,500\) mm\(^4\), as the theorem requires.
  6. The principal second moments are also the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} I_{\mathrm{z}} & I_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ I_{\mathrm{yz}} & I_{\mathrm{y}} \end{pmatrix}\) (definition 2.59): the zeros of the determinant \((I_{\mathrm{z}} - \lambda)(I_{\mathrm{y}} - \lambda) - I_{\mathrm{yz}}^2 = (307\,500 - \lambda)(107\,500 - \lambda) - 10^{10}\) are \(\lambda = 207\,500 \pm 100\,000\sqrt2\ \text{mm}^4\), which is \(66\,079\) and \(348\,921\) mm\(^4\), the same as in step 5.

We will need the principal axes of a cross section for bending in two planes. For cross sections with an axis of symmetry, such as the rectangle and the I-section, nothing needs to be turned, because this axis is already principal.

5.5 Stress and stiffness in bending

We now have two parts of the beam. From equilibrium we know the internal forces in every cross section, the axial force \(N\), the shear force \(V\) and the bending moment \(M\) (section 5.2). From kinematics we know the strain, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = u' - y\,v''\) (theorem 5.15), where \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\) are the displacements of the points of the axis. The link between them is missing. How large is the stress in the fibre at height \(y\) above the axis, and how are \(N\) and \(M\) related to the displacements \(u\) and \(v\)? We need the answer because we shall compute the deflection of the beam from \(M(x)\), and from the same stress check whether the steel carries the load. All calculations will be done on the beams of section 5.1.3, a flat steel bar of width \(b = 20\) mm and height \(h = 40\) mm, standing on its edge.

The path is short. From the strain and Hooke's law we get the stress, where we must say what we assume about the other stress components. We then add the stress over the cross section, as lemma 5.9 and corollary 5.19 say, and obtain \(N\) and \(M\) in terms of the displacements. This shows where in the cross section the axis must be placed. Finally we invert the relation and compute the stress from \(N\) and \(M\). The addendum at the end of the section shows what changes if the beam is heated unevenly.

5.5.1 From strain to stress

The question is how large the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is in the fibre (definition 1.24) that lies along the axis \(x\) at height \(y\). Hooke's law for an isotropic material (theorem 3.11) links the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) with all three normal strains at once. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) we would therefore need \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) as well as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), or else the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). What do we know about them?

The beam is thin. The upper and lower faces are free, except where the distributed load \(q\) acts on the upper one, and the side faces are entirely free. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is therefore zero on the lower face, on the upper face by the condition on that face it equals the pressure of the load, and in between it takes values between the two. Let us check how large it is. The simply supported beam of section 5.1.3 carries \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m over a width \(b = 20\) mm, which is a pressure \(q_0/b = 50\) kPa. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in the same beam will reach \(93{,}75\) MPa (we compute it later in this section), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is at most \(0{,}05\,\%\) of that value. The same holds for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), since the side faces are free. The cross section \(20 \times 40\) mm is not a state of plane stress, so this is only an approximation. The elastic calculation shows how good it is. For a beam under a uniform load, SADD (PDF p. 175, plane stress) finds that the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at the outer fibres differs from the elementary value by \(w/5\), where \(w\) is the pressure of the load on the upper face, whatever the dimensions of the beam. For our beam this gives a difference \(w/5 = 10\) kPa, which is \(0{,}011\,\%\) of the largest stress.

We therefore take a step which we call assumption 6 (the numbers of the assumptions are the same as in the table that collects them at the end of the chapter): in each fibre the stress is uniaxial, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). The shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) does not follow from Hooke's law, as we shall see below, but from equilibrium (in the next section). For the normal stress of a fibre, however, what we learned in the tensile test holds. The fibre is in the same state as the bar of the test, in which the only nonzero stress component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so by lemma 3.6 on uniaxial stress we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (equation (3.6)). The material is here linearly elastic, homogeneous and isotropic (definitions 3.3, 3.5, 3.4) and the stresses are below the yield strength (definition 2.7). This is assumption 7. With the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = u' - y\,v''\) from theorem 5.15 we obtain

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, y) = E\,\big(u'(x) - y\,v''(x)\big) . \tag{5.21}\]

The stress is a linear function of the height \(y\). The meaning of the two terms is the same as for the strain. The term \(E\,u'\) is a stress that stretches all fibres of the cross section equally, and the term \(-E\,y\,v''\) is proportional to the height and therefore stretches one side of the cross section and shortens the other (figure 5.32). For \(v'' < 0\), as at the clamp of a cantilever, the upper fibre is stretched and the lower compressed, for \(v'' > 0\) it is the other way round.

Let us test this on the cantilever of section 5.1.3. Later in this section we shall derive that its curvature at the clamp is \(v''(0) = -0{,}02392\) 1/m (radius of curvature \(41{,}8\) m). At the clamp we therefore have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -y\,v''(0)\) equal to \(+4{,}78\cdot 10^{-4}\) at the top of the cross section (\(y = 20\) mm) and \(-4{,}78\cdot 10^{-4}\) at the bottom. By equation (5.21) with \(E = 196\) GPa the stress is \(\pm 93{,}75\) MPa, \(43\,\%\) of the yield strength \(220\) MPa.

Assumption 6 has a cost that we must state. Assumption 4 of section 5.3.2 says that the fibres on a normal keep their length, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). By lemma 3.6, however, a fibre in uniaxial stress has the transverse strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\), which is not zero if \(\nu \neq 0\). Both statements hold together only for \(\nu = 0\). The model is therefore not entirely consistent and stays so in every book that uses it. CM (PDF p. 309) writes explicitly in the derivation that in the relation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\mu + \lambda)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) he took \(\nu = 0\), but not in the relation \(2\mu = 2G = E/(1 + \nu)\). What would happen if, instead of assumption 6, we kept \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\)? Hooke's law (theorem 3.11) would give \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,(1 - \nu)/\big((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\big)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), for \(\nu = 0{,}3\) this factor is \(1{,}346\) and the stress would be \(35\,\%\) larger. That would hold only if someone prevented the cross section from changing its shape. The side faces are free, so the fibre contracts transversally when it is stretched, as in the tensile test. The upper fibre at the clamp of the cantilever stretches along its length by \(4{,}78\cdot 10^{-4}\) and contracts transversally by \(\nu \cdot 4{,}78\cdot 10^{-4} = 1{,}43\cdot 10^{-4}\) of its width, which for a width of \(20\) mm is \(2{,}9\) µm. This is unimportant for the displacements we compute, so we neglect the transverse strains. The stress of the fibre is therefore taken from the uniaxial state (assumption 6), and the displacements from the kinematics of the beam. That the model works well in spite of this inconsistency is already shown by the comparison with the elastic solution above: for a slender beam the difference in stress is \(0{,}011\,\%\).

One more contradiction. By Hooke's law \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), so the shear force \(V = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,dA\) would have nothing to arise from. At the same time, by the equilibrium of a piece of the beam (corollary 5.11), \(V = -M'\) is not zero if the moment changes. This is an inconsistency which EP (p. 74) and CM (PDF p. 309) call a flaw of the Euler-Bernoulli model. Both books resolve it in the same way: they do not compute the shear stress from Hooke's law but from equilibrium, and the shear force from \(V = -M'\). We shall do the same in the next section. For now we are interested only in the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\).

5.5.2 Neutral axis

From history

In calculating the breaking force Mariotte took the same point of rotation of the cross section as Galileo, at the edge of the cross section (TIMO, PDF p. 31). We met Coulomb and his memoir of 1773 in section 1.1. As a member of the military engineering corps he spent nine years in charge of construction works on the island of Martinique, which led him to the mechanical properties of materials, and his memoir also covered bending (TIMO, PDF p. 55). He first tested sandstone. The strength in shear was equal to the strength in tension, and bars for bending, 1 inch deep, 2 inches wide and 9 inches long, broke at a force of 20 pounds (TIMO, PDF p. 56-57).

In his theory he considered a rectangular cantilever and its cross section, and concluded that the fibres of the upper part of the cross section are in tension and those of the lower part are compressed (TIMO, PDF p. 57). He resolved the forces in the fibres into a horizontal and a vertical component and wrote three equations of statics: the sum of the horizontal forces across the cross section is zero, the sum of the vertical forces equals the applied load, and the moment of all fibre forces about a chosen axis equals the moment of the load about the same axis (TIMO, PDF p. 57-58). He noticed that these equations do not depend on how the forces in the fibres depend on the elongations (TIMO, PDF p. 58). He could therefore use them for a material that follows Hooke's law up to fracture and for a perfectly rigid material. For the first he obtained the equation \(S h/6 = Q l\), where \(S\) is the strength of the bar in tension, \(h\) its depth, \(l\) the arm of the force \(Q\) and \(Q\) the breaking force (TIMO, PDF p. 58). For a perfectly rigid material with uniformly distributed forces he obtained \(S h/2 = Q l\) (TIMO, PDF p. 58). The breaking force calculated from this equation was somewhat larger than the measured one, so he concluded that the point of rotation cannot lie at the edge but inside the cross section, where part of the cross section is in compression (TIMO, PDF p. 58). Coulomb applied statics correctly and had a clear picture of the distribution of forces over the cross section (TIMO, PDF p. 58). Engineers understood his results only after more than forty years (TIMO, PDF p. 78).

After the death of his uncle Gauthey in 1807, Navier edited and published the three volumes of his unfinished work on bridges and canals, the second volume in 1813 (TIMO, PDF p. 79). In a note on page 18 of the second volume he gave the complete theory of bending of prismatic bars (TIMO, PDF p. 79). He did not know Coulomb's work. He thought, as Mariotte and Jacob Bernoulli had done, that the position of the line in the cross section where the fibres neither lengthen nor shorten does not matter, and for that line he took the tangent to the edge of the cross section on the concave side (TIMO, PDF p. 79). In the first printed edition of his book on the strength of materials in 1826 he assumed that the bar bends in the plane in which the forces act, so his calculation holds only for beams with a plane of symmetry loaded in that plane, and that the cross sections remain plane during bending (TIMO, PDF p. 81-82). With the three equations of statics he concluded that this line passes through the centroid of the cross section (TIMO, PDF p. 82). We see the reason from the first equation. The force in a fibre is proportional to its distance from the line, and in bending without an axial force the sum of all longitudinal forces across the cross section must be zero. This holds exactly when the line passes through the centroid, since the centroid is the point about which the contributions of area on both sides balance.

Let us return to the question of the section: where in the cross section lie the fibres that neither lengthen nor shorten in bending, and how large is the stress elsewhere.

So far we have left open where in the cross section the axis of the beam lies, the line from which we measure the height \(y\) and on which the displacements \(u\) and \(v\) are defined. Up to now we took cross sections with a symmetry, where it lies at mid-height. But what if the cross section is not symmetric, like the letter T? Let us see what happens if we choose the axis anywhere. Let \(y\) be measured from some line in the cross section, let \(S = \int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,dA\) be the first moment of area (statični moment prereza) about it (definition 5.20), and \(I_0 = \int_{\mathrm{A}} y^2\,dA\) the second moment of area about it. If we insert the stress (5.21) in \(N\) and \(M\) of lemma 5.9, we get \(N = E\,(A\,u' - S\,v'')\) and \(M = E\,(I_0\,v'' - S\,u')\). For \(S \neq 0\) the axial and bending deformations are coupled. An axial force would also bend the beam, and a moment would stretch it. For \(S = 0\) they separate. By the definition of the centroid (definition 5.21) and by the first step of the proof of lemma 5.22, the first moment about a line at height \(c\) above the original origin equals \(S_{\mathrm{z}} - cA = A\,(y_{\mathrm{T}} - c)\), that is the area times the distance of the centroid from the line. This is zero exactly when \(c = y_{\mathrm{T}}\), so when the line passes through the centroid. Therefore \(S = 0\) exactly when the line passes through the centroid, and we place the axis of the beam through the centroids of the cross sections (assumption 8). With this we complete definition 5.1, which placed the axis at mid-height for cross sections with symmetry: there mid-height is exactly the centroid.

Lemma 5.33 Separation of axial and bending parts (osna in upogibna togost se ločita)
