Let a beam be made of a linearly elastic, homogeneous, isotropic material with modulus of elasticity \(E\), let the stress in the fibres satisfy equation (5.21) (assumption 6) and let \(y\) be the height above a line \(\ell\) in a cross section of area \(A\) which is a rectangle or a union of rectangles. Let \(S = \int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,dA\) and \(I_0 = \int_{\mathrm{A}} y^2\,dA\). Then

\[N = E\,\big(A\,u' - S\,v''\big) , \qquad M = E\,\big(I_0\,v'' - S\,u'\big) . \tag{5.22}\]

If \(\ell\) passes through the centroid of the cross section, then \(S = 0\), \(I_0 = I\) is the second moment of area of the cross section (definition 5.26) and

\[N = EA\,u' , \qquad M = EI\,v'' . \tag{5.23}\]
Proof

We insert the stress (5.21) in the expressions for \(N\) and \(M\) of lemma 5.9 and corollary 5.19 and compute the integrals over the cross section.

  1. By lemma 5.9 for a rectangular cross section and by corollary 5.19 for a union of rectangles, \(N = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,dA\) and \(M = -\int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,dA\). For \(y\) measured from \(\ell\), \(M\) is the moment about \(\ell\).
  2. By equation (5.21), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,(u' - y\,v'')\). On a cross section at fixed \(x\) the quantities \(u'\) and \(v''\) are constants, since they are functions of \(x\) only, and \(E\) is constant by homogeneity. Hence by linearity of the integral over the cross section (section 5.4.1) we can take them out.
  3. The first integral is \(N = E\,u' \int_{\mathrm{A}} dA - E\,v'' \int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,dA = E\,(A\,u' - S\,v'')\).
  4. The second integral is \(M = -E\,u' \int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,dA + E\,v'' \int_{\mathrm{A}} y^2\,dA = E\,(I_0\,v'' - S\,u')\).
  5. If \(\ell\) passes through the centroid, then by lemma 5.22 the first moment is \(S = 0\). The integral \(\int_{\mathrm{A}} y^2\,dA\) is by definition 5.26 the second moment of area \(I\), since \(\ell\) is an axis through the centroid. With this the equations (5.23) are proved.

Source: EP (2.5.8) to (2.5.11) (pp. 74-75, there \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(D_{\mathrm{xx}}\) for an \(E\) that varies over the cross section). The sign of \(M\) is opposite to that of EP by D1. CM (PDF p. 310, before (7.3.30)).

What does the theorem say if the modulus of elasticity is not constant over the cross section? Then the integrals acquire weights, \(A_{\mathrm{xx}} = \int E\,dA\), \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} = \int y\,E\,dA\) and \(D_{\mathrm{xx}} = \int y^2 E\,dA\) (EP, (2.5.9), p. 74), and the centroid must be computed with the weight \(E\). This is the case of composite beams of several materials, for example a bimetallic strip. We stay with one material.

Now we can name the line where the stress vanishes.

Definition 5.34 Neutral axis (nevtralna os)

The neutral axis of a cross section of the beam at \(x\) is the set of points of the cross section at which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\). If \(v''(x) \neq 0\), it is the line at height \(y_{\mathrm{n}} = u'/v''\), parallel to the axis \(z\).

Source: SADD (PDF p. 577) calls the neutral axis (nevtralna os) the axis through the centroid on which the stress in bending is zero. The general form with \(y_{\mathrm{n}} = u'/v''\) is derived here.

We get the height \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) from equation (5.21), \(E\,(u' - y\,v'') = 0\). If the axis passes through the centroid and \(N = 0\), then by lemma 5.33 \(u' = N/(EA) = 0\) and \(y_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\): the neutral axis is the axis of the beam itself, the line through the centroids. This happens for the beams of section 5.1.3, since \(N = 0\) for them. If \(N \neq 0\), then by the lemma \(u' = N/(EA)\) and \(v'' = M/(EI)\), so \(y_{\mathrm{n}} = N\,I/(A\,M)\) and the neutral axis is no longer on the axis: it moves towards the side that the moment compresses.

For a cross section with a symmetry the centroid is at mid-height, so the neutral axis is at mid-height. For the letter T it is not. Take the T-section of example 5.25: web \(20 \times 60\) mm, flange \(80 \times 20\) mm on top, \(80\) mm high in all, area \(A = 2800\) mm². The centroid was computed there as the average of the centroids of the two rectangles weighted by area (lemma 5.23). It is at \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = 370/7 = 52{,}86\) mm from the bottom edge and \(27{,}14\) mm from the top edge, so not at mid-height (\(40\) mm). The second moment of area about the centroidal axis is by theorem 5.28 the sum of the contributions of the two rectangles, each being its own moment (lemma 5.27) plus \(A\,d^2\) for the distance \(d\) of its centroid from the centroid of the cross section:

\[I = \frac{20 \cdot 60^3}{12} + 1200\,\big(52{,}86 - 30\big)^2 + \frac{80 \cdot 20^3}{12} + 1600\,\big(70 - 52{,}86\big)^2 = 1{,}510\cdot 10^{6}\ \text{mm}^4 .\]

Let \(N = 0\) and \(M = 500\) N m, as in the largest cross sections of all three beams of section 5.1.3. By the lemma \(u' = 0\) and \(v'' = M/(EI)\), so by (5.21) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -M\,y/I\) with the height \(y\) above the centroid. At the top (\(y = 27{,}14\) mm) it is \(-9{,}0\) MPa, compression, at the bottom (\(y = -52{,}86\) mm) \(+17{,}5\) MPa, tension. At mid-height (\(y = 40 - 52{,}86 = -12{,}86\) mm) the stress is \(+4{,}3\) MPa and not zero (figure 5.33). The bottom, which is farther from the centroid, has a \(1{,}95\) times larger stress than the top, because the stress is proportional to the distance from the neutral axis and the ratio of the distances is \(52{,}86 : 27{,}14 = 1{,}95\).

5.5.3 Bending moment and curvature

From history

Galileo and Mariotte investigated the strength of beams, not their deflection (TIMO, PDF p. 34). Toward the end of the seventeenth century the calculus with infinitely small quantities was developing fast. Jacob Bernoulli (1654 to 1705) and his brother sought applications for it in examples from mechanics and physics (TIMO, PDF p. 33). One of these examples was the shape into which an elastic bar bends (TIMO, PDF p. 33-34).

Jacob Bernoulli followed Mariotte in the position of the axis of rotation of the cross section and took a cantilever of rectangular cross section with depth \(h\) and width \(b\), loaded by \(P\) at the free end (TIMO, PDF p. 34). The cross section turns about the axis \(A\), and the elongation of the fibres between two neighbouring cross sections is proportional to the distance from \(A\). By Hooke's law the resultant of the forces in the fibres of the cross section equals \(\tfrac12 m\,\Delta\,\mathrm{d}s\,b h/\mathrm{d}s\), where \(\mathrm{d}s\) is the length of a small piece of the bar, \(\Delta\,\mathrm{d}s\) the elongation of the farthest fibre and \(m\) a constant depending on the material (TIMO, PDF p. 34). Its moment about \(A\) must equal the moment \(P x\) of the load about the same axis (TIMO, PDF p. 34). Since the ratio of the fibre elongation to the length \(\mathrm{d}s\) equals \(h\) divided by the radius of curvature \(r\) of the bar, he obtained an equation of the form \(P x = C/r\), where \(C = m b h^3/3\) is a constant determined by the material and the cross section (TIMO, PDF p. 35). Because of the wrong position of the axis of rotation, its expression was wrong. The general form is correct, however: the curvature of the bent bar at each point is proportional to the bending moment at that point (TIMO, PDF p. 35).

Euler accepted this statement of Bernoulli without discussion (TIMO, PDF p. 38-39). He called the constant \(C\) the absolute elasticity. He did not explain its physical meaning, only wrote that it depends on the properties of the material and that for rectangular bars it is proportional to the width and to the square of the depth (TIMO, PDF p. 40). That square was a mistake, since \(C\) is proportional to the third power of the depth, as Bernoulli's expression shows (TIMO, PDF p. 40-41). Navier reached the same relation differently in his book of 1826. From plane cross sections and statics he derived that the curvature equals the moment divided by the product of the modulus \(E\) (the ratio of the load per unit of cross-sectional area to the elongation per unit of length) and the second moment of area \(I\) of the cross section about the line without elongation (TIMO, PDF p. 82). For small deflections he wrote it as \(E I\,\mathrm{d}^2 y/\mathrm{d}x^2 = M\) (TIMO, PDF p. 83). What Bernoulli and Euler wrote with the constant \(C\) is the product \(E I\) in Navier, and in him each part of the constant got its meaning: \(E\) describes the material, \(I\) the cross section.

Let us return to the question of the section: how the moment and the stress in a beam are connected with bending, that is, with the curvature of its axis. Navier's equation is the answer that we shall now derive from our assumptions.

Lemma 5.33 says what happens when the stress is known. Let us turn the question round: for known \(N\) and \(M\) from equilibrium, what is the stress? We solve both equations (5.23) for \(u'\) and \(v''\) and insert into (5.21). Let us state the result as a theorem.

Theorem 5.35 Stress and deformation in bending (napetost in deformacija pri upogibu)

Let a beam have its axis through the centroids of the cross sections, let the displacements satisfy theorem 5.15, let the fibres be in uniaxial stress (assumption 6) and let the material be linearly elastic, homogeneous and isotropic with modulus of elasticity \(E\). Let \(A\) be the area and \(I\) the second moment of area of the cross section about the axis \(z\) through the centroid, and \(N\) and \(M\) the internal force and moment of definition 2.5, lemma 5.9 and corollary 5.19. Then

\[N = EA\,u' , \qquad M = EI\,v'' , \tag{5.24}\]

and the stress in the cross section at \(x\) at height \(y\) above the axis is

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{N}{A} - \frac{M\,y}{I} . \tag{5.25}\]
Proof

The relations (5.24) are proved by lemma 5.33, then we invert them and insert into the stress.

  1. By lemma 5.33, for an axis through the centroid \(N = EA\,u'\) and \(M = EI\,v''\). These are the equations (5.24).
  2. The area \(A\) is positive. The second moment of area \(I = \int_{\mathrm{A}} y^2\,dA\) is the integral of a function that is nonnegative and zero only on the line \(y = 0\) of area zero, so \(I > 0\). Also \(E > 0\). Hence we may divide and get \(u' = N/(EA)\) and \(v'' = M/(EI)\).
  3. We insert into the stress (5.21): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\big(N/(EA) - y\,M/(EI)\big) = N/A - M\,y/I\).

Source: EP (2.5.12), (2.5.15), (2.5.16) (pp. 74-75, in EP \(M_{\text{EP}} = \int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,dA = -M\) and \(z\) is our \(y\), so \(M\) in (2.5.12) and (2.5.16) has the opposite sign to that in (5.24) and (5.25)), SADD (D.6) to (D.8) (PDF pp. 577-578, \(M_{\text{SADD}} = M\), \(\sigma = -My/I\) and \(d^2v/dx^2 = M/(EI)\) for \(v\) upward), ONATE2 (1.5) (PDF p. 34, \(M = EI\,d^2w/dx^2\), the same sign as ours), CM (7.3.30), (7.3.31) (PDF p. 310, \(M_{\text{CM}} = -M\)). The translation of signs between the sources was checked with SymPy from our definitions.

The theorem says two things. First, \(M = EI\,v''\) means that the moment is proportional to the curvature \(\kappa = v''\) (definition 5.16), with the property of the cross section and the material \(EI\) as the coefficient. Second, the stress is the sum of a uniform part \(N/A\) and a part that is linear in \(y\) and proportional to \(M\).

Definition 5.36 Axial and bending stiffness (osna in upogibna togost)

The product \(EA\) of the modulus of elasticity and the area of the cross section is the axial stiffness of the beam, and the product \(EI\) of the modulus of elasticity and the second moment of area of the cross section about the axis \(z\) through the centroid is the bending stiffness. Their units are N and N m².

Source: EP (2.5.9), (2.5.10) (p. 74, there \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(D_{\mathrm{xx}}\)), CM (PDF p. 310). The names axial and bending stiffness were promised by section 3.7 of chapter 3.

Why do we call \(EI\) a stiffness? From \(M = EI\,v''\) we have \(EI = M/v''\): this is the moment that we need for a unit of curvature. Take the beam of section 5.1.3, where \(E = 196\) GPa and \(I = bh^3/12 = 1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\) m⁴. We get \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m². A curvature of \(1\) 1/m, that is a circular arc of radius \(1\) m, would need a moment of \(20\,907\) N m. The curvature at the clamp of the cantilever, \(0{,}0239\) 1/m, corresponds to a moment of \(500\) N m. The axial stiffness \(EA = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N is the force that would stretch the bar by \(100\,\%\) (\(\varepsilon = 1\)), if the material could bear it. For \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\) the force is \(156{,}8\) kN. Why \(I\) is decisive is shown by \(h^3\) in \(I = bh^3/12\) (lemma 5.27): if we double the height, \(EI\) grows eightfold, while \(EA\) grows only twofold for the same use of material.

Let us test the theorem on both beams of section 5.1.3. For the cantilever, clamped at \(x = 0\), with a force of \(500\) N downward at the end \(x = L = 1\) m, by section 5.2.2 we have \(N = 0\) and \(M(x) = -F\,(L - x)\), so at the clamp \(M(0) = -500\) N m. The curvature at the clamp is \(v''(0) = M(0)/(EI) = -500/20\,906{,}7 = -0{,}02392\) 1/m, the radius of curvature \(41{,}8\) m. The stress at the top of the cross section (\(y = h/2 = 20\) mm) by (5.25) is

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\frac{M\,y}{I} = \frac{500\ \text{N m} \cdot 0{,}020\ \text{m}}{1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4} = 93{,}75\ \text{MPa} ,\]

tension, and at the bottom it is \(-93{,}75\) MPa, compression (figure 5.34). This is \(43\,\%\) of the yield strength, so we are in the region where linear elasticity holds. The tension is at the top because at the clamp \(v'' < 0\) and the upper fibres stretch (figure 5.32). For the simply supported beam with the uniform load \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m the largest moment at mid-span is \(M = +500\) N m, equal in magnitude, but the stress has the opposite sign: on the upper side it is \(-93{,}75\) MPa, compression, and on the lower \(+93{,}75\) MPa, tension. The same number is no coincidence. For all three beams we chose the load so that the largest moment is the same (section 5.2.2), and by the theorem the stress depends only on the moment and the cross section.

What does \(M = EI\,v''\) mean on a piece of the beam? Figure 5.35 shows a piece of the beam with moments on both faces. The moment on the right face is the moment that the part of the beam to the right of it exerts on the piece, that is the moment of the stresses on the face with outward normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) (lemma 5.9), and on the left face it is equal and opposite. When \(M > 0\), the beam bends as the figure shows: \(v'' > 0\), the fibres at the bottom are stretched and at the top compressed. If we reverse the moment, the curvature reverses.

Why is the cross section in the shape of the letter I so popular? Take the cross section of section 5.4.3: height \(200\) mm, flanges \(100 \times 10\) mm, web \(180 \times 6\) mm, \(A = 3080\) mm², \(I = 2{,}098\cdot 10^{7}\) mm⁴. The same moment \(500\) N m gives at the outer edge by (5.25) the stress \(500 \cdot 0{,}100/(2{,}098\cdot 10^{-5}) = 2{,}38\) MPa, at the junction of web and flange \(2{,}14\) MPa. A rectangle of the same area, \(20 \times 154\) mm, would have \(I = 6{,}087\cdot 10^{6}\) mm⁴, so \(3{,}45\) times less, and a stress of \(6{,}32\) MPa. Material far from the axis carries the most moment, because \(y^2\) grows with distance, so the I-section is \(3{,}45\) times stiffer for the same area (figure 5.36).

We proved the theorem from the model. Is the model really accurate for bending? Let us check it for pure bending (section 5.3.1), where the argument from symmetry showed that the cross sections stay plane. The exact elastic solution for pure bending of a straight beam with a rectangular cross section (SADD, Example 8.2, PDF pp. 171-172, plane stress) gives a stress that equals the elementary one, and a displacement of the axis that is also equal (SADD (8.1.22), (8.1.23)). In pure bending the elementary stress (5.25) is therefore exact. The difference between the model and the elastic solution appears only under shear loading, which the next section treats.

5.5.4 Temperature and bending

For the uniaxial state we have already seen that a freely heated piece stretches without stress (theorem 3.15). A beam, however, can be heated unevenly: for example, if the sun heats the upper flange of a bridge beam and the lower one stays in the shade. What happens then?

Hooke's law with temperature, in the uniaxial form, for a fibre in which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) (assumption 6), is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E + \alpha\,\Delta T\), where \(\alpha\) is the coefficient of thermal expansion (first row of equation (3.16)). EP (2.4.19), p. 70, writes the same relation in general form with the stiffness matrix. Let us denote the change of temperature by \(\theta(x, y)\) and assume that it is linear over the height, \(\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{m}}(x) + g(x)\,y\), where \(\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\) is the change of temperature on the axis and \(g\) the temperature gradient over the height, in K/m. A linear one is the simplest distribution with a gradient. How the temperature is really distributed over a body is treated by chapter 14.

Theorem 5.37 Bending caused by temperature (upogib zaradi temperature)

Let the assumptions of theorem 5.35 hold for the beam, let \(E\) and \(\alpha\) not depend on temperature and let the change of temperature be \(\theta(x, y) = \theta_{\mathrm{m}}(x) + g(x)\,y\). Then

\[N = EA\,(u' - \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}}) , \qquad M = EI\,(v'' + \alpha\,g) , \tag{5.26}\]

and the stress is still \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A - M\,y/I\). If \(N = M = 0\), then \(v'' = -\alpha\,g\), \(u' = \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\).

Proof

The procedure is as for lemma 5.33, except that the thermal part is subtracted in the stress.

  1. In the uniaxial state, by Hooke's law with temperature, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E + \alpha\,\theta\) (theorem 3.15, first row of equation (3.16), for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\)), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \alpha\,\theta)\).
  2. With \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = u' - y\,v''\) (theorem 5.15) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\big(u' - \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}} - y\,(v'' + \alpha\,g)\big)\).
  3. By lemma 5.9 and corollary 5.19, \(N = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,dA\). From step 2, \(N = E\,(u' - \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}})\,A - E\,(v'' + \alpha\,g) \int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,dA\), and since the axis passes through the centroid, the integral is zero (lemma 5.22). This is the first equation (5.26).
  4. By the same lemma, \(M = -\int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,dA = -E\,(u' - \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}}) \int_{\mathrm{A}} y\,dA + E\,(v'' + \alpha\,g) \int_{\mathrm{A}} y^2\,dA = EI\,(v'' + \alpha\,g)\). This is the second equation.
  5. From step 3, \(u' - \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}} = N/(EA)\), from step 4, \(v'' + \alpha\,g = M/(EI)\). We insert into step 2: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A - M\,y/I\). For \(N = M = 0\) we have \(u' = \alpha\,\theta_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(v'' = -\alpha\,g\).

Source: The relation of stress and strain: EP (2.4.19) (p. 70). The result for the beam is not from the sources, it is derived from theorem 3.15, checked with SymPy.

The theorem shows that the stress is still expressed by \(N\) and \(M\) as before. The temperature only shifts the zeros of the axial and bending deformation: the beam is free of stress when \(v'' = -\alpha\,g\), not when \(v'' = 0\). The curvature \(-\alpha g\) we call the free curvature, the curvature that the beam takes when nothing restrains it.

Let us test this on our cantilever. Let the upper edge be \(20\) K warmer than the lower, \(\theta = g\,y\) with \(g = 20/0{,}040 = 500\) K/m and \(\theta_{\mathrm{m}} = 0\) (on the axis the temperature does not change). The free curvature is \(v'' = -\alpha g = -15\cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 500 = -7{,}5\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/m. The upper fibre has the free strain \(\alpha \cdot 10\ \text{K} = 1{,}5\cdot 10^{-4}\), the lower \(-1{,}5\cdot 10^{-4}\). The cantilever is clamped at \(x = 0\) (\(v(0) = v'(0) = 0\)) and has no load. Equilibrium (section 5.2) gives \(N = M = 0\) along the whole length. Theorem 5.37 therefore gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) everywhere, and the beam bends: \(v'' = -\alpha g\), \(v'(x) = -\alpha g\,x\) and \(v(x) = -\alpha g\,x^2/2\). The free end at \(x = L = 1\) m falls by \(\alpha g L^2/2 = 3{,}75\) mm. The upper fibres are longer, so the cantilever bends downward. There is no stress, because nothing restrains the bending.

Now let us clamp the same beam at both ends (\(v = v' = 0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and the axis cannot stretch). Without load over the span \(V' = -q = 0\) and \(M' = -V\), so \(M\) is a linear function of \(x\), and by theorem 5.37 \(v'' = M/(EI) - \alpha g\) is linear. Integrating a linear function twice gives a cubic polynomial \(v\). Since \(v = v' = 0\) at both ends gives it double zeros at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), it would have to be divisible by the polynomial of fourth degree \(x^2 (x - L)^2\), so it is zero and \(v'' = 0\). Similarly \(u(0) = u(L) = 0\) gives \(u' = 0\). By theorem 5.37 we then have \(N = 0\) and \(M = EI\,\alpha g = 20\,906{,}7 \cdot 7{,}5\cdot 10^{-3} = 156{,}8\) N m. The stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -M\,y/I = -E\,\alpha\,g\,y\), at the top \(-E\alpha\,\Delta T/2 = -29{,}4\) MPa (compression, the warm fibre would like to stretch) and at the bottom \(+29{,}4\) MPa, which is \(13\,\%\) of the yield strength. The clamps must carry a moment of \(156{,}8\) N m, without any external load. For comparison: if the beam clamped at both ends were heated evenly by \(20\) K (\(\theta_{\mathrm{m}} = 20\) K, \(g = 0\)), the stress would be \(-E\alpha\theta_{\mathrm{m}} = -58{,}8\) MPa, twice as much as for a temperature difference of \(20\) K over the height, where \(\theta\) at the edges is \(\pm 10\) K (figure 5.37).

What have we learned in this section? The stress in a beam is a linear function of the height above the centroidal axis, and has the form (5.25). The moment is proportional to the curvature, and the constant of proportionality is the bending stiffness \(EI\). On the steel bar \(20 \times 40\) mm at \(M = 500\) N m we got \(93{,}75\) MPa, \(43\,\%\) of the yield strength, and with an I-section of equal area only \(2{,}38\) MPa. The next section shows how the beam carries the shear force \(V\).

5.6 Shear stresses in bending

By lemma 5.9 the shear force \(V\) is the integral of the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) over the cross section, \(V = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) (for a rectangle, and by corollary 5.19 for a figure made of rectangles). Take the cantilever of section 5.1.3, a flat steel beam with a \(20 \times 40\) mm cross section and length \(L = 1\) m, loaded at its free end by a force \(F = 500\) N downwards. Here \(V = -500\) N in every cross section. Some shear stress must therefore exist in the cross section. The beam model, however, assumed that cross sections stay perpendicular to the axis, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) (section 5.3.2), and by Hooke's law (theorem 3.11) it follows that \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). Hooke's law and the shear force contradict each other. We resolve this by not computing \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) from the deformation but from equilibrium. In this section we answer the questions how the shear stress is distributed over the height of the cross section, how large it is and how good this computation is.

From history

Coulomb pointed out the shear stresses in a cantilever and wrote that they matter only in short beams (TIMO, PDF p. 149). Young wrote that solid bodies differ from liquids in resisting shear. Vicat gave many cases in which this resistance is decisive and criticized the theory of bending because it ignores shear stresses (TIMO, PDF p. 149). The first edition of Navier's book in 1826 says nothing about them. The second edition in 1833 has an article on the bending of short beams, in which the shear stress at the built-in end is taken as an average over the cross section, and the way to combine it with the longitudinal bending stresses is unsatisfactory (TIMO, PDF p. 149). The exact solution was given by Saint-Venant in his memoir on bending, but only for a few of the simplest cross-section shapes. For more complicated shapes engineers had to use the approximate, simple solution presented by D. J. Jourawski (1821 to 1891) (TIMO, PDF p. 149).

He developed the theory of shear stresses in rectangular beams while designing wooden bridges for the railway between St. Petersburg and Moscow between 1844 and 1850, and presented it in 1854 to the Russian Academy of Sciences, which awarded him the Demidov prize for the work (TIMO, PDF p. 149, footnote). He graduated in 1842 from the Institute of Engineers of Ways of Communication in St. Petersburg and immediately got work on building this railway (TIMO, PDF p. 149-150). In 1844 he was given the design and construction of a bridge over the river Werebia (spelling as in the source), with nine spans, a total length of 180 feet, 170 feet above the water (TIMO, PDF p. 150). For this bridge he had to use wooden beams of great depth and built-up wooden beams. Wood is very weak in shear along the fibres, so Jourawski correctly concluded that shear stresses in such beams must not be neglected (TIMO, PDF p. 150). The literature had nothing on calculating them, so he had to work them out himself (TIMO, PDF p. 150).

He started with the simplest case, a rectangular cantilever with a load at the free end. He reasoned that the normal stresses across the cross section at the built-in end tend to cause shear in the neutral plane \(00\) (TIMO, PDF p. 150). The shear force \(T\) in this plane equals the resultant of the normal stresses of the upper half of the cross section at the built-in end. The normal stress is largest at the edge, \(\sigma_{\max} = 6 Q l/(b h^2)\), and falls to zero toward the neutral plane. The resultant in the upper half is therefore \(\tfrac12\sigma_{\max}\cdot\tfrac12 b h = 3 Q l/(2h)\), where \(Q\) is the load, \(l\) the length of the bar, \(b\) the width and \(h\) the depth of the cross section. The plane \(00\) has area \(l b\), so the shear stress is \(T/(l b) = 3 Q/(2 b h)\) (TIMO, PDF p. 151). He calculated the stresses in any horizontal plane \(ss\) above the plane \(00\) in a similar way (TIMO, PDF p. 151). For a uniformly distributed load he showed that the shear stress along the horizontal plane is no longer constant but grows with the distance from the free end (TIMO, PDF p. 151). With the same idea he calculated the forces on each connecting element of built-up wooden beams and from them the required dimensions of the elements (TIMO, PDF p. 151). He also calculated the rivet spacing in built-up iron beams and in the Conway and Britannia tubular bridges. He showed that the number of rivets could be reduced considerably, because the transverse force on the tube falls from the ends toward the middle of the span, and the rivet spacing in the middle can therefore be larger (TIMO, PDF p. 151). Saint-Venant praised his approximate method and adapted it to a rectangular beam whose depth is much larger than its width (TIMO, PDF p. 151).

Let us return to the question of the section: how the shear force \(V\) is distributed over the cross section as shear stress. Jourawski's reasoning, the equilibrium of the part of the beam above a horizontal cut, we shall now derive for an arbitrary cross section. For a rectangular cross section our result must give in the neutral plane the same value as Jourawski's, \(3 Q/(2 b h)\) for a load \(Q = |V|\), and we shall indeed obtain it in section 5.6.2.

5.6.1 Equilibrium of part of a slice

Let us first look at the simplest case in which shear stress appears. Two equal boards, each \(20 \times 20\) mm, are laid one on top of the other and loaded as a beam. If they are not glued, each bends on its own and at the ends they slide along each other, like cards in a deck (figure 1.5). If we glue them, the glue prevents the sliding by pulling them together with a stress that lies in the horizontal plane of the joint and points along the axis \(x\). The glued and the free beam also do not bend alike: the second moment of area of the \(20 \times 40\) mm cross section is \(1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\), and the sum of the second moments of the two free boards is \(2{,}667\cdot 10^{-8}\) m\(^4\). At the same curvature the glued beam therefore carries a moment four times as large. A beam made of one piece is like a glued one in every horizontal plane, since the material does not slide there, and so there is a shear stress in every such plane.

How large this stress is we compute by cutting the beam in thought also along a horizontal plane. Take a straight prismatic beam (the cross section does not change along the axis) whose cross section has the axis \(y\) as an axis of symmetry, with the axis \(x\) through the centroids of the cross sections and with the load in the plane \(x\)-\(y\), as in the previous sections. We use the assumptions of theorem 5.35, and we take the axial load to be zero: the load on the surface and the body force have no component in the direction \(x\), so \(q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). Otherwise the equilibrium of forces in the direction \(x\) would contain one more term for the load. Equilibrium of a piece of the beam tells us how large the stress must be. Imagine a slice between the cross sections at \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) and cut it with the plane \(y = y_0\). We consider the part of the slice above this plane (figure 5.38). The longitudinal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) act on the faces of this part. Since the bending moment changes along the beam, the stresses on the right face (\(x + \Delta x\)) are not the same as on the left one (\(x\)), and their difference is not balanced. It is balanced by the shear stress on the lower face of the part, that is, on the cut.

For the computation we need the first moment of the part of the cross section above the cut. We shall use it in the examples too, so we introduce it with a definition. The first moment of the whole cross section about an axis through the centroid is zero (lemma 5.22), but the first moment of a part of the cross section is not.

Definition 5.38 First moment of a partial area (statični moment dela prereza)

Let \(A\) be the cross section of a beam in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) with the axis \(x\) through the centroid, and let \(y_0\) be the height at which we cut the cross section by a horizontal line. Denote by \(A^*(y_0)\) the part of the cross section above this line, that is, the points of the cross section with \(y \ge y_0\). The first moment of a partial area (statični moment dela prereza) is the number

\[S(y_0) = \int_{\mathrm{A}^*(\mathrm{y}_0)} y\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{5.27}\]

with unit m\(^3\). The width of the cross section \(b(y_0)\) is the total length of that part of the line \(y = y_0\) which lies in the cross section.

Source: SADD (D.9) and the text before it (PDF p. 580), EP (2.5.19), (2.5.20) (p. 76). Both books write this number \(Q\), in this book it is \(S\) as in section 5.4.2.

The first moment of a partial area is the product of the area of the part and the height of its centroid, \(S(y_0) = A^*\,y_{\mathrm{T}}^*\), where \(y_{\mathrm{T}}^*\) is the coordinate \(y\) of the centroid of the part \(A^*\) (definition 5.21). How does \(S\) change with \(y_0\)? For \(y_0\) at the top of the cross section the part is empty and \(S = 0\). For \(y_0\) at the bottom \(A^*\) is the whole cross section and \(S = 0\), because the whole cross section has first moment zero. When we increase \(y_0\) by \(\Delta y_0\), we lose a strip of height \(\Delta y_0\) and width \(b(y_0)\) at height \(y_0\), which contributes \(y_0\,b(y_0)\,\Delta y_0\), so \(\mathrm{d}S/\mathrm{d}y_0 = -y_0\,b(y_0)\). Below the axis \(y_0 < 0\) and \(S\) grows, above the axis it falls. Therefore \(S \ge 0\) for all \(y_0\) and it is largest at the axis, \(y_0 = 0\). Figure 5.39 shows this for a rectangle.

Equilibrium of a part of the slice gives us only the total force across the cut, that is, the integral of the shear stress over the width of the cut. We obtain the stress from it only with an additional assumption, that it is uniform across the width of the cut \(b(y_0)\), and we use it only to replace the integral by the product \(b\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The assumption does not hold exactly: near a free side face the stress may change. In section 5.6.3 we shall show how large the error is for our beam.

Theorem 5.39 Jourawski's formula for shear stress (Jourawskijeva enačba za strižno napetost)

Let the beam be straight and prismatic with a plane of symmetry \(x\)-\(y\), the axis \(x\) through the centroids of the cross sections and the load in this plane. Let the assumptions of theorem 5.35 hold. The load on the surface and the body force have no component in the direction \(x\), so \(q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). Let \(N\) and \(M\) be differentiable functions of \(x\) on the interval considered and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) continuous in \(x\). Let \(b(y_0) > 0\) be the width of the cross section at height \(y_0\) and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) be uniform across the width along this cut. Then at every point of the cross section at height \(y_0\)

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(x, y_0) = \frac{V(x)\,S(y_0)}{I\,b(y_0)} , \tag{5.28}\]

where \(S(y_0)\) is the first moment of the part of the cross section above \(y_0\) (definition 5.38), \(I\) is the second moment of area (definition 5.26) and the signs hold by the convention by which \(V\) and \(M\) mean the forces on the face with outward normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) (definition 5.7).

Idea

The part of the slice above the cut is in equilibrium. The longitudinal stresses on its two faces differ, because the moment differs, and the difference must be balanced by the shear stress on the cut. We know the stresses on the faces from theorem 5.35, so from the difference we obtain the stress on the cut.

Proof

We must show that the shear stress on the cut equals \(V S/(I b)\). We write the equilibrium of forces in the direction \(x\) for the part of the slice above the cut and divide it by \(\Delta x\).

  1. Let \(P\) be the part of the slice between the cross sections \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) above the plane \(y = y_0\). It is a part of a body in equilibrium, so by definition 2.3 the sum of the forces on it is zero. The force across a face is the stress vector times the area, and by Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24) we obtain the stress vector from the stress components. For a face with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the component \(x\) of the stress vector is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and for a face with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) it is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) (definition 2.25).
  2. The faces of the part \(P\) are: the right face at \(x + \Delta x\) with normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the left face at \(x\) with normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the cut at \(y_0\) with normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), because it points out of the part \(P\), which lies above it, downwards, the upper face of the beam and the two side faces. By assumption the load on the surface and the body force have no component \(x\), so these faces and the volume of the part \(P\) contribute nothing in the direction \(x\).
  3. The sum of the components \(x\) is therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} &\int_{\mathrm{A}^*} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x + \Delta x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{A}^*} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}A \\ &\quad - \int_{\mathrm{x}}^{x + \Delta x}\!\int \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}(\xi, y_0, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}\xi = 0 . \end{aligned} \tag{5.29}\]
    The first term has the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the second the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the third has a minus sign because of the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the inner integral runs over the width of the cut.
  4. By the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.36) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and by assumption this is uniform across the width. The inner integral is therefore \(b(y_0)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}(\xi, y_0)\). Denote \(\Phi(x) = \int_{\mathrm{A}^*} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}A\). Equation (5.29) then says
    \[\Phi(x + \Delta x) - \Phi(x) = b(y_0)\int_{\mathrm{x}}^{x + \Delta x} \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}(\xi, y_0)\,\mathrm{d}\xi .\]
  5. We divide by \(\Delta x\) and let \(\Delta x \to 0\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, part 2) the right-hand side approaches \(b(y_0)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}(x, y_0)\), because by assumption \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is continuous in \(x\). The left-hand side therefore approaches it too, so \(\Phi\) is differentiable and
    \[\Phi'(x) = b(y_0)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}(x, y_0) .\]
  6. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A - M y/I\) from theorem 5.35. Since the cross section is the same at every \(x\), \(A^*\), \(A\), \(I\) and \(S\) do not depend on \(x\), and
    \[\Phi(x) = \frac{N(x)}{A}\,A^* - \frac{M(x)}{I}\,S(y_0) , \qquad \Phi'(x) = \frac{N'}{A}\,A^* - \frac{M'}{I}\,S(y_0) .\]
  7. By corollary 5.11 \(N' = -q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(M' = -V\) (a vertical load on the surface has no component \(x\), so it gives no couple about the axis, \(m = 0\)). Therefore \(\Phi'(x) = V\,S(y_0)/I\).
  8. Steps 5 and 7 give \(b(y_0)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = V S/I\), and since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) (step 4), this is equation (5.28).
Explanation

The sign follows from the convention, not from the source: \(M' = -V\) is a consequence of \(V\) being the force that the part at larger \(x\) exerts on the part at smaller \(x\) (section 5.2.3). Since \(S \ge 0\) for all \(y_0\) (section 5.6.1), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) has the sign of the force \(V\) in the whole cross section, so on the face with normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) it points in the direction \(y\) just as \(V\) itself does. The assumption of uniformity across the width is the one that the beam model cannot derive. How well it holds we shall see in section 5.6.3.

Source: SADD (D.9) (PDF pp. 579-580), EP (2.5.19) (p. 76). The sign is derived from the convention of this book. SADD has \(V\) with the opposite sign (its \(V\) is \(-V_{\mathrm{y}}\) in ours), so its \(\tau = V_{\mathrm{SADD}}\,Q/(I t)\) has the opposite sign to our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the same magnitude. EP has the axis \(z\) upwards and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The name after Jourawski: TIMO PDF pp. 149-150.

We check the equation on the cantilever. At \(V = -500\) N, \(I = 1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\) and \(b = 20\) mm the first moment of the part of the cross section above the axis (\(y_0 = 0\)) is \(S(0) = 20 \cdot 20 \cdot 10 = 4000\) mm\(^3 = 4\cdot 10^{-6}\) m\(^3\) (an area \(20 \times 20\) mm\(^2\) with its centroid 10 mm above the axis). By equation (5.28)

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(0) = \frac{-500 \cdot 4\cdot 10^{-6}}{1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 0{,}02}\ \text{Pa} = -0{,}9375\ \text{MPa} .\]

The minus sign means that on the face with normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the shear stress points downwards. This is correct, since the part at larger \(x\) must act on the part at smaller \(x\) downwards to be in equilibrium with the force of \(500\) N downwards at the free end.

We call equation (5.28) Jourawski's formula. The syllabus of the course (item MK 9) calls it Grashof's equation (Grashof equation), but none of the sources of this book supports this name. Timoshenko ascribes the approximate elementary solution for shear stresses in beams to Jourawski (TIMO PDF pp. 149-150). His account of Grashof's book on elasticity and strength (TIMO PDF pp. 141-142) lists the bending and torsion of prismatic bars, the longitudinal tensile force in the bending of a beam with two pins, shells and plates, but it does not mention the equation for shear stress.

5.6.2 Rectangular cross section

How is the shear stress distributed over the height? Equation (5.28) depends on the height \(y_0\) only through \(S(y_0)\) and \(b(y_0)\), and for a rectangle \(b\) is constant. So we check how \(S(y_0)\) changes.

Corollary 5.40 Shear stress in a rectangular cross section (strižna napetost v pravokotnem prerezu)

For a rectangular cross section of width \(b\) and height \(h\) with the axis \(x\) through the centroid, under the conditions of theorem 5.39

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(x, y_0) = \frac{V(x)}{2I}\Big(\frac{h^2}{4} - y_0^2\Big) = \frac{3V(x)}{2A}\Big(1 - \frac{4 y_0^2}{h^2}\Big) , \qquad |y_0| \le \frac h2 , \tag{5.30}\]

where \(A = b h\). The stress is a parabola over the height, zero at the top and bottom of the cross section, with its largest magnitude on the axis, \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(x, 0)| = 3|V|/(2A)\).

Proof

We must show the shape of the stress and its largest value. We compute \(S(y_0)\) and insert it into equation (5.28).

  1. The part of the cross section above \(y_0\) is a rectangle of width \(b\) and height \(h/2 - y_0\). By definition 5.38 and by Fubini's theorem (theorem 4.9)
    \[S(y_0) = \int_{\mathrm{y}_0}^{h/2} y\,b\,\mathrm{d}y = \frac b2\Big(\frac{h^2}{4} - y_0^2\Big) .\]
  2. The width is \(b(y_0) = b\) and \(I = b h^3/12\) (lemma 5.27). Equation (5.28) gives
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{V}{I b}\cdot\frac b2\Big(\frac{h^2}{4} - y_0^2\Big) = \frac{V}{2I}\Big(\frac{h^2}{4} - y_0^2\Big) ,\]
    which is the first form. The second follows, because \(\dfrac{1}{2I}\cdot\dfrac{h^2}{4} = \dfrac{6}{b h^3}\cdot\dfrac{h^2}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2 b h}\).
  3. The expression \(h^2/4 - y_0^2\) is a quadratic function, which is zero at \(y_0 = \pm h/2\) and largest at \(y_0 = 0\), where it equals \(h^2/4\). There \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}| = 3|V|/(2A)\).

Source: SADD (D.10), (D.11) (PDF p. 581), EP (2.5.20), (2.5.21) (p. 76). EP denotes the height of the cross section by \(2h\), so it has \(h^2 - z^2\) and \(3V/(4bh)\), where this book has \(h^2/4 - y_0^2\) and \(3V/(2bh)\). The proof is not from the source.

Why is the distribution a parabola? The first moment \(S\) is the area of the part above the cut, \(b\,(h/2 - y_0)\), times the height of its centroid, \((h/2 + y_0)/2\). Both are linear in \(y_0\), and the product of two linear functions is a quadratic function. The area is zero at the top, and at the bottom the centroid falls on the axis, so \(S\) is zero at both end points. Figure 5.40 shows the distribution.

The values for our cantilever (\(V = -500\) N, \(h = 40\) mm) by equation (5.30) at \(y_0 = 0\), \(5\), \(10\), \(15\) and \(20\) mm are \(-0{,}9375\), \(-0{,}8789\), \(-0{,}7031\), \(-0{,}4102\) and \(0\) MPa. Let us also check that this is a distribution of the shear force. By lemma 5.9 we must have \(\int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = V\). The integral is

\[\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} \frac{V}{2I}\Big(\frac{h^2}{4} - y^2\Big)\,b\,\mathrm{d}y = \frac{V b}{2I}\Big(\frac{h^3}{4} - \frac{h^3}{12}\Big) = \frac{V b}{2I}\cdot\frac{h^3}{6} = V ,\]

since \(I = b h^3/12\). The force carried by the shear stress is indeed \(V\), as it must be.

How large is this stress compared with the bending stress? At the clamp \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}|_{\max} = 93{,}75\) MPa (section 5.5.3) and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}|_{\max} = 0{,}9375\) MPa, so exactly 1 %. This is no coincidence. For a cantilever with a force \(F\) at the end, at the clamp \(M = FL\) and \(V = F\), so

\[\frac{|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}|_{\max}}{|\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}|_{\max}} = \frac{3F/(2bh)}{6FL/(b h^2)} = \frac{h}{4L} , \tag{5.31}\]

at \(L/h = 25\) that is \(1/100\). Why is the ratio equal to the height divided by the length? The bending stress is proportional to the moment, and this to the lever arm \(L\), whereas the shear stress is proportional to the force alone and has no lever arm. A longer beam has the same \(V\) and a larger \(M\), so the shear stress relatively disappears. For the simply supported beam of section 5.1.3 with load \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m the largest shear stress at the support is \(1{,}875\) MPa (there \(V = 1\) kN, the moment is zero), the bending stress at mid-span is \(93{,}75\) MPa, the ratio is \(h/L = 0{,}02\), but it is reached at two different places.

A beam in the shape of the letter I has the same \(V\) distributed differently. Take the cross section of section 5.4.3, of height 200 mm, with flanges \(100 \times 10\) mm and a web \(180 \times 6\) mm, and \(V = 1\) kN. The section is a figure made of three rectangles, so \(V = \int_{\mathrm{A}} \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) holds for it too (corollary 5.19). By equation (5.28) on the axis \(S = 100\cdot 10\cdot 95 + 6\cdot 90\cdot 45 = 119\,300\) mm\(^3\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1000 \cdot 119\,300/(2{,}098\cdot 10^7 \cdot 6)\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 0{,}948\) MPa. At the edge of the web, where it meets the flange, \(S = 100\cdot 10\cdot 95 = 95\,000\) mm\(^3\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}755\) MPa, and in the flange at the same \(S\) and \(b = 100\) mm only \(0{,}045\) MPa. The stress jumps, because at the same \(S\) the width \(b\) changes abruptly from 6 mm to 100 mm. The average in the web, \(V/(6 \cdot 180\ \text{mm}^2) = 0{,}926\) MPa, is close to the largest value \(0{,}948\) MPa, and the web carries \(95{,}4\) % of the shear force, which we obtain by integrating the stress over the web. This is why for I-beams we compute as if the web carried the shear force with uniform stress and the flanges carried the moment. Figure 5.41 shows the distribution.

Where are the longitudinal and the shear stress present at the same point? At the point of the cantilever at the clamp at height \(y = 10\) mm, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 46{,}875\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}703\) MPa, and there are no other components in the plane. The principal stresses are the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & 0\end{pmatrix}\) (definition 2.60), \(46{,}886\) and \(-0{,}011\) MPa, and the principal direction is rotated by \(0{,}86^\circ\) from the axis \(x\). The shear stress therefore hardly changes the principal stresses. On the axis, however, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}9375\) MPa, that is, pure shear, with principal stresses \(\pm 0{,}9375\) MPa in directions rotated by \(45^\circ\). The largest shear stress is on the axis and the largest bending stress at the edge of the cross section, and nowhere are both large at the same time.

5.6.3 How accurate the formula is

Equation (5.28) follows from equilibrium and from the assumption of uniformity across the width, and it contains the beam model with plane cross sections. How good is it? SADD has three cases.

In section 8.1 of SADD, in example 8.3 (PDF pp. 173-175), the plane stress state of a beam with uniform transverse load is computed, and the shear stresses given by elasticity are equal to those of equation (5.28). The longitudinal stresses differ, the difference at the outer fibres is \(w/5\), where \(w\) is the load per unit area of the upper face, and it does not depend on the dimensions of the beam. At a ratio of span to height of 4 the difference is about 1 %. In example 9.9 (PDF pp. 279-280) the rectangular cross section is treated in three dimensions. Besides the term of equation (5.28), elasticity gives a correction with the factor \(\nu/(1 + \nu)\). At \(\nu = 0\) the correction vanishes, and so it does (relative to the elementary term) for a very narrow or a very wide rectangle, where the elastic solution passes into the result of equation (5.28). For our cross section with half-width \(a = 10\) mm and half-height \(c = 20\) mm equation (9.9.19) at \(\nu = 0{,}3\) gives a correction on the axis of \(-1{,}9\) % of the elementary value \(|V|\,c^2/(2I)\). We computed the sum in the equation on a computer, its terms fall quickly because of \(\operatorname{sech}(n\pi c/a)\). Equation (9.9.18) also tells how the correction changes across the width: at the side edge, \(x = \pm a\), it is \(+3{,}8\) % and on the axis \(-1{,}9\) %, so the assumption of uniformity across the width does not hold exactly, the difference is about 6 % of the elementary value. At \(\nu = 1/2\) SADD calls the differences sizeable (p. 280). In example 9.8 (PDF pp. 277-278) the cross section is a circle, and the differences are small according to SADD. For our beam at \(\nu = 0{,}3\) the equation is therefore wrong by about 2 % on the axis and by about 4 % at the edge, and this is the price of the assumption of uniformity across the width.

The shear stress has one more consequence that must be stated. The deformations are now no longer zero. By Hooke's law (theorem 3.11, definition 3.9) the shear strain is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/G\). On the axis of the cantilever \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}9375\ \text{MPa}/75{,}38\ \text{GPa} = 1{,}24\cdot 10^{-5}\), which is 2,6 % of the longitudinal strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 4{,}78\cdot 10^{-4}\) at the edge at the clamp. The shear strain is a parabola over the height, at the edge it is zero. The plane cross sections that the beam assumes therefore do not stay plane: the cross section warps (figure 5.43). Let us derive by how much.

Derivation 5.41 Warping of the cross section of a cantilever (izbočenje prereza konzole)

Goal: find the displacement field \((u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}})\) in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) for a cantilever with a force \(F\) downwards at the end, whose stresses are those computed by theorem 5.35 and equation (5.28), and from it the warping of the cross section. We assume that the field lies in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) and that we obtain the displacements by integrating the strains. The fibres are in uniaxial stress (\(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\)), so Hooke's law (theorem 3.11, equation (3.12)) gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). With this we give up assumption (b) of section 5.3.2 about transversals of equal length, because the transversals stretch because of the Poisson effect.

1
\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{F (L - x)\,y}{E I} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{G} = -\frac{F}{2 G I}\Big(\frac{h^2}{4} - y^2\Big) .\]
Hint

From \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -M y/I\) with \(M = -F(L - x)\) (section 5.2.2) and from theorem 3.11 with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) we have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The shear strain is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/G\) by definition 3.9 and by equation (5.30) with \(V = -F\).

2
\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{F y}{E I}\Big(L x - \frac{x^2}{2}\Big) + f(y) , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\frac{\nu F (L - x)\,y^2}{2 E I} + g(x) .\]
Hint

We integrate \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) over \(x\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) over \(y\). The integration constants are functions of the other variables, \(f(y)\) and \(g(x)\).

3
\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]
Hint

The definition of the engineering shear strain, \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (chapter 1).

4
\[\underbrace{g'(x) + \frac{F}{E I}\Big(L x - \frac{x^2}{2}\Big)}_{\text{only } \mathrm{x}} = -\underbrace{\Big[ f'(y) - \frac{(2 + \nu)\,F\,y^2}{2 E I} + \frac{(1 + \nu)\,F h^2}{4 E I}\Big]}_{\text{only } \mathrm{y}} .\]
Explanation

We insert steps 1 and 2 into step 3 and collect the terms that depend only on \(x\) on one side and those that depend only on \(y\) on the other. Here we use \(1/G = 2(1 + \nu)/E\).

5
\[f(y) = \frac{(2 + \nu)\,F\,y^3}{6 E I} - \Big[\frac{(1 + \nu)\,F h^2}{4 E I} + c_0\Big]\,y + c_1 .\]
Explanation

The left side is a function of \(x\) only and the right of \(y\) only, and they are equal for all \(x\) and \(y\), so each is a constant. We denote the left side by the constant \(c_0\), and the right side is then \(-c_0\). From the right side we obtain \(f'(y)\) and integrate. The constants \(c_0\) and \(c_1\) are determined by the clamp (how the beam is attached), and the whole linear part of \(f(y)\) only means a rotation of the cross section as a whole.

What warps is therefore the term \((2 + \nu)\,F y^3/(6 E I)\), which is not linear in \(y\). The linear part rotates the cross section, the cubic one bends it. All steps are possible, so the displacement field exists and the strains derived from it are compatible by the definition of compatible strains. This is the field that EP computes for a cantilever with a point force at the end (example 2.5.1).

Source: EP example 2.5.1 (pp. 78-80), field (p80-b9) in the axes of the book EP (\(x_3\) upwards). The derivation is in our axes and with signs by the convention of this book.

For our beam (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(I = 1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^4\)) the cubic term at the edge of the cross section (\(y = 20\) mm) is \(0{,}073\ \mu\text{m}\). The deviation of the cross section from the plane through its two edges (\(y = \pm 20\) mm) is largest at \(y = \pm h/(2\sqrt3) = \pm 11{,}5\) mm, \(0{,}028\ \mu\text{m}\). The displacement of the edge of the cross section at the free end due to rotation is \(0{,}239\) mm, so the cubic term at the edge is \(0{,}03\) % of this displacement. The flatness of the cross sections therefore holds very well, because the beam is long: the shear strain is proportional to \(V\), which does not depend on \(L\), whereas the longitudinal displacement due to rotation is proportional to \(L\). For a short and thick beam the ratio is different, which the Timoshenko beam takes into account by including the shear strain in the model (section 5.13).

5.7 The deflection curve equation (enačba upogibnice)

For the cantilever and the simply supported beam we got the reactions from the equilibrium of the whole beam, the internal forces \(V\) and \(M\) from the equilibrium of parts, and the curvature from \(M = EI\,v''\). The deflection \(v\) came last. Is there another way, in which we compute the deflection directly from the load? We need the answer for a beam where equilibrium alone does not suffice, and such a beam is the propped cantilever (podprta konzola).

Take the same steel strip \(20 \times 40\) mm as before, of length \(L = 2\) m, with \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m². Let it be clamped (vpetje) at \(x = 0\) and held up at \(x = L\) by a roller support (pomična členkasta podpora), and let it carry the uniform load \(q = -q_0\), \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m, downward. The clamp gives two forces and a couple, the support one force, four unknown reactions in all, while there are only three equilibrium equations in the plane (definition 5.6). Because the load points vertically, the horizontal equation is satisfied if the horizontal reaction at the clamp is zero. What remains are the equations for the vertical forces and for the moments about the clamp. Let \(A\) be the vertical reaction at the clamp, \(M_{\mathrm{v}}\) the couple at the clamp (positive if it turns counterclockwise) and \(R\) the reaction at the support, both forces upward. Equilibrium gives

\[A + R - q_0 L = 0 , \qquad M_{\mathrm{v}} + R\,L - q_0 L\,\frac{L}{2} = 0 , \tag{5.32}\]

so \(A = 2000 - R\) and \(M_{\mathrm{v}} = 2000 - 2R\) (forces in N, moment in N m). Every \(R\) gives a pair that satisfies equilibrium. For \(R = 0\) this is the cantilever without a support with \(M_{\mathrm{v}} = q_0 L^2/2 = 2000\) N m. For \(R = 1000\) N we get \(M_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\), the clamp acts as a pin and we have the simply supported beam. Which value of \(R\) is the right one, equilibrium does not say. The deformation says it: the support at \(x = L\) prevents the end of the beam from sinking, so \(v(L) = 0\). This is a condition on the deflection, so we must find the deflection from the load.

From history

Navier's equation \(E I\,\mathrm{d}^2 y/\mathrm{d}x^2 = M\) had been used since Euler's time for the deflection of cantilevers and symmetrically loaded simply supported beams (TIMO, PDF p. 83). Navier applied it to any transverse load: since the moment differs in different parts of the beam, the deflection in different parts is described by different equations (TIMO, PDF p. 83). For a beam loaded at a point \(C\) he denoted the angle that the tangent at \(C\) makes with the horizontal by \(\alpha\) and expressed the deflections of both ends with this angle. From the equality of the two deflections he obtained \(\tan\alpha\) (TIMO, PDF p. 83). He knew the deflection of a cantilever, so he could write the deflection equations for both parts of the beam (TIMO, PDF p. 83).

Navier was the first to develop a general method for statically indeterminate problems. He showed that problems are indeterminate only as long as the bodies are considered perfectly rigid. When elasticity is taken into account, equations expressing the conditions of deformation can always be added to the equations of statics, and so we get enough equations for all unknowns (TIMO, PDF p. 83). He explained this with the example of a load carried by several bars in one plane. If the bars are perfectly rigid, we may choose arbitrary values for the forces in all bars except two and compute the last two from statics, so the problem is indeterminate. If elasticity is taken into account, the elongations of the bars and the forces in them are functions of the two components of the displacement of the point where the bars meet. Two equations of statics then determine the displacement and from it all the forces (TIMO, PDF p. 83-84). For bending he started with a beam built in at one end and simply supported at the other (TIMO, PDF p. 84). He denoted the unknown support force at the simply supported end by \(Q\) and for each part of the beam wrote the deflection equation with a moment that depends on \(Q\). By integrating, and by requiring that the two parts have a common ordinate and tangent where they meet, he obtained the deflection, and \(Q\) from the condition that the deflection at the simply supported end is zero (TIMO, PDF p. 84-85). His calculation has no moment and shear force diagrams, which might explain why he sometimes fixed the place of the largest moment wrongly (TIMO, PDF p. 85).

Let us return to the question of the section: how we get the deflection of a beam built in at one end and simply supported at the other directly from the load, when equilibrium alone does not suffice. Navier's path is the same as ours: we express the moment with the unknown, integrate the deflection equation and determine the unknowns from the conditions at the ends and at the joints.

5.7.1 From the load to the deflection

We already know every link of the path from the load to the deflection, each one separately. The load \(q\) changes the shear force: a piece of beam without point forces is in equilibrium if \(V\) changes over the piece by the opposite of the load force, and this is said by the relation \(V' = -q\) (corollary 5.11). For the simply supported beam with \(q = -q_0\) we have \(V' = q_0 = 1000\) N/m, so over \(2\) m \(V\) grows from \(-1000\) N to \(+1000\) N. The shear force changes the moment, \(M' = -V\) (the same corollary): the moment grows while \(V\) is negative and falls when it becomes positive. The moment gives the curvature, \(v'' = M/(EI)\) (theorem 5.35). The curvature is the change of the slope \(v'\), and the slope is the change of the deflection \(v\). The graph of the function \(v\), the curve into which the axis of the beam bends, is called the deflection curve (upogibnica). If we know \(q\), we get it by four integrations (figure 5.44).

The signs in the relations \(V' = -q\) and \(M' = -V\) are a consequence of the choice of the side of the cross section with which we defined \(V\) and \(M\) (definitions 5.7 and 5.8). Let us check them on the cantilever with the force \(F = 500\) N downward at the end: there \(V = -500\) N and \(M(x) = -F\,(L - x)\), so \(M' = F = 500\) N and indeed \(M' = -V\). The load \(q\) is zero for the cantilever, \(V' = 0\) and \(M\) is linear, as it must be.

The relation \(v'' = M/(EI)\) and both relations from the section on internal forces hold under conditions that we now collect in a theorem. The theorem is the equilibrium of a piece of beam, written with one unknown deflection.

Theorem 5.42 Deflection curve equation (enačba upogibnice)

Let the beam be straight and prismatic (the cross section and the material do not change along the axis, so \(EI\) and \(EA\) are constant) and satisfy the assumptions of theorem 5.35 (Euler-Bernoulli model, linearly elastic material, axis through the centroids of the cross sections). On an open interval \((a, b)\) of the axis let there be no point forces and couples and no distributed couples (\(m = 0\)), let the load \(q\) be continuous on \((a, b)\), and let the function \(v\) be four times differentiable. Then

\[\big(EI\,v''\big)'' = q \quad \text{on } (a, b) , \tag{5.33}\]

If the axial load \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\) is also continuous and \(u\) is twice differentiable, then on \((a, b)\) also

\[-\big(EA\,u'\big)' = q_{\mathrm{x}} . \tag{5.34}\]

Here \(q\) is positive upward and \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\) positive in the direction of the axis \(x\).

Proof

We show that the equations are only another way of writing the relations among \(q\), \(V\), \(M\) and \(v\) from theorem 5.35 and corollary 5.11.

  1. By theorem 5.35 \(M = EI\,v''\) on \((a, b)\). So the function \(EI\,v''\) equals the moment \(M\) on the whole interval \((a, b)\).
  2. The load \(q\) is continuous on \((a, b)\), so by corollary 5.11 (equation (5.13) with \(m = 0\)) \(V' = -q\) and \(M' = -V\). The signs follow from the definition of \(V\) and \(M\) on the side of larger \(x\), the check is on the cantilever above.
  3. From step 2 it follows that \(M'' = (M')' = (-V)' = -V' = q\).
  4. Insert \(M = EI\,v''\) from step 1: \((EI\,v'')'' = M'' = q\). Since the beam is prismatic, \(EI\) is constant and \((EI\,v'')'' = EI\,v''''\). This is (5.33).
  5. For the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) (theorem 5.35) and by corollary 5.11 (equation (5.13), \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\) continuous on \((a, b)\)) \(N' = -q_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the equilibrium of a piece of the axis, as lemma 4.75 makes it for a bar. Since \(EA\) is constant, \(-EA\,u'' = -(EA\,u')' = -N' = q_{\mathrm{x}}\). This is (5.34).

Source: EP (2.5.17) and (2.5.18) (p. 75), CM (7.3.32) (PDF p. 310). The source CM (7.3.32) writes both equations with variable \(EI(x)\) and \(EA(x)\), EP (2.5.18) the first one with variable \(EI\). We wrote them for the prismatic beam. The sources use the opposite sign of \(M\) to ours (EP \(M = \int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) with the axis \(z\) upward, CM \(M = \int y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\)), and the same \(V\) as we do. In the second derivative the sign of \(M\) cancels, so the equation is the same in all three notations (EP: \(-M_{\mathrm{EP}}'' = q\) and \(M_{\mathrm{EP}} = -M\)). The proof from \(V' = -q\) and \(M' = -V\) is not literally from the sources, they derive the equation from the equilibrium of a slice.

Extension to a variable cross section (a named simplification). If the cross section changes along the axis, \(EI(x)\) and \(EA(x)\) are functions of \(x\) and EP (2.5.18) (p. 75) writes \(\big(EI(x)\,v''\big)'' = q\). Our proof stays the same up to step 4, where \(EI\) may not be taken out of the derivative. The extension needs a cross section that changes slowly along the axis: we proved theorem 5.35 and the relation \(M = EI\,v''\) for a prismatic beam, and for a variable cross section they remain good only approximately, if the height of the cross section changes little over a length of one height. How little, this book does not estimate, and it does not use the extension: all beams in this chapter are prismatic.

The proof showed that the deflection curve equation is the same statement as the chain in figure 5.44, written with one unknown function. The first part goes from the load to the moment: \(q \to V \to M\), and this is equilibrium. The second part is kinematics and material: \(M \to v''\). The last claim of the theorem is the bar of chapter 4. Equation (5.34) is \(N' + q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) with \(N = EA\,u'\) and constant \(EA\), so the equilibrium of the bar (lemma 4.75). The axial and the bending equation are not coupled, because the axial force and the moment come separately from theorem 5.35.

Equation (5.33) connects the unknown function \(v\) with its derivatives and not only with its values. The highest derivative in it is the fourth. What this means, when it has a solution and when only one, we say in the next section (section 5.8.1), which also names equations of this kind. Already now we can see what else we need to know. Every integration in the chain adds a constant: the integral of \(q\) is \(V\) up to a constant, the integral of \(V\) is \(M\) up to a constant, and then follow two more integrations for \(v'' \to v' \to v\). Altogether there are four constants.

Let us try this on the simply supported beam with a uniform load (\(L = 2\) m, \(q = -q_0\)). We already know the moment from the equilibrium of parts, \(M = \tfrac12 q_0\,x\,(L - x)\), so we start at \(v'' = M/(EI)\) and have two integrations before us:

\[\begin{aligned} v'' &= \frac{q_0}{2EI}\,\big(L x - x^2\big) , \\ v' &= \frac{q_0}{2EI}\left(\frac{L x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right) + c_1 , \\ v &= \frac{q_0}{2EI}\left(\frac{L x^3}{6} - \frac{x^4}{12}\right) + c_1\,x + c_2 . \end{aligned} \tag{5.35}\]

The two steps of the chain, from \(q\) to \(V\) and from \(V\) to \(M\), would add two more constants. Here the equilibrium of the whole beam determined them (the reactions are \(1\) kN). The constants \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) stay open: they cannot be got from the load alone, since we add \(c_1 x + c_2\), which is a displacement and a rotation of the beam as a rigid body (definition 1.11), and the function \(v''\) stays the same. They are determined by the position of the beam, that is, by the supports.

5.7.2 Conditions at the ends of the beam

The open constants are determined by conditions at the ends of the beam. In chapter 4 we met the same for the bar: the equation \(N' + q = 0\) holds in the interior, and the conditions \(u(0) = 0\) and \(N(L) = F\) are at the ends. We called the first essential or geometric (bistveni ali geometrijski), the second natural or force (naravni ali silni) condition (section 4.4.7). In the next section we shall collect such conditions at the ends together with the equation. For a beam the unknown is \(v\) and the conditions also concern its derivatives. So that we do not write them just by feeling, let us ask what a support prescribes at its end.

At every end of the beam there are three pairs of quantities: displacement and axial force \((u, N)\), deflection and shear force \((v, V)\), and slope and moment \((v', M)\). The product of the members of a pair is work: the axial force on the displacement, the shear force on the deflection, the moment on the slope (a couple on the angle of rotation, the slope is a ratio of lengths without a unit). At an end we cannot prescribe both members of a pair: if the support holds the end in place, the displacement is prescribed, and the force is a reaction that we get only from the computation. If nothing holds the end, the force is prescribed and the displacement is the result. So at every end exactly one member of each pair is prescribed. CM (7.3.33), (7.3.34) says this too.

We get the signs from the definitions 5.7 and 5.8, where \(V\) and \(M\) are the force and the moment with which the part on the side of larger \(x\) acts on the part on the side of smaller \(x\). At the right end \(x = L\) the cross section is an outer cross section with the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so there \(V(L)\) is simply the force that acts on the end, and \(M(L)\) simply the couple that acts on the end. If the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) (positive upward) and the couple \(M_0\) (positive counterclockwise) act on the end, then

\[V(L) = F_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad M(L) = M_0 . \tag{5.36}\]

At the left end \(x = 0\) the outer cross section has the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The force that acts on the end is, by the law of action and reaction, opposite to \(V(0)\), so the applied force there is \(-V(0)\) and the couple \(-M(0)\). CM (7.3.33) writes the same pairs with its own signs and uses \(-v'\) for the rotation. We derive the signs from our definitions and do not copy them.

The conditions of the beams that we know, one by one:

  • clamp (vpetje): \(v = 0\) (the end does not move) and \(v' = 0\) (the cross section does not rotate: by theorem 5.15 a point at height \(y\) moves in the direction \(x\) by \(-y\,v'\), so the rotation of the cross section is tied to \(v'\) and for \(v' = 0\) there is none). The reaction \(V\) and the moment \(M\) are unknown,
  • pin or roller support (nepomična ali pomična členkasta podpora): \(v = 0\), the rotation is free, so there is no couple and \(M = 0\), which by theorem 5.35 means \(v'' = 0\). The reaction \(V\) is unknown,
  • free end: \(V = F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M = M_0\) (equation (5.36)), \(v\) and \(v'\) are unknown.

So an end has two conditions, the two ends together four. This is exactly the number given by the fourth derivative in equation (5.33), as we counted four constants. For our beams the conditions are these:

  • cantilever (\(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -500\) N, \(M_0 = 0\)): \(v(0) = 0\), \(v'(0) = 0\), \(M(L) = 0\), \(V(L) = -500\) N,
  • simply supported beam: \(v(0) = 0\), \(M(0) = 0\), \(v(L) = 0\), \(M(L) = 0\),
  • propped cantilever: \(v(0) = 0\), \(v'(0) = 0\), \(v(L) = 0\), \(M(L) = 0\).

For the cantilever both conditions with forces are prescribed at the free end, \(V(L)\) and \(M(L)\). From there downward along the chain of section 5.7.1 we get \(V\) and \(M\) without constants, and the deflection then from the conditions at the clamp. For the propped cantilever only \(M(L) = 0\) is prescribed at the end \(x = L\), and the force \(V(L) = R\) is unknown. The chain from \(q\) to \(M\) therefore cannot be computed before we know \(R\). The missing datum is given by the condition \(v(L) = 0\). This is the difference between a statically determinate and an indeterminate beam (definition 5.6), seen in the conditions. The solution of the propped cantilever is found in section 5.9.4. For checking we state that we get \(R = 750\) N, \(A = 1250\) N and \(M_{\mathrm{v}} = 500\) N m, in agreement with equation (5.32) (\(2000 - 2 \cdot 750 = 500\)).

Let us also try the conditions on the simply supported beam of equation (5.35). The condition \(v(0) = 0\) gives \(c_2 = 0\). The condition \(v(L) = 0\) gives

\[\frac{q_0}{2EI}\left(\frac{L^4}{6} - \frac{L^4}{12}\right) + c_1 L = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad c_1 = -\frac{q_0 L^3}{24\,EI} = -0{,}01594 . \tag{5.37}\]

This is the slope of the beam above the left support, \(v'(0) = c_1\), and it is negative, because the beam descends from the support. The conditions for the moment, \(M(0) = M(L) = 0\), are already satisfied, since \(M = \tfrac12 q_0\,x\,(L - x)\). The deflection at the middle is

\[v\!\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = -\frac{5\,q_0 L^4}{384\,EI} = -9{,}965\ \text{mm} , \tag{5.38}\]

which is 0,5 % of the length of the beam. The largest slope is \(0{,}0159\) and its square \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), so the assumption of small slopes (\(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\)) from section 5.3.3 is satisfied. The result was given by equilibrium, theorem 5.42 and two conditions.

So far the load was continuous everywhere. What happens under a point force, where theorem 5.42 does not hold? The function \(q\) is not a function there, since a force on zero length is not a force per unit length. So we cut the beam into two parts, solve each with equation (5.33), and join the pieces with conditions at the point. Take the simply supported beam of length \(L = 2\) m with the force \(F = 1\) kN downward at the middle, \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -1000\) N at \(x_0 = 1\) m. The reactions are \(500\) N each. The shear force is \(V = -500\) N to the left and \(V = +500\) N to the right of the force, the moment is \(M = 500\,x\) on the left and \(M = 500\,(L - x)\) on the right, \(500\) N m in the middle (figure 5.46). The shear force jumps by \(+1000\) N, the moment is continuous with a pointed peak.

Lemma 5.43 Matching conditions at a point force (pogoji pod točkovno silo)

Let the beam satisfy the assumptions of theorem 5.35. At an interior point \(x_0\) of the axis let a point force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) act and no couple, and on both sides of \(x_0\) let the load \(q\) be continuous and bounded near \(x_0\) and \(m = 0\). Let the point where the force is applied lie on the surface of the beam, and let the displacement field be continuously differentiable at all interior points of the beam (section 1.15.6). Then \(v\), \(v'\) and \(M\) are continuous at \(x_0\), and the shear force jumps by

\[V(x_0^+) - V(x_0^-) = -F_{\mathrm{y}} . \tag{5.39}\]
Proof

We show that \(v\) and \(v'\) come from the continuity of the displacement field, and \(M\) and \(V\) from the lemma on the jump.

  1. We apply theorem 5.15 separately to the piece of the beam left of \(x_0\) and to the piece right of it. Each is a box as in the theorem, and its interior points are interior points of the beam, where the field is continuously differentiable. So for \(x \ne x_0\) we have \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = v(x)\) and \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = u(x) - y\,v'(x)\) with the same function \(v\) on each side.
  2. The displacement field is continuously differentiable also at the interior points of the cross section at \(x_0\) (the point where the force is applied lies on the surface), and so continuous (lemma 1.91). The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 0, 0) = v(x)\) is therefore continuous also at \(x_0\), so the limits \(v(x_0^-)\) and \(v(x_0^+)\) are both equal to \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x_0, 0, 0)\). So \(v\) is continuous.
  3. For two heights \(y_1 \ne y_2\) of the cross section \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y_1, 0) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y_2, 0) = -(y_1 - y_2)\,v'(x)\) for \(x \ne x_0\). The left side is a continuous function of \(x\) also at \(x_0\), because the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous (step 2). So the limits \(v'(x_0^-)\) and \(v'(x_0^+)\) are both equal to \(-(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x_0, y_1, 0) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(x_0, y_2, 0))/(y_1 - y_2)\) and \(v'\) is continuous.
  4. The load and the point force satisfy lemma 5.12. It gives \(M(x_0^+) - M(x_0^-) = -M_{\mathrm{p}} = 0\) and \(V(x_0^+) - V(x_0^-) = -F_{\mathrm{y}}\). So the moment is continuous and the shear force jumps by \(-F_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Source: The continuity of the displacement field at interior points is an assumption from section 1.15.6, and the jump is lemma 5.12 (EP p. 74, relation of \(V\) and \(q\)). The proof is not from a source.

Let us look at the consequences on the beam with the central force. The jump of \(V\) is \(1000\) N and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -1000\) N, so indeed \(V^+ - V^- = -F_{\mathrm{y}}\). Since \(M\) is continuous, the curvature \(v'' = M/(EI)\) is continuous too, and its derivative jumps, because \((EI\,v'')' = M' = -V\) and \(V\) jumps. So \(v''\) has a pointed peak at \(x_0\), the same as \(M\), the graph of \(v'\) has no corners and the graph of \(v\) has no sharp corner: under the force the beam does not break, only the rate of change of the curvature jumps. The slope is \(v' = 0\) at \(x_0\) by symmetry and the beam has its lowest point there, \(v(x_0) = -F L^3/(48\,EI) = -7{,}972\) mm.

If there were a point couple \(M_0\) on the beam, the moment would jump, not the shear force (lemma 5.12). The conditions under the force (continuity of \(v\), \(v'\), \(M\) and the jump of \(V\) by equation (5.39)) are four at the joint of two pieces, just as the conditions at an end are four at the end of the beam. With two pieces we have eight constants and eight conditions: four at the ends and four under the force. We write the solution piece by piece in section 5.8.4.

5.8 Mathematics: ordinary differential equations (matematika: navadne diferencialne enačbe)

For the hanging bar we started from the known displacement \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), obtained the strain by differentiation and the force by equilibrium. The way led from a function to its derivatives. For the beam the situation is reversed. We know the load, and the deflection we look for is a function about which we only know how its fourth derivative is related to the load (theorem 5.42). What is such an equation, when does it have exactly one solution, and how do we find it when only the fourth derivative is given? We answer these questions in this section. First we name the equations whose unknown is a function. Then we prove that for our case we can solve them to the end, and count how many conditions we need so that the solution is no longer one of many but a single one. At the end we show what to do when a point force acts on the beam.

5.8.1 An equation for an unknown function (enačba za neznano funkcijo)

In chapter 1 we knew the solution and only checked it. Take again the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hanging under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) vertical, pointing down from the fixed top. By lemma 4.75 on the equilibrium of a bar, \(N' + q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), where \(q_{\mathrm{x}} = \rho g A\) is the weight per unit length, and by Hooke's law \(N = E A\,u'\). If \(E A\) is constant, it follows that

\[E\,u''(x) = -\rho g . \tag{5.40}\]

This is the equation for the displacement \(u\). The input is the position \(x\) on the bar, the output the displacement of the point, a number in metres. The equation does not say how large \(u(x)\) is. It only says that the second derivative of \(u\) equals the same number at every point, \(-\rho g/E = -3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). The expression from chapter 1, \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), satisfies the equation, since \(u'' = -2a = -3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). The question is whether it is the only function that does.

The beam is the same. The steel beam of section 5.1.3, 20 mm wide and 40 mm high, has \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m² and self weight \(q = -61{,}21\) N/m (downward, the axis \(y\) points up). By theorem 5.42 we have

\[EI\,v''''(x) = q(x) , \qquad v''''(x) = -2{,}928 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{-3} . \tag{5.41}\]

The unknown is the deflection \(v\), a function with input \(x\) and output numbers in metres, and the equation relates its fourth derivative to a given number on the right. Both equations have the same form: an unknown function of one variable \(x\) and its derivatives appear in them. The exact name and the definition are below. The equilibrium equations of chapter 2, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), contain partial derivatives of functions of several variables \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) and are of a different kind, which we do not need here.

Definition 5.44 Ordinary differential equation (navadna diferencialna enačba)

Let \(I\) be an open interval, \(n\) a natural number and \(\Phi\) a function with \(n + 2\) numbers as input and one number as output. An ordinary differential equation (navadna diferencialna enačba) of order \(n\) is an equation

\[\Phi\big(x, y, y', \dots, y^{(n)}\big) = 0 , \tag{5.42}\]
