The derivation showed that the elementary stress \(-My/I\) is corrected by a term that changes neither the force nor the moment in the cross section, but only reshapes the distribution over the height, and that the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), which the model neglected, was equal to \(-p\) on the upper face (figure 5.85). SADD states that the difference at the outer fibres is \(p/5\), independent of the beam dimensions. Its share of the largest stress \(M c/I = 3pl^2/(4c^2)\) is \((4/15)\,(c/l)^2\). For \(l/c = 4\) this is \((4/15)/16 = 1{,}7\) %. The same ratio follows from figure 8.4 in SADD (PDF p. 175): at \(l/c = 4\) the largest stress at the outer fibre is about \(12\,p\), and the difference \(p/5 = 0{,}2\,p\) is therefore 1,7 % of that value. SADD writes in the text on the same page that the difference is "about only 1 %". This is a rounded description of the figure, not a computation: its own formulas give 1,7 %, and that is why we state this number. For our beam with \(l/c = 50\) it is 0,011 %: the load \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m on the width of 20 mm is a pressure \(p = 50\) kPa, the difference \(p/5 = 0{,}01\) MPa, the largest stress 93,75 MPa. The pattern is simple. The difference \(p/5\) is the same for every beam, while the largest stress grows as \((l/c)^2\), so the share is ever smaller.

A correction of the deflection as well. For a uniformly loaded simply supported beam, plane elasticity gives a midspan deflection larger than the elementary one by the factor \(1 + (12/5)(4/5 + \nu/2)(h/L)^2\) (SADD (8.1.37), PDF p. 177). At \(L/h = 50\) the factor is 1,0009, at \(L/h = 25\) it is 1,0036, and at \(L/h = 10\) it is 1,0228. The term with \(4/5\) comes from the shear force, the term with \(\nu/2\) from the Poisson effect, which the elementary theory neglects.

All ten assumptions together can be reviewed on one map. For the cantilever with a force at the free end and the steel of the book we draw each of the limits as a line in the plane of slenderness \(L/h\) and tip deflection relative to the length, \(v/L\) (figure 5.86). There are four limits, but the first three are drawn, because the fourth is an estimate without a number that we could draw.

  1. The shear part of the deflection exceeds 1 % of the bending part: \(L/h < 8{,}8\) (assumption 5).
  2. The slope exceeds \(0{,}1\), so \(v/L > 0{,}067\) (assumption 3).
  3. The stress exceeds the yield stress (assumption 7). For a cantilever with a force at the end \(\sigma = 3E\,v\,h/(2L^2)\), which follows from \(v = FL^3/(3EI)\) and \(\sigma = FLh/(2I)\). At \(\sigma = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) we get \(v/L = (2\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/(3E))\,(L/h) = 7{,}5\cdot 10^{-4}\,L/h\), a straight line on a logarithmic scale.
  4. Slenderness below about 10 (assumption 1), where three-dimensional effects at the clamp and at the force take up most of the beam. The limit is an estimate, not a computation (EP, p. 71: ratio 10 to 100).

The yield line meets the slope limit at \(L/h = 0{,}067/(7{,}5\cdot 10^{-4}) = 89\). At slenderness below 89 the elastic computation fails because of the material, before the geometry shows. Our cantilever (\(L/h = 25\), \(v/L = 0{,}0080\)) reaches 43 % of the yield stress and is far from the other limits.

5.15.2 Testing the model

The map tells us when the model fails, but from the same assumptions on which it is built. The real test is a comparison with measurement. No book of the project treats this test, so the section is assembled from computations of this chapter and of chapter 3 (section 3.1.1, measuring the strain on a test specimen), not from a source. What follows is therefore a plan of a test, not an established procedure, and every number below is computed from the model.

The question is whether the cantilever of our flat steel under 500 N really takes the shape that the model predicts, and whether it has at the clamp the stress that the model predicts. We clamp it at one end in a rigid table, hang a weight of mass \(500/9{,}81 = 51\) kg at the free end and measure two things (figure 5.87). First, the tip deflection with a dial gauge that touches the upper face above the free end. Second, the strain with strain gauges (merilna lističa), electrical resistors whose resistance changes in proportion to the stretch of the sheet they are glued to, on the upper and lower faces.

The model predicts the following. The tip deflection is \(v(L) = -F L^3/(3EI) = -7{,}97\) mm. The strain of the upper fibre at the clamp is \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E = 4{,}78\cdot 10^{-4}\). We must not glue the gauges onto the clamp itself, because assumption 1 does not hold there (three-dimensional state at the clamp), so we glue them one cross-section height, \(x_0 = 40\) mm, from the clamp or further. At \(x_0 = 50\) mm the moment is \(M = F(L - x_0) = 475\) N m and the strain is \(4{,}54\cdot 10^{-4}\), on the lower face of the same size with the opposite sign. A second pair of gauges at \(x = 450\) mm has the strain \(2{,}63\cdot 10^{-4}\). The ratio of the two is \(475/275 = 1{,}73\): it is independent of \(E\) and of \(I\) and checks that the moment falls in direct proportion to the distance from the force.

What would tell us in the test that the model is wrong? Whatever differs from the prediction by more than the sources of uncertainty explain. There are several of them, and we can estimate each with the model itself. The sizes of the errors that we assume in the list (dial resolution 0,01 mm, error of the height and width 0,05 mm, error of the length 1 mm, weight offset 10 mm, error of the modulus 5 %) are our assumptions about typical equipment and workshop, not data from a source or from a measurement. Only their effect on the deflection is computed from the model.

  • Dial gauge reading. A resolution of 0,01 mm is 0,13 % of the deflection 7,97 mm.
  • Cross-section dimensions. The height is measured to 0,05 mm. Since \(I \propto h^3\) and \(v \propto 1/I\), this means 0,375 % of the deflection. The same error of the width means 0,25 %.
  • Length. The deflection grows as \(L^3\). An error of 1 mm in 1000 mm means 0,3 %.
  • Point of application of the force. If the weight hangs 10 mm from the end, the tip deflection is 7,85 mm instead of 7,97 mm, so 1,5 % less.
  • Elastic modulus. The deflection is proportional to \(1/E\). We must measure the modulus of the steel on a specimen from the same bar (section 3.1.1): an error of 5 % of the modulus is 5 % of the deflection, 0,4 mm.
  • Compliance of the clamp. A rotation \(\varphi\) of the clamp adds \(\varphi L\) to the tip deflection. A rotation of \(8\cdot 10^{-5}\) rad, so 0,0046 degrees, already adds 1 %. We do not know such a rotation in advance, so we estimate it only from the measurement.
  • Weight of the bar. We either take it into account, or we set the gauge and the strain gauges to zero after the bar is installed. For the steel density \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ (section 3.1.5) the self weight alone gives a deflection \(\rho g A L^4/(8EI) = 0{,}366\) mm, which is 4,6 % of the deflection due to the force. Since the model is linear, the displacement due to the weight equals the difference of the readings.

From the list we see two things. First, the error of the clamp and of the position of the force is larger than the shear correction at our slenderness: the shear part of the deflection is 0,125 % at \(L/h = 25\), and none of these measurements separates it from noise. We cannot test this with this cantilever, while the shear part would show at \(L/h = 5\) (3,1 %). Second, we check the linearity of the model with several load steps, for example 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 N: the deflection and the strain must lie on a straight line through the origin. A deviation from the line shows slip of the clamp or a nonlinearity that the model does not capture.

5.16 Connections

The abbreviations of subjects are the same as in section 1.19.

  • The Euler-Bernoulli equation and boundary conditions: beam finite elements with Hermite interpolation functions (AK, MK, chapter 12), the virtual work equation for a beam and the computation with trial functions (chapter 6), plates as the two-dimensional version (MK, chapter 18).
  • Virtual work and natural boundary conditions: the virtual work equation in integral form (chapter 6), Hamilton's principle and dynamic boundary conditions (VD, DSK, chapters 8 and 13).
  • The Timoshenko beam: shear locking (AK, chapter 12), Mindlin plates (chapter 18), rotary inertia in vibration (DSK, chapter 13).
  • Moments of inertia and principal axes: torsion (MK, VD, chapter 16), rotor shafts (DSK, chapter 24).
  • Deflection and compliance: compliant links of robots (DSK, chapter 28), influence coefficients (chapter 10).
  • Frames: spatial frames and assembly (AK, MK, chapter 12), symmetry of frames (MK, chapter 19).
  • Limits of the theory: plane solutions of elasticity for beams with the Airy function (VT, MK, chapter 11), the hierarchy of models (AK, chapter 17).
